                              Biblical Types
The Bible is not as full of types as some would have us believe—that is,
types that can be proved by Scripture. Some make nearly every person and
event of the Old Testament typical. Such a method of intepretation leads to
confusion and a wrong understanding of the Word of God. Searching for
hidden meaning in every passage and pressing the typical teaching so far
imperils the literal teachings and soundness of many Biblical truths.

Everything in Scripture intended as a divine type is confirmed by at least
two or three plain statements in God's Word. "In the mouth of two or three
witnesses" applies to this subject as much as any other doctrine of the Bible
(Deut. 19:15; Matthew 18:16; 2 Cor. 13:1). This work recognizes types as
distinct from parables, symbols, allegories, riddles, and figurative
statements otherwise. We deal with typology only as defined below,
accepting only those types that harmonize with all the essential
characteristics.

                      Definition of Biblical Types
A type is a preordained representation wherein certain persons, events, and
institutions of the Old Testament stand for corresponding persons, events,
and institutions of the New Testament Types are pictures or object lessons
by which God has taught His redemptive plan. They are a shadow of things
to come, not the image of those things (Col. 2:17; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews
10:1). The Mosaic system, for example, was a kind of kindergarten in
which God's people were trained in divine things and taught to look forward
to the realities of things yet to come.

                      Five Greek Words Defined
1. Tupos (GSN-5179), translated "print" (John 20:25); "figure" (Acts 7:43;
   Romans 5:14); "form" (Romans 6:17); "fashion" (Acts 7:44); "manner"
   (Acts 23:25); "pattern" (Titus 2:7; Hebrews 8:5); "ensample" (2 Cor.
   10:11; Phil. 3:17; 1 Thes. 1:7; 2 Thes. 3:9; 1 Peter 5:3); and "example"
   (2 Cor. 10:6; 1 Tim. 4:12).

2. Antitupon (GSN-499), translated "like figure" (1 Peter 3:21) and "figure"
   (Hebrews 9:24).

3. Hupodeigma (GSN-5262), translated "pattern" (Hebrews 9:23);
   "ensample" (2 Peter 2:6); and "example" (John 13:15; Hebrews 4:11;
   Hebrews 8:5; James 5:10).

4. Parabole (GSN-3850), translated "figure" in only two places, referring to
   "types" (Hebrews 9:9; Hebrews 11:19). This word is mostly limited to
   the "parable" or "illustration" in the New Testament Types are
   illustrations, but they are also the pre-ordained shadow or likeness of
   things to come, while parables may be illustrations of something in the
   past, present, or future. Scriptural types and prophecy are the same in
   substance, differing only in form. This fact distinguishes between types,
   parables, symbols and other forms of human expression. See the notes at
   ▪ Matthew 13:3,11.

5. Skia (GSN-4639), translated "shadow" three times, referring to "types"
   (Col. 2:17; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 10:1). The English word "type" best
   corresponds with skia (GSN-4639) because it means a shadow, a limited
   idea or likeness of the reality that it foreshadows.
It is clear from the above scriptures that New Testament writers used the
word "type" with some degree of freedom; yet they had one general idea in
common, namely, that all types show a likeness existing between two
persons, events, or institutions. The one resembles the other in some
essential feature. In typology these two are called type and antitype, and the
link that binds them is the correspondence or similarity of the one to the
other. The type is the preordained shadow of the antitype. The type is the
object lesson, the temporary and shadowy resemblance of some predicted
person, event, or institution. The antitype is the fulfillment of that which has
been predicted.

                Six Essential Characteristics of Types
1. There must be one or more points of resemblance between the type and
   the antitype (Col. 2:14-17; Hebrews 10:1).

2. The type must be prophetic in all points of resemblance with the antitype.
   It must truly prefigure something to come (John 3:14; Romans 5:14; Col.
   2:14-17; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:23-24; Hebrews 10:1; 1 Peter 3:21).

3. The type is merely the shadow of the realities to come, not the realities
   typified (Col. 2:14-17; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 10:1).

4. The type is always earthly while the antitype could be earthly or
   heavenly (Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:24; 1 Peter 3:21).

5. Since both type and antitype must be pre-ordained as part of the same
   plan of God, they cannot be chosen by man, picked out simply because
   certain details resemble some future truth (Romans 5:14; Hebrews 9:23-
   24; Hebrews 10:1-21).

6. The only authority for types and their application is Scripture. More than
   a mere resemblance is needed to constitute a type. In true typology no
   meaning should be accepted without positive scriptural support.
   Historical events that bear some resemblance to New Testament truths
   should not be taken as true types unless substantiated by two or three
   plain passages proving a connection (2 Cor. 13:1). This would require at
   least a plain scripture on the antitype as well as the type.
A genuine type is a true figure or shadow of the reality to come—the
antitype (John 3:14; Romans 5:14; Hebrews 9:23-24; Hebrews 10:1; 1 Peter
3:21). Centuries or even millenniums may lie between them but the shadow
is never lost and the figure is never destroyed. The fulfillment or reality
always comes. Furthermore, a type has its own meaning apart from the
antitype (John 3:14 with Numbers 21). The details of a type (as with
parables, allegories, and symbols) are not to be stressed; nor are they to be
interpreted apart from the antitype; only the intended truth should be
emphasized.

                         Four Classes of Types
1. Typical Persons:

   (1) Adam was a type of Christ who was yet to come (Romans 5:12-21; 2
      Cor. 15:45-49).

   (2) Melchizedek was a type of the eternal priesthood of Christ (Genesis
      14:18-24; Hebrews 5:5-9; Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:1-10,17); a type
      of combined kingship and priesthood (Hebrews 7:1-3 with Zech.
      6:12-13); and a type of eternal existence (Hebrews 7:3,6 with Micah
      5:1-2; John 1:1-3; Hebrews 1:8).

   (3) Abraham offering up his only promised son was a type of God
      offering His only begotten Son (Genesis 22; John 3:16; Hebrews
      11:17-19).

   (4) Isaac was a type of the resurrection of Christ (Genesis 22; Hebrews
      11:19).

   (5) Moses was a type of Christ as the prophet of God (Deut. 18:15-19;
      Acts 3:19-26), and of faithfulness (Hebrews 3:1-6).

   (6) Aaron was a type of the high priesthood of Christ (Hebrews 5:1-5).

   (7) Jonah was a type of the death, burial, descension (into the lower parts
      of the earth for three days), and resurrection of Christ (Jonah 2;
      Matthew 12:40; Ephes. 4:8-10).
2. Typical Events:

   (1) The flood was typical of baptism (1 Peter 3:20-21).

   (2) Some of the events during Israel's wandering in the wilderness were
      typical of things Christians would face (2 Cor. 10:1-13).

   (3) The lifting up of the brazen serpent in the wilderness was typical of
      the crucifixion of Christ and benefits of the cross to be realized by
      others (John 3:14; Numbers 21).

3. Typical Acts:

   (1) Smiting the rock as in Exodus 17 was typical of Christ being
      crucified or smitten for people (2 Cor. 10:4).

   (2) Smiting the rock the second time instead of speaking to it was typical
      of crucifying Christ afresh (Numbers 20; 2 Cor. 10:4; Hebrews 6:6).

   (3) Rejecting the chief cornerstone was typical of the rejection of Christ
      (Isaiah 28:16; Matthew 21:42).

   (4) The many acts of the priests in the tabernacle worship were typical of
      various aspects of redemption through Christ: killing animals;
      shedding and sprinkling blood; burning incense; the showbread;
      lighting lamps; and the daily and yearly rituals were all typical acts,
      fulfilled in Christ and His redemptive work (Hebrews 7:11-28;
      Hebrews 8:1-6; Hebrews 9:1-28; Hebrews 10:1-22).

4. Typical Institutions:

   (1) The whole Mosaic institution of offerings and worship was typical of
      things to come in the sacrifice and redemptive work of Christ and the
      worship of God in the true way (Exodus 12-13; Exodus 25:1-40:38;
      Hebrews 7-10).

   (2) The Aaronic priesthood, the garments of the priests, and other
      aspects of the ministry of the law were typical of Christ and His
      redemptive work (Exodus 28-29; Hebrews 7-10).
   (3) The sabbath for Israel was typical of the eternal rest in Christ and of
      that which is to come for all the redeemed (Exodus 20:8-11; Exodus
      31:12-18; Deut. 5:15; Hebrews 4).

   (4) The feasts of Israel were typical of various aspects of redemption
      through Christ (Exodus 12; Leviticus 23; 2 Cor. 5:7; Hebrews 5-10).

   (5) The temple and all the rituals of worship carried on in it were typical
      of the same things that the tabernacle and its worship were typical of.

   (6) The tabernacle and temple, their compartments, and furniture were
      themselves typical of the heavenly tabernacle Christ entered into
      (Hebrews 8:1-5; Hebrews 9:1-10,23-24).

                         Interpretation of Types
1. Only the point or points of resemblance between the type and the
   antitype should be emphasized; they should not be used as the basis of
   other doctrines which they do not typify.

2. Types should be understood and interpreted only in the light of their
   antitypes.

3. Plain historical events should not be made typical simply because there
   are some points of resemblance between them and New Testament
   truths.

4. The type and the antitype must agree with each other as well as with all
   related scriptures.

5. The historical sense of Scripture or the literal meaning of the words
   telling of the type or antitype should never be destroyed.

6. All "hidden" meanings of the words should be avoided, for such
   explanation only leads to confusing interpretations.

            How Much of the Old Testament Is Typical?
That the above mentioned Old Testament persons, events, acts, and
institutions are types is proved by plain statements in the New Testament
How much more, if any, of the Old Testament is typical is speculation.
Portions of the Old Testament are typical only as the New Testament
affirms them as such. Anything beyond this should be considered as
illustration in teaching. Many applications can be taken from similarities
between Old Testament facts and New Testament truths; but to make these
types and antitypes is not allowed by Scripture. True types meet all the
above requirements on definition, essential characteristics, etc.

Biblical characters are often presented as types. While they make
interesting studies, they are not true biblical types, because they lack
identification as such in the New Testament. The life of Joseph compared to
that of Christ is such an example. Not recognized as type and antitype in
Scripture, the two lives nevertheless have many similarities and the facts
about them make impressive illustrations.

              Similarities between Joseph and Christ
1. Both were familiar with the shepherd's life (Genesis 37:2; John 10).

2. Loved by Father (Genesis 37:2; John 17:24).

3. Hated by brethren (Genesis 37:8; John 15:25).

4. Brethren did not believe in them (Genesis 37:20; John 7:5).

5. Their rule rejected (Genesis 37:8; John 19:15).

6. They were envied (Genesis 37:11; Mark 15:10).

7. Their sayings were observed (Genesis 37:11; Luke 2:51).

8. They were sent to brethren (Genesis 37:13; Luke 20:13).

9. They went after brethren (Genesis 37:14; John 1).

10. Brethren conspired against them (Genesis 37:18; Matthew 26:15).
11. They were stripped (Genesis 37:23; Matthew 27:28).

12. Brethren sat down to watch them in sufferings (Genesis 37:25; Matthew
   27:36).

13. Each was sold for money (Genesis 37:28; Matthew 26:15).

14. Under testing, both went to Egypt (Genesis 37:36; Matthew 2:14-15).

15. The Lord was with them (Genesis 39:2; John 16:32).

16. Fully trusted (Genesis 39:4-8; John 3:35)

17. Men blessed for their sake (Genesis 39:5; Ephes. 1:3)

18. Compassionate (Genesis 40:7; Luke 23:17)

19. Servants (Genesis 40:4; Luke 22:27)

20. Both asked men to think of them (Genesis 40:14; 2 Cor. 11:24).

21. They were anointed (Genesis 41:38; Acts 10:38).

22. They ruled their own house (Genesis 41:40; Hebrews 3).

23. They were sovereigns (Genesis 41:44; John 15:5).

24. Enemies bowing to them (Genesis 41:43; Phil. 2:10).

25. Each began a great work at thirty years of age (Genesis 41:46; Luke
   3:23).

26. People were told to obey both (Genesis 41:55; John 2:5).

27. They opened storehouses (Genesis 41:56; Luke 24:27-52).

28. They supplied all countries (Genesis 41:57; Rev. 5:9-10; Rev. 7:9-17).

29. They knew people (Genesis 42:7-8; John 2:24-25).
30. Brethren knew them not (Genesis 42:8; John 1:10).

31. Each wept (Genesis 42:17; John 11:35).

32. They met all needs (Genesis 42:25; Phil. 4:19).

33. They made themselves known to brethren (Genesis 45:1; Luke 24:31).

34. They introduced themselves (Genesis 44:3; Acts 9:5).

35. They invited people to come to them (Genesis 44:18; Matthew 11:28).

36. They were discovered to be alive after they were thought dead (Genesis
   44:26; Acts 25:19; Rev. 1).

37. They bought people (Genesis 47:23; 2 Cor. 6:20).

38. They comforted people (Genesis 50:19; John 14:11).

39. They told people not to fear (Genesis 50:19; Matthew 14:27; Matthew
   17:7; Matthew 28:10).

40. They forgave brethren and made promises to them in the end (Genesis
   50:17-21; Luke 24:47-51; Acts 1:8-14).

                     Examples of So-Called Types
Eve, Rebekah, Ruth, and other women of the Old Testament are sometimes
taken to be types of the church and the bride of Christ, but these are not
substantiated in the New Testament. The primary New Testament picture of
the church is the body of Christ; as such, it is referred to as a man (Ephes.
2:14-15; Ephes. 4:13). See 2 Cor. 10:16; 2 Cor. 12:12,27; Ephes. 1:21-22;
Col. 1:18,24. Regarding Christ's bride, Rev. 21:9-10 makes it plain that "the
bride, the Lamb's wife" is "that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending
out of heaven from God." See ▪ Rev. 21:2,9-10, notes. Some attempt to
prove the doctrine of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by the fact that Noah's
ark had three stories. They seek to prove the doctrine of the rapture before
the tribulation by the fact that Enoch was translated before the flood, even
though it was 669 years before the flood. Others, teaching about the bride of
Christ, say He will not marry all the church, or that all in the church are not
the bride, simply because Isaac did not marry all the family of Laban. The
objection to this method of interpretation is that it wrests the scriptures out
of their natural and historical setting and intent. It destroys the simplicity of
the Word of God, detracts from its trustworthiness and leads men to believe
there is a hidden and mysterious meaning to every detail of Scripture. The
safe way is to prove every doctrine with plainly related passages, and use
any historical event or resembling detail as an illustration of some point in
teaching. Innumerable applications can ri ghtly be made apart from the
authentic types and antitypes, but that is all they are—illustrations or
applications.

These commands do not include the 106 in Genesis, only those beginning
with the life of Moses. They are divided into 4 sections, as follows:

1. The 203 commands to Moses before the Ten Commandments were given.
   Most of these were personal commands directing Moses in his war with
   Pharaoh, the exodus, and the journey to Sinai (Exodus 3:5,10,14-16,18;
   Exodus 4:3-4,6-7,12,15-17,19,21-22,27; Exodus 6:6,11,13,29; Exodus
   7:2,9,15,19; Exodus 8:1,5,16,20; Exodus 9:1,8,13,22; Exodus

   Exodus 14:2,13,15-16,26; Exodus 15:25; Exodus 16:4-5,9,16,19,23,25-
   26,29,32-33; Exodus 17:5-6,14; Exodus 19:3,10,12-15,20-24).

2. The Ten Commandments, including 37 statements (Exodus 20:3-17;
   Deut. 5:1-21).

3. The 155 commands in the first section of the Mosaic covenant—those
   between the Ten Commandments and the dedication and sealing of the
   book of the covenant with the blood of animals (Exodus 20:18-24:8).

4. The 2,345 commands which are additions to the book of the law of

                    SUMMARY OF EXODUS
                           ____________________
Date and Place: Written as part of the law during the eleven months at Mt.
Sinai—about 1688 B.C.

Author: Moses, the lawgiver and leader of Israel during the exodus and the
wilderness wanderings.

Proof of Authorship: See Two Objections to Mosaic Authorship, and
Sixteen Proofs that Moses Wrote the Pentateuch.

Theme: The Pentateuch was originally one book, written on one scroll,
called Ha-Towrah (HSN-8451), "The Law," and Cepher (HSN-5612) Ha-
Towrah (HSN-8451), "The Book of the Law." Over time, it was divided
into five sections called "The Five Parts of the Law," each section named by
the leading Hebrew word or words in the first verse. The title of this book
was Ê¼Elleh (HSN-428) Shemowth (HSN-8034), "These the Names," or
simply Shemowth (HSN-8034), "Names." Exodus signifies a "departure" or
"going out," referring to the leading event of the book, the going out of
Egypt by the children of Israel. The structure of the book in the first few
sentences shows that it is a continuation of Genesis. It introduces another
great epoch in the history of Israel. What Genesis sets forth in prophecy,
Exodus records in history. It records the prophetic increase of Israel during
the 145 years between Joseph and the Exodus; the persecution and
oppression of Israel in Egypt; their deliverance by the power of God; the
exodus from Egypt; the giving of the law; the building of the tabernacle;
and the beginning of the Aaronic priesthood. It sketches the early life of
Moses and his call to lead Israel out of Egypt; tells of the plagues which
made Pharaoh willing to let Israel leave; and records the fundamental
principles of the constitution of the Jewish nation. It gives the history of the
political and religious organization of Israel as a people of God and a
mighty nation among men. The book may be divided into two main parts:
Historical (Exodus 1:1-19:25) and Legislative (Exodus 20:1-40:38).

Purpose: To continue the history of Israel in fulfillment of the covenant—
the promises and prophecies given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
concerning their seed; to show the time, circumstances, and purpose of the
law given by Moses to Israel; and to record the organization of the nation
and the establishment of a visible form of worship with God dwelling in the
midst of His people.
Statistics: 2nd book of the Bible; 40 chapters; 1,213 verses; 32,692 words;
1,089 verses of history; 129 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 2 verses of
unfulfilled prophecy; 58 questions. Exodus has 73 separate messages from
God (Exodus 3:12,14; Exodus 4:2,4,6,7,11,14,19,21,27; Exodus 5:1;
Exodus 6:1,10,13; Exodus 7:1,8,14; Exodus 8:1,5,16,20; Exodus
9:1,8,13,22; Exodus 10:1,12,21; Exodus 11:1,9; Exodus 12:1,43; Exodus
13:1; Exodus 14:1,15,26; Exodus 16:4,11,28,32; Exodus 17:5,14; Exodus
19:3,9,10,20,21,24; Exodus 20:1; Exodus 23:20; Exodus 24:1,12; Exodus
25:1; Exodus 30:11,17,22,34; Exodus 31:1,12; Exodus 32:7,9,33; Exodus
33:1,11,14,17,19; Exodus 34:1,5,9,27; Exodus 40:1); 827 commands; 240
predictions; 28 promises; and 35 of 42 miracles by Moses.

Ten General Facts about Offerings:

1. Two classes of offerings:

   (1) Sweet savor offerings (Leviticus 1:1-3:17)

   (2) Non-sweet savor offerings (Leviticus 4:1-6:7)

2. Two classes to offer them:

   (1) Individuals (Leviticus 1:2,10; Leviticus 2:1; Leviticus 3:1)

   (2) The public (Leviticus 4:13-21; Leviticus 16:1-34; Numbers 19)

3. Two kinds of offerings:

   (1) Purely voluntary (Leviticus 1:1-3:17)

   (2) Commanded (Leviticus 4:1-6:7)

4. Mode of offerings:

   (1) Burnt offerings were wholly burned with fire (Leviticus 1:6-17;
      Leviticus 6:8-12) except in cases where a part was reserved for the
      priests

   (2) Meat offerings were to be partly burned and partly for priests
      (Leviticus 2:1-16; Leviticus 6:14-18)

   (3) Meat offerings for priests were to be wholly burned (Leviticus 6:19-
      23)

   (4) Peace offerings were to be partly burned and partly eaten by priests
      and offerer (Leviticus 3:1-17; Leviticus 7:11-21,28-38)

   (5) Sin offerings were to be burned, partly inside and partly outside of
      the camp (Leviticus 4:1-35; Leviticus 6:24-30; Leviticus 8:14-17)

   (6) Trespass offerings were to be partly burned and partly eaten
      (Leviticus 5:1-6:7; Leviticus 7:1-10)

   (2) Sheep and lambs (Leviticus 1:1-13; Leviticus 3:7-11)

   (3) Goats and kids (Leviticus 1:10-13; Leviticus 4:27-35)

   (4) Pigeons (Leviticus 5:7-10; cp. Genesis 15:9)

   (5) Turtledoves (Leviticus 5:7-10)

6. Other kinds of sacrifices:

   (1) Fine flour (Leviticus 2:1-4)

   (2) Oil and frankincense (Leviticus 2:1-4)

   (3) Baked and fried cakes (Leviticus 2:4-9)

   (4) Firstfruits of crops (Leviticus 2:12-16)
    (5) Silver (Leviticus 5:15)

    (6) Drinks (Leviticus 23:13; Exodus 29:40-41)

    (7) Material things (Leviticus 27:1-34)

7. Laws concerning animal offerings:

    (1) To be clean animals (Genesis 8:20)

    (2) To be perfect (Leviticus 22:18-25)

    (3) To be at least eight days old (Leviticus 22:27; Leviticus 23:12)

8. Place of slaughter: at the door of the tabernacle and near the altar
   northward (Leviticus 1:11; Leviticus 3:2; Leviticus 6:25; Leviticus 7:2)

9. Mode of killing: like that of slaughtering other animals. The throat was
   cut and the blood caught in a basin. The animal was then skinned and cut
   up (Leviticus 1:5-6; Leviticus 4:8-12,19-21). The blood was sprinkled
   and poured out before God (Leviticus 1:5,11; Leviticus 3:2; Leviticus
   4:6,7,18).

10. Purpose of sacrifices: to make atonement and have access to God (see
   Atonement). ÷

a [meat offering] With one exception (Leviticus 2:1), every instance of
    "meat offering" comes from the Hebrew minchah (HSN-4503), gift;
    oblation; present; sacrifice. Leviticus 2:1 combines minchah (HSN-4503)
    with qorban (HSN-7133), a sacrificial present, something brought near the
    altar. In all these passages "meat offering" could be better translated "food
    offering," for they were all of grains, vegetables, fruits, and similar
    products. No blood was shed, for these offerings were not typical of
    Christ's sacrifice for sin. They mainly expressed appreciation to God for
    remission of sin. No leaven or honey was to be offered with them, for both
    cause fermentation, the first stage of decay (Leviticus 2:11; 2 Cor. 5:8).
    Salt was permitted as an emblem of purity, permanence, and preservation
    of life—the opposite of leaven. Salt was also used in covenants. See
    Fifteen Great Covenants.

               Seventeen Commands—Meat Offerings
1. A meat offering shall be fine flour with oil and frankincense upon it
   (Leviticus 2:1)

2. Bring it to priests who shall take some of it and burn for a memorial
   (Leviticus 2:2)

3. The rest shall belong to the priests as something most holy to eat
   (Leviticus 2:3)

4. Bring unleavened cakes of fine flour mingled with oil (Leviticus 2:4)

5. Bring baked pan cakes unleavened and mingled with oil (Leviticus 2:5)

6. Part them in pieces and pour oil on them (Leviticus 2:6)

7. Bring fried pan cakes of fine flour with oil (Leviticus 2:7)

8. Bring such meat offerings to the Lord (Leviticus 2:8)

9. The priests shall bring them to the brazen altar and burn a memorial
   portion in the fire (Leviticus 2:8-9)

10. The rest shall belong to the priest as his part to eat (Leviticus 2:10)

11. Do not offer meat offerings with leaven or honey (Leviticus 2:11)

12. Offer your firstfruits to the Lord to be burned upon the altar (Leviticus
   2:12)

13. Season every meat offering with salt
14. With all offerings offer salt (Leviticus 2:13)

15. Bring the firstfruits as an offering to the Lord (Leviticus 2:14)

16. Pour oil upon it and lay frankincense upon the meat offering of the
   firstfruits (Leviticus 2:15)

17. Priests shall burn a memorial part of it in the fire as a burnt offering on
   the brazen altar (Leviticus 2:16)

The meat offerings typified something altogether different from the burnt
offerings and sin offerings. The latter typified sin and a Savior, while the
meat offerings simply acknowledged that the offerer was grateful to God
for a Savior and forgiveness, and recognized that he owed everything to
God, including the fruit of his labors. They were thank offerings for God's
blessing and provision for sin, not offerings of atonement for sin.

Many special offerings are mentioned, nearly all male sacrifices, implying
by figure and type the responsibility of Adam, not Eve, as God's agent;
emphasizing the iniquity of fathers, not mothers; and symbolizing the
Redeemer who came as a Man (1 Tim. 2:4-5). Female offerings simply
implied that the woman had a part in the transgression of man and was also
provided for in redemption. Females were used only in peace offerings
(Leviticus 3) and in minor sin offerings of a personal nature—never in the
whole burnt offerings or any that definitely symbolized Christ as the sin-
bearer for all men.

a [this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings]
                Ten Commands—the Peace Offerings
1. Thanksgiving peace offerings shall be unleavened cakes mingled with
   oil, unleavened wafers anointed with oil made of fine flour and fried
   (Leviticus 7:11-12).

2. Besides the cakes the offerer shall offer unleavened bread with the
   sacrifice of a thanksgiving or peace offering (Leviticus 7:13).

3. He shall offer one unleavened cake, one wafer, one fried cake, and one
   loaf of leavened bread as a heave offering for the priest who sprinkles
   the blood of the peace offering (Leviticus 7:14).

4. The flesh of the peace offering shall be eaten the same day it is offered;
   nothing shall be left of it until morning (Leviticus 7:15).

5. If the sacrifice of one's offering is a vow or voluntary offering, it shall be
    eaten the same day it is offered, and the next day also, but the remainder
    shall be burned on the third day (Leviticus 7:16-17).

6. If any flesh is eaten on the third day, it won't be accepted, neither shall it
    be imputed to the offerer, but shall be an abomination and sin to the one
    who eats (Leviticus 7:18). The reason for this was that the meat would
    begin to putrefy. Since it was holy, to expose it to decay was a crime
    against God to whom it was consecrated. Avoiding decay typified the
    fact that the body of Christ would not see corruption (Psalm 16:10; Acts
    2:27-30).

7. The flesh that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten; it shall be
   burned with fire (Leviticus 7:19).

8. All that are clean shall eat of the flesh of the peace offerings.

9. The person with uncleaness on him shall die if he eats the flesh of peace
   offerings (Leviticus 7:20).

10. The person who touches any unclean thing and then eats of the flesh of
   the peace offerings shall die (Leviticus 7:21).
b [peace offerings] Three kinds of peace offerings:

1. Thanksgiving offerings (Leviticus 7:11-15)

2. Vow offerings (Leviticus 7:16-21)

a [sprinkled it uipon Aaron, and upon his garments, ...]

              The Sprinkling of Blood and Anointing Oil
The sprinkling of the blood and anointing oil together on the bodies and
garments of the priests was a fitting conclusion for their consecration and of
the entire rite of sanctification. Blood had been applied before this to the
bodies (Leviticus 8:23-24) and to the altar (Leviticus 8:14-15). Aaron had
already been anointed as high priest (Leviticus 8:10-13), so the new part of
the ritual did not cleanse from sin, sanctify, or bless in any way except to
show the necessity of continued trust in the blood and the need for
continued a nointing with the Spirit. The outward ritual of anointing with
oil signified the choice of God, the calling of God, and the impartation of
power for the particular work one was called to do. Priests, prophets, and
kings were all anointed. If they carried out their calling they had God's
support. If they sinned and failed, they received the curse of God until they
repented and came back to the original calling and fulfilled it. If they never
came back, the curse of God remained on them forever. This is exemplified
even among angels who were once anointed (Ezekiel 28:11-17; Isaiah
14:12-14; Matthew 24:41; Rev. 12:10-12; Rev. 20:10), as well as demons
and men. See Twenty-one Examples of Beings Fallen from Grace.

   2:22; John 2:3-10).

3. It was permitted in moderation under the law of Moses (Deut. 14:26)

4. Nazarites were forbidden to drink it (Numbers 6).

5. It was used in drink offerings to God (Exodus 29:40; Leviticus 23:13;
    Numbers 15:5-10; Numbers 28:14).

    Deut. 14:26; Deut. 29:6; Judges 13:4,7,14; 1 Samuel 1:15; cp. Luke
    1:15)

7. It makes the eyes red (Genesis 49:12).

8. Is a mocker (Proverbs 20:1).

9. It is not to be used when red (Proverbs 23:31).

10. It is not for kings (Proverbs 31:4).

11. It was often mixed with spices and other drinks (Proverbs 9:2; Proverbs
   23:30; Song 8:2; cp. Mark 15:23)

12. It was offered by Melchizedek to Abraham (Genesis 14:18).

a [leprosy]

                                  Leprosy
Leprosy, as it is known today, begins with an eruption of small reddish
spots which are said to be soon covered by a thin, smooth scale of whitish
color. In a little while, this falls off, leaving the skin beneath red and
uneven. As the circles increase in size, the skin recovers its healthy
appearance toward the center; fresh scales are formed which are thicker and
cause the center to seem depressed. The disease generally affects the knees
and elbows, but sometimes it extends over the whole body. Though it is said
to scarcely affect general health, it does cause skin to be thickened about the
joints, impeding free motion of the limbs. Leprosy is common to both
sexes, to almost all ages, and all ranks of society. It is always difficult to
treat, and, when it is longstanding, may be pronounced incurable. On the
other hand, it may last for years and then disappear. A person with such a
plague would no doubt be pronounced clean by the priest.

Among ancient people, "leprosy" was the name for many varieties of skin
disease (including modern leprosy), some of which caused the Hebrews to
be ceremonially unclean. It was possible to spread the contagious type
when the ulcers were running. Lepers in Israel were required to live
separated and cry out, "Unclean! Unclean!" if approached by others
(Leviticus 13:45). In the middle ages elephantiasis was thought to be
leprosy. This serious ailment also appears as spots over the skin, and
progresses to impair sensibility of the skin . It can produce facial deformity
and baldness, falling out of lashes, brows and beard; and cause joints of the
toes to ulcerate and fall off. After years of suffering, the victim dies either
from exhaustion or the effects of the disease internally.

The Hebrew word for "leprosy" is tsaraÊ½ath (HSN-6883), meaning "to
smite" or "strike." In Greek, "leprosy" (lepra (GSN-3014)) comes from a
word meaning "to scale." Anyone in Israel seemingly stricken with such a
disease was required to appear before the priest for diagnosis. It was his
duty to determine whether the person was the victim of scall, scab, other
non-contagious inflammation, or the loathsome plague of contagious
leprosy itself.

                      Seven Symptoms of Leprosy
1. White rising of the skin, white hair, raw flesh (Leviticus 13:2,10,14-15)

2. Thin white scales or scabs on the body like layers of snow (Leviticus
   13:2; Exodus 4:6; Numbers 12:10; 2 Kings 5:27)

3. Bright spots, white and somewhat reddish (Leviticus 13:2,19)

4. Skin depressed, white hair in the spots (Leviticus 3,20-22)

5. Hot burning raw flesh, spreading white bright spots, somewhat reddish,
   white hair (Leviticus 13:24-25)

6. Spreading deep spots in the skin with yellowish thin hair (Leviticus
   13:29-34)

7. White reddish sore (Leviticus 13:42-44)

1. When the plague of leprosy is in a man he shall be brought to the priest.

    13:16).

   shall pronounce the man clean (Leviticus 13:17).

In Leviticus 13:2-17 there are either two kinds of disease or two stages of
one kind:

1. That which partially covers the body, is raw and open, emitting
   corruption (Leviticus 13:10-11,14-15).

2. That which is dry and scaly, and therefore not so contagious (Leviticus
   13:13,16-17).

a [And the leper in whom the plague is, ...]

                  Six Commands concerning a Leper
1. He shall rip his clothes (a sign of mourning).

2. He shall go with his head bare.

3. He shall put a covering on his upper lip (a cloth on his mouth as a corpse
   in death).

4. He shall cry out "Unclean! Unclean!" when he comes near other people
   (to protect them from the disease)

5. He shall be considered to be defiled and unclean all the days of his
   plague (Leviticus 13:46).

6. He shall stay separated from clean and healthy people (even relatives) all
   the days of his plague.

To all people the leper was a living portrayal of sin, of which death was the
penalty. He carried about perpetual signs of mourning for the dead, himself
being an example of living death. He was not only lost and ruined because
of what he had done, but on account of what he was. The sinner must not
only confess what he has done, but also admit there is no righteousness in
him (Psalm 51:5; 2 Cor. 5:21; Ephes. 2:1-8; 1 John 1:9).

a [This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing]

             Eighteen Commands—Ceremonial Cleansing
1. One who is healed of leprosy shall be brought to the priest who shall go
   on the outside of the camp to meet him (Leviticus 14:2-3).

2. The priest shall examine him, and if the plague is healed, then he shall
   command that two live birds, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop be
   obtained for the who who is to be cleansed (ceremonially, Leviticus
   14:3-4).

3. The priest shall command one bird to be killed in an earthen vessel over
   running water (Leviticus 14:5).

4. He shall take the living bird, the cedar wood, the scarlet, and the hyssop,
   and shall dip them and the living bird in the blood of the dead bird, then
   sprinkle it seven times on the cleansed leper, pronouncing him clean, and
   let the living bird go free in the open field (Leviticus 14:6-7).

5. The leper shall wash his clothes, shave himself, bathe in water, and
   remain outside the camp for seven days (Leviticus 14:8).

6. On the seventh day he shall shave the hair of his head, beard, and
   eyebrows, and wash his clothes and body in water and be clean
   (Leviticus 14:9).

7. On the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without blemish, one
   female of the first year without blemish, three tenth deals of fine flour
   (1.5 gallons) and a log of oil, and accompany the priest to the door of the
   outer court of the tabernacle (Leviticus 14:10-11).

8. The priest shall offer one lamb as a trespass offering and wave it with the
   log of oil for a wave offering before God (Leviticus 14:12).

9. He shall slay the lamb at the north side of the brazen altar (Leviticus
   14:13; Leviticus 1:11).

10. The priest shall take some of the blood and put it on the tip of the right
   ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the great toe of the right foot of the
   leper (Leviticus 14:14).
11. The priest shall pour some of the log of oil in his own left hand
   (Leviticus 14:15).

12. He shall dip his right finger in the oil and sprinkle it seven times before
   God (Leviticus 14:16).

13. The rest of the oil he shall put on the tip of the right ear, right thumb,
   and right great toe of the man, and on the blood on these parts (Leviticus
   14:17).

14. The remnant of oil in the priest's hand shall be put upon the head of the
   leper (Leviticus 14:18).

15. The priest shall offer the other male lamb for a sin offering and make
   atonement for the leper (Leviticus 14:18-19).

16. He shall then kill the female lamb for a burnt offering (Leviticus 14:19-
   20).

17. The priest shall offer the burnt offering and the meal offering of flour
   and oil upon the brazen altar (Leviticus 14:20).

18. The priest shall thus make an atonement for the leper and he shall be
   clean.

     Seven Commands—Ceremonial Cleansing for the Poor
1. A poor man healed of leprosy shall take one lamb, one tenth deal of flour
   mingled with oil, a log of oil (1 part), two turtledoves or pigeons, and
   bring them to the priest at the door of the tabernacle, on the eighth day
   (Leviticus 14:21-23).

2. The priest shall take the lamb and the oil and wave them before the Lord
   (Leviticus 14:24).

3. He shall kill the lamb for a trespass offering and put some of the blood on
   the tip of the right ear, right thumb, and right great toe of the leper
   (Leviticus 14:25).

4. The priest shall pour the oil in the palm of his own left hand and sprinkle
   some of it with his right finger seven times before God (Leviticus
   14:27).

5. He shall put some of the oil on the physical parts of the leper where the
   blood has been applied (Leviticus 14:28).

6. He shall pour the rest of the oil upon the head of the leper (Leviticus
   14:29).

7. He shall offer one of the pigeons or turtledoves for a sin offering, the
   other for a burnt offering with the meat offering, and make atonement for
   the leper (Leviticus 14:30-31).
A comparison of the above items to be offered by the poor man with those
of the more prosperous one (note, ▪ Leviticus 14:2) shows that some of each
thing sacrificed was to be given by rich and poor alike. The same number of
birds and the same amount of oil were required of both, but the flour was
less for the poor man, and the lambs went from three to one. The whole
lamb, it seems, was waved before God in both cases. This went to the priest
for his services after the blood was properly shed and applied (Leviticus
14:21-32). Whereas in the case of the rich man, one bird was set free, both
were killed for the poor man, to provide a sin offering and a burnt offering
instead of lambs (Leviticus 14:4-7,21-22).

The things offered were brought to the tabernacle door on the eighth day
and all rituals were completed before the leper was pronounced as clean.

b [running water] Realizing that bacteria can multiply as much as 281.5
    trillion times in 24 hours, we see the wisdom of the commands to wash in
    running water instead of stagnant water; to destroy certain vessels that
    were prone to harbor contamination; to quarantine persons with symptoms
    of contagious disease until a diagnosis could be made; to declare clothing,
    beds, chairs, saddles, and other things touched by the diseased to be
    unclean; and to require both physical and ceremonial cleansing before a
    person stricken with a contagious ailment could be restored to society.
    Through divine knowledge, Moses was thousands of years ahead of his
    time in bacteriological science, treatment of disease, sanitation and health
    laws. This gave the Jews the benefit of wisdom concerning physical
    fitness which no other nation of that time had.

1. Speak to Aaron telling him not to come into the most holy place at all

3. He shall put on his holy garments—linen coat, breeches, girdle, mitre

4. He shall wash his flesh with water before putting them on.

5. He shall take two kids of the goats for a sin offering, and a ram for a
   burnt offering for the congregation (Leviticus 16:5).

6. He shall offer his bullock for a sin offering, and make atonement for

12. He shall bring the incense within the veil and burn it upon the fire

a [cast lots] This was done by the Urim and Thummim. The Septuagint
    reads: "Aaron shall cast lots on the goats, one lot, For the Lord, and one
    lot, For escape." The priest, standing before the two goats, would put his
    hands into the pocket and take a lot in each one. The lot in his right hand
    was for the goat before him, on the right, and the one in his left hand was
    for the goat on the left.

b [two goats] According to tradition, the two goats were to be the same in
    size, color, and value, and as nearly alike as possible. Both were presented
 to the Lord by the high priest and then the lots were cast to determine
 which one should die and which should live (Leviticus 16:8-10,15-22).

c [scapegoat] Hebrew: Ê½azaÊ¼zel (HSN-5799), from Ê½ez (HSN-5795),
 goat, and Ê½azal (HSN-235), "to go away," meaning the goat of
 departure. Used in Leviticus 16:8,10,26. We must depend on this simple
 meaning for a true understanding of this chapter.

                    Ten Fallacies about the Scapegoat
1. that Ê½azaÊ¼zel (HSN-5799) means the Devil.

2. that it refers to a demon in the wilderness being sacrificed to.

3. that God places the sins upon Satan who will be the final sin-bearer and
    be annihilated with all sins upon him.

4. that Ê½azaÊ¼zel (HSN-5799) refers to some personal being opposite
    Jehovah to whom the goat is sent.

5. that the goat is sent to Ê½azaÊ¼zel (HSN-5799) and is not `aza'zel itself.

6. that it represents all evil.

7. that it is the personification of all that is great and terrible.

    sacrificed to him, thus satisfying his demands.

To teach the above and other such fallacies mystifies the simple gospel truth
expressed here in type. The two goats represented and completed one
atonement for sin. The goat which died typified the death of Christ and the
one which lived typified His resurrection. They represented the same idea
as the two birds, one of which was killed and the other turned loose in the
open fields (Leviticus 14:4-8,50-53). When the goat was led into the
wilderness atonement was complete; the sins transferred figuratively on the
goat were already atoned for, and the blood was sprinkled before the Lord.
No other sacrifice could be allowed for sin after this on the day of
atonement, signifying that when Christ died and entered into heaven there
was no more sacrifice for sin.

When people lost sight of God and began to worship the planets, demons,
and hero gods, they practiced horrifying acts of cruelty, obscenity, and
perversion (unnatural sexual acts). Even sons and daughters were burned in
the fire (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 3:26-27; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 17:17,31;

ancient nations shed human blood before their deities. Molech means
"king." This was the name of the main god of Ammon—called Chemosh by
Moabites (see Biblical Facts about False Gods). Molech was worshiped in
Egypt as Amun, or Amun-Ra, "the king of gods." What was supposed to be
his likeness was a statue of brass resting on a pedestal or throne of brass—
his head crowned and resembling that of a calf, and his arms extended as if
to embrace all who came near. Children were his victims. The statue was
heated red hot by fire inside and children were shaken over the flames or
passed through the hot arms in dedication to it, to receive Molech's favor. It
was believed that all children not so dedicated would die in infancy. Many
were actually burned alive in the idol (see the scriptures above). It seems
that King Ahaz was dedicated to Molech (2 Kings 16:3,19-20; 2 Chron.
28:3).

To Spue Out
The term "spue out" is used in Rev. 3:16 of backslidden Christians. See
Leviticus 18:28; Leviticus 20:22; Jeremiah 25:27. The word "spue" here is
from the Hebrew qowÊ¼ (HSN-6958), "spue out; vomit up." Since one
cannot spue out anything which was not at one time possessed by him, it
indicates that even the Gentiles were once in God's favor before being
spued out. This is proved in Romans 1:21-32 where it says of Gentiles that
"when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were
thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was
darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and
changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image ... for this cause
God gave them up unto vile affections"—that is, the homosexual sins as
referred to in Leviticus 18:22; Leviticus 20:13. When they went into
depravity, apostasy, and the abominations of Leviticus 18 and Romans 1,
He spued them out and later spued Israel out for committing the same sins.
This He will do to anyone who follows the former apostates in the practice
of sin. See Backsliding.

God warned Israel that He would spue them out also if they practiced the
sins of nations that they were dispossessing (Leviticus 18:28-30). He would
be an unjust tyrant, if He saved one group of people and judged another
who were committing the same sins which were worthy of death. He told
Moses that He would blot out of the Book of Life any person who sinned
against Him (Exodus 32:32-33). This is the rule under both law and grace.
See Twenty-one Examples of Beings Fallen from Grace and 210 Plain Laws
and Warnings.

That God did reject Israel and spue the nation out when they backslid and
went into the sins of the Canaanites is clear. He raised up sixteen different
judges to deliver them from seven servitudes to other nations because of sin
(see notes a-y, Dispensation of Law). He cursed the nation because of sin

rejected Christ and the gospel, He scattered them among the nations where
they have been for many centuries. That Israel was in grace and had

                                    Profaning
From the meanings of the Hebrew and the English word "profane"
(meaning secular; uninspired; vulgar; common; blasphemous; godless;
impious; irreligous; unconsecrated; unholy; unsanctified; wicked; worldly)
we understand what God meant by the following laws:

                          Five Commands to Priests
1. A priest shall not profane himself (Leviticus 21:4).

2. He shall not profane the name of God (Leviticus 21:6; cp. Leviticus
   18:21; Leviticus 19:12; Leviticus 20:3; Leviticus 22:2,32).

3. A priest shall not marry a profane woman (Leviticus 21:7,14).

4. He shall not profane the sanctuary (Leviticus 21:12,23; cp. Ezekiel
   23:39; Ezekiel 25:3)).

5. Priests shall not profane the holy things (Leviticus 22:15; cp. Leviticus
   22:9; Ezekiel 22:26).
                        Ten Examples of Profaning
1. Israel profaning the sabbaths (Neh. 13:17; Ezekiel 22:8,26; Ezekiel
    23:38).

2. Prophets and priests profaning God (Jeremiah 23:11-15; Ezekiel 22:25-
   26).

3. Zedekiah is called the profane wicked prince of Israel (Ezekiel 21:25).

4. Profaning the sanctuary (Ezekiel 25:3).

5. Profaning God's holy name (Ezekiel 36:20-23; Amos 2:7; Malachi 1:12).

6. Profaning the holiness of God (Malachi 2:11).

7. Profaning the holy covenant (Malachi 2:10).

8. Lucifer was cast out as profane when he sinned (Ezekiel 28:16).

9. Priest profaning the temple (Matthew 12:5; cp. Acts 24:6).

10. Esau was a profane person, a fornicator (Hebrews 12:16).

b [himself] A priest profaned himself when he became backslidden in
    heart, irreverent, ungodly, unholy, defiled, unclean, wicked, or worldly—
    more interested in secular things than in his duty to God.

                            Sickness in Israel
None of Aaron's seed or any of the nation otherwise needed to be leprous or
diseased, according to God's covenants; that is, if the people would carry
out their obligations to Him. At Marah a covenant of healing was made
with the whole nation which conditionally guaranteed both healing and
continued health (see note, ▪ Exodus 15:26). On their obedience God
promised to take away sickness from their midst (Exodus 23:25).
Sicknesses were promised only as a result of sin (Leviticus 26; Deut. 28).
God healed everyone so that there was not a feeble person in all their tribes
(Psalm 105:37; Psalm 107:20). Thus, Israel had a perfect beginning as a
nation leaving Egypt and could have continued in this state had they not
rebelled. The laws about diseases in Leviticus 13-15, etc. and the references
to possible leprosy and other diseases were made in view of the fact that, if
Israel failed, they would be needed. Even when Israel went into sin, God
promised repeatedly to heal them should they turn to Him (Psalm 34:9-10;
Psalm 84:11; Psalm 91:1-12; Psalm 103:3; Isaiah 58; etc.). When the
Messiah came to restore Israel and save the nation, He healed everyone who
came to Him for healing, without exception. No less than 23 times the
Gospels record that He healed them all (note, ▪ Matthew 13:58). Thus, God
sought to renew Israel and start them out with a new beginning as in the
days of Moses. True to the prophecy in Deut. 18, He sent them a prophet
like Moses.

                          The Feasts of Jehovah
The Eight Feasts of Jehovah:

1. The weekly sabbath feast (Leviticus 23:2-3)

2. The yearly passover feast (Leviticus 23:4-5)

3. The yearly feast of unleavened bread (Leviticus 23:6-8)

4. The yearly feast of firstfruits (Leviticus 23:9-14)

5. The yearly feast of Pentecost (Leviticus 23:15-21)

6. The yearly feast of trumpets (Leviticus 23:23-25)

7. The yearly feast of atonement (Leviticus 23:26-32)

8. The yearly feast of tabernacles (Leviticus 23:33-34)

Three commands—the Feasts of Jehovah:

1. Speak to Israel concerning the feasts of Jehovah (Leviticus 23:2).

2. Proclaim My feasts to be holy convocations.

3. Proclaim the feasts in their proper seasons (Leviticus 23:4).

Three Yearly Feast Gatherings for All Males:

1. The feasts of the passover, unleavened bread, and firstfruits were
   observed in the same season at the same gathering (Exodus 12; Exodus
   23:14-17).

2. The feast of Pentecost (Leviticus 23:15-21; Exodus 23:16)
3. The feast of tabernacles (Leviticus 23:33-44; Exodus 23:16; Exodus
   34:18-22). This was preceded by two other feasts which all males
   attended. By gathering fifteen days earlier they could attend all three
   which required a total of twenty-one days—the feast of trumpets, the
   great day of atonement, and feast of tabernacles (Leviticus 23:23-44; 2
   Chron. 8:13).

Eight Other Feasts of the Jews:

1. A septennial (recurring every seven years) or sabbatical feast (Leviticus
   25)

2. The feast of the new moon, the first crescent moon after its transition (1
   Chron. 23:31; 2 Chron. 2:4; 2 Chron. 8:13; 2 Chron. 31:3; Ezra 3:5; Neh.
   10:33; Isaiah 1:13-14; Hosea 2:11; Col. 2:14-17)

3. The feast of Purim, to celebrate the deliverance from Haman (Esther 9)

4. The feast of dedication, or the restoration of the temple, which was
   profaned by Antiochus Epiphanes (John 10:22). This was also called the
   feast of lights.

5. The feast of branches, to commemorate the taking of Jericho by Joshua.
   It is not mentioned in Scripture.

6. The feast for the death of Nicanor (1 Macc. 7:48 of the Apocrypha)

7. The feast for the discovery of the sacred fire (2 Macc. 1:18)

8. The feast of carrying wood to the tabernacle, called Xylophory
   (Josephus, Wars of the Jews, II:17:6)

a [out of your habitations two wave loaves] This simply means that in a
    place of dwelling they should bake two loaves, not that two loaves were to
    come from each house for the priests. This would have made thousands of
    loaves, more than the priests could use. This could be translated "from
    your dwelling," or "place of abode," referring to abode in the general
    sense; or "from the assembly," referring to the loaves being from the
    public at public expense and dedicated to God for the priests who were on
    duty at this time.

b [wave loaves] All food offerings were for the priests in appreciation of
    their service (Leviticus 2:2-3,8-10,14-16).

c [tenth deals] A tenth deal was a half gallon. They must have been very
    large loaves, for each contained about four pounds of flour raised with
    leaven (Leviticus 23:17). According to the Mishna (the writings of the
    oral law), the length of a loaf was 7 handbreadths (about 28 inches), the
    width 4 handbreadths (about 16 inches), and the depth equal to 7 fingers'
    width (about 6 or 7 inches).

d [they shall be baken with leaven] No bread made with leaven (yeast)
    could be burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:11). So, the object was not a
    burnt offering. This was a present to God from the best produce of the
    earth in the form most useful to sustain human life. It was a thanksgiving
    offering for God's blessings on the crops of the year. Besides these, there
    were hundreds, even thousands, of other loaves brought to the feast, not as
    offerings for the priests' use but for the people attending on that day.

e [firstfruits] Referring to the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, not the barley
    which was earlier. In warmer parts of Palestine barley ripened about the
    middle of April, whereas the wheat crop did so the last of May or first part
    of June, being reaped by the time of the feast of Pentecost (Leviticus
    23:17).

    forty-ninth year of the period, and the eighth or jubilee being the fiftieth

    to enjoy a rest from work in the fields (Leviticus 25:8-13).

    (Leviticus 25:47-49).

3. The redemption price was reckoned by the number of years the Hebrew
   had already served and the number of years he was yet to serve,
   according to a yearly servant's wage (Leviticus 25:48-53).

4. If the slave who sold himself for a debt for longer than six years was not
    redeemed by any of the above means, he was to continue until the year
    of jubilee and then be set free from further obligation to his debt
    (Leviticus 25:54-55).

a [chastise you seven time for your sins]

                         Five Degrees of Chastening
1. The eight curses of physical destruction by disease and war (Leviticus
   26:16-17).

2. The seven curses on agriculture—no more blessings upon the land to
   produce abundantly as promised in Leviticus 26:4-5 for obedience
   (Leviticus 26:18-20). These were additional plagues to those of Leviticus
   26:16-17, and more severe, as proved by the statement of Leviticus
   26:18, "And if ye will not yet for all this (eight curses of Leviticus
   26:16-17) hearken unto Me, then I will punish you seven times more for
   your sins." Before God could punish Israel seven times more, it was
   necessary for the nation to be punished a previous time; so the seven
   times could not represent the whole length of the times of the Gentiles
   (as sometimes taught) or a period of 2,520 years (seven times 360 years),
   even if the expression referred to the years of such a period of Israel's
   chastening. The previous years of the eight curses of Leviticus 26:16-17
   would have to be accounted for in the reckoning as well as the four
   different times in this chapter when punishment seven times is promised.
   If the expression means 2,520 years the first time it is used to warn of
   punishment, it means the same when it is used to warn of additional
   punishment. In four such cursings we should have four times 2,520 years
   or 10,080 years for the times of the Gentiles before the dispersion of
   Israel among the nations (Leviticus 26:27-39), and this did not happen.
   The theory then falls apart; so we look on the seven times as a figurative
   statement expressing more severe punishment from time to time, just as
   if a parent would say, "I will punish you seven times harder if you still
   refuse to obey." See The Times of the Gentiles.

3. The six curses of destruction by multiplying wild animals against Israel,
   which God promised would not happen (in Leviticus 26:6) if they
   obeyed (Leviticus 26:21-22). These also were additional to the first eight
   curses and the first seven times of Leviticus 26:16-20, as proved by
   Leviticus 26:21, "And if ye walk contrary unto Me, and will not hearken
   unto Me; I will bring seven times more plagues upon you according to
   your sins."

4. The six curses of avenging His covenant by war, famine, and pestilence,
   which God promised He would not send (in Leviticus 26:7-10), if they
   would obey (Leviticus 26:23-26). These were additional to the eight
   curses of Leviticus 26:16-17, and those of the two previous seven times
   of Leviticus 26:18,21, as proved in Leviticus 26:23-24, "And if ye will
   not be reformed by Me by these things (the previous plagues or curses),
   but will walk contrary unto Me; then will I also walk contrary unto you,
   and will punish you yet seven times for your sins."

5. The twenty-seven curses bringing complete national destruction and
   dispersion among the nations, which God promised (in Leviticus 26:11-
   13) that He would not allow if they obeyed (Leviticus 26:29-39). This is
   the fourth seven times warning of curses and these too were additional to
   the eight of Leviticus 26:16-17 and others as proved in Leviticus 26:27-
   28, "And if ye will not for all this (all the curses and more curses before
   this) hearken unto Me, but walk contrary unto Me; then I will walk
     contrary unto you also in fury; and I, even I, will chastise you seven
     times for your sins."

                           Special Vows to God
The "singular vow" was a special, voluntary vow to God. Most vows were
made in cases of illness and danger, or under an emotional impulse—either
in thanksgiving for blessings received, or pleading for those desired. A man
might dedicate himself, his wife, his children, or his servants. The law
simply ordained that a religious tax, according to age and sex, be paid for
special vows, the money to be for the priests.

a [if it be a beast, whereof men bring an offering unto the LORD]

            Six Commands—Vows Regarding Animals
1. If a man makes a special vow and dedicates a beast to God in connection
    with his vow, it shall be holy to Jehovah.

2. He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad or a bad for a good
   (Leviticus 27:10).

3. If he insists on a change, then the first beast and the one he wished to
    exchange for it shall both be holy.

4. If a man dedicates an unclean beast to Jehovah which is not acceptable
    for sacrifice, then he shall present it before the priest (Leviticus 27:11).

5. The priest shall estimate its worth and the value he places on it shall
   stand (Leviticus 27:12). The beast was to be sold for that amount.

6. If the man will at all redeem it for himself then he shall add twenty
    percent to its value and give the full amount to the priest; and the beast
    shall be his own again (Leviticus 27:13).

All vows were voluntary. No man was forced to make a vow, but he was
under obligation to pay one after making it (Numbers 30:2; Eccles. 5:4-6).
According to Psalm 15:4, one of the characteristics of a righteous man is
that he keeps his word. A person should not use vows to obtain an answer
to prayer or to bring about some desire. Faith is the thing that will produce
answers to prayer, not unnecessary vows. Jephthah made a rash vow and
had reason to regret it (Judges 11:29-31). He would have defeated his
enemies without it, for God would have given him victory. Israelites vowed
to destroy Benjamites and refuse wives to the remnant, and they were sorry
later (Judges 20-21).

                  SUMMARY OF LEVITICUS
                            ____________________

Date and Place: Written as part of the law of Moses at Sinai about 1,686
B.C.

Author: Moses, the lawgiver and leader of Israel.

Proof of Authorship: See Two Objections to Mosaic Authorship, and The
Sixteen Proofs Moses Wrote the Pentateuch.

Theme: Leviticus is the book of the detailed walk, worship, and service of
the redeemed people of God. Exodus tells of the exodus from Egypt, the
giving of the law, the establishment of the priesthood, and the building of
the tabernacle. Leviticus reveals the giving of the laws concerning sacrifices
and offerings; the consecration of the priesthood; the full establishment of
the tabernacle worship; the holiness of God's people in body, soul, and
spirit; the relationship of Israel to the Lord; the feasts of the Lord; the
record of God dwelling in the tabernacle in the midst of His people; and the
proper means of approach and fellowship with God.

Statistics: 3rd book of the Bible; 27 chapters; 859 verses; 24,541 words; 3
questions; 58 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 6 verses of unfulfilled prophecy;
799 verses of history; 795 commands; 26 promises; 125 predictions; and 35
messages from God (Leviticus 1:1; Leviticus 4:1; Leviticus 5:14; Leviticus
6:1,8,19,24; Leviticus 7:22,28; Leviticus 8:1,10:8; Leviticus 11:1; Leviticus
12:1; Leviticus 13:1; Leviticus 14:1,33; Leviticus 15:1; Leviticus 16:1;
Leviticus 17:1; Leviticus 18:1; Leviticus 19:1; Leviticus 20:1; Leviticus
21:1,16; Leviticus 22:1,17,26; Leviticus 23:1,9,23,26,33; Leviticus 24:1;
Leviticus 25:1; Leviticus 27:1).

In 38 years the 5 tribes (Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Ephraim, Naphtali) had a
loss of 61,020 soldiers, whereas the other 7 tribes had a total gain of 59,200.
Simeon's loss of 37,100 was the most, being more than half of the
combined losses of all the other tribes. This may be due to many Simeonites
being destroyed in the plague of the 24,000 killed because of adultery
(Numbers 25:1-9). It was Zimri, the chief of Simeon, that led men in this
sin (Numbers 25:14-15).

Besides the sentence of death which took the last of those who rebelled at
the entrance of Canaan, there were 10 different plagues recorded in
Numbers, which took their toll as well. In one of them (Numbers 16:44-50),
a total of 14,700 were killed; in another (Numbers 25:9) a total of 24,000.
Israel suffered 3 plagues described as consuming "them that were in the
uttermost parts of the camp" (Numbers 11:1), smiting "the people with a
very great plague" (Numbers 11:33), and fiery serpents biting so many that
"much people of Israel died" (Numbers 21:6). If these only took 14,700
each there would have been a loss of 44,100 in the 3 plagues. Along with
the losses of 14,700 and 24,000 in the other 2 plagues, there would have
been a total of 82,800 people killed in 5 plagues alone.

The total number of soldiers in the first column (603,550) shows a gain of
3,550 in 12 months over the 600,000 men of war that left Egypt (Exodus
12:37). The rebellion took place after this increase causing all of the
603,550 (except Caleb and Joshua) to incur the death sentence and perish
within a 40-year period. The total figure of the second column then,
represents practically a new generation of soldiers coming up in 38 years,
actually a gain of approximately 601,730.

The following is a breakdown after the 38 years, according to maternal
lineage:

Leah's Six Sons:

1. Judah—an increase of 1,900

2. Issachar—an increase of 9,900

3. Zebulun—an increase of 3,100

4. Levi—an increase of 1,000

5. Reuben—a decrease of 2,770
6. Simeon—a decrease of 37,100

The tribes of Leah's sons (including Levi who wasn't counted with the men
of war) had a gain of 15,900 through the years and a loss of 39,870 which
gave them a net decrease of 23,970 in the second count. Concerning Levi's
increase of 1,000 see note, ▪ Numbers 3:39.

Rachel's Two Sons:

1. Benjamin—an increase of 10,200

2. Joseph:

  (1) Manasseh—an increase of 20,500

  (2) Ephraim—a decrease of 8,000

The tribes of Rachel's sons had a gain of 30,700 and a loss of 8,000 which
gave them a net increase of 22,700.

Zilpah's Two Sons:

1. Asher—an increase of 11,900

2. Gad—a decrease of 5,150

Net increase: 6,750

Bilhah's Two Sons:

1. Dan—an increase of 1,700

2. Naphtali—a decrease of 8,000

Net decrease: 6,300

With the Levites having a gain of 1,000 and being counted, the tribes as
listed above had increases totaling 29,450 from Rachel's sons (22,700) and
Zilpah's sons (6,750) with decreases totaling 30,270 from Leah's sons
(23,970) and Bilhah's sons (6,300). This gave Israel a net loss of 820
between the numberings.

The Breakdown by Camps:

In the east camp of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, all increased; in the south
camp of Reuben, Simeon, and Gad—where Korah's rebellion (Numbers
16:1-35) and Zimri's sin (Numbers 25:1-18) were committed—all
decreased; in the west camp both Benjamin and Manasseh increased while
Ephraim (next to the rebellious south camp) decreased; and in the north
camp Dan and Asher increased while Naphtali decreased.

a [numbered among the children of Israel]

         The Twenty-four Lists of the Tribes in Scripture
1. The tribal heads by birth (Genesis 29:32-30:24).

2. The list of tribal heads according to the wives of Jacob (Genesis 35:23-
   26).

3. The list of tribal heads according to the wives, giving the number of
   children of each head (Genesis 46:8-24).

4. The first list by prophecy (Genesis 49:3-28).

5. The list of those who went into Egypt with Jacob (Exodus 1:1-6). Joseph
   is omitted because he was already in Egypt. Levi is mentioned in these
   first five lists because his tribe did not yet serve as ministers of the
   twelve. The tribe of Levi is not mentioned in the next four lists because
   they served in the priesthood by that time.

6. The list naming census takers and heads of the twelve tribes making up
   the nation of Israel (Numbers 1:4-16).

7. The list by the numbering of the tribes (Numbers 1:20-46).

8. The list by encampment around the tabernacle (Numbers 2:2-32).

9. The list by offerings of the tribes at the dedication of the altar (Numbers
   7:12-84).

10. The list by order of march on the journeys (Numbers 10:14-28). Levi is
   included and given a place in the march.

11. The list by spies chosen to spy out Canaan (Numbers 13:3-17). Levi is
   not included here.

12. The list by numbering of the tribes in the plain of Moab (Numbers 26:4-
   56). Levi is again numbered here, after the twelve tribes, as in the first
   numbering (cp. Numbers 26:57-65 with Numbers 3:1-4:49).

13. The list by dividers of the land of Canaan (Numbers 34:16-29). Levi is
   not included because they did not inherit any of the land.

14. The list by order of position on Mount Gerizim and Ebal (Deut. 27:12-
   14). The original twelve sons of Jacob are listed here—including Levi
   and Joseph (who stands in the place of Ephraim and Manasseh)—
   because they represent the fathers of all the tribes, as before Levi was
   chosen to the priesthood.

15. The second list by prophecy and blessing of the tribes. Levi is included
   but Simeon is omitted for some unknown reason (Deut. 33:6-29).

16. The list by actual division of the land of promise (Joshua 13:1-21:45).
   Levi is included, not as receiving a portion to compare with the twelve
   tribes, but as being given certain places among them.
17. The list by failure to inherit all the land of promise (Judges 1:1-36).

18. The list by cooperation with Deborah and Barak (Judges 5:14-18).
   Judah and Simeon are not mentioned because they were not in the war
   with the other tribes. Levi is not mentioned because they were ministers,
   not soldiers.

19. The list of original sons of Jacob before Manasseh and Ephraim (1
   Chron. 2:1-2).

20. The list of the tribes and their descendants from Jacob to David,
   including Levi (1 Chron. 2:3-9:44). Zebulun and Dan are omitted for
   some unknown reason.

21. The list by tribes of those who were numbered to help David (1 Chron.
   12:1-40). Levites are included because they also helped him.

22. The list by heads of tribes under David, king of Israel (1 Chron. 27:16-
   22). Levi is represented; Gad and Asher are omitted; and Manasseh is
   listed as having two heads to the tribe—East and West Manasseh.

23. The list by choice of God in future and eternal restoration, and by
   division of the land of promise as it will be in eternity (Ezekiel 48). Levi
   is included here to show his portion of the eternal land under the
   Messiah. This makes thirteen tribes recognized by God in the end.

24. The list by sealing of God in the foreheads of all that are servants of
   God at the time when 144,000 are protected through the trumpet
   judgments and are caught up to heaven as the man-child of Rev. 12:5
   (Rev. 7:1-8; Rev. 14:1-5). Dan is excluded because they won't be
   servants of God at the time, and Levi is included.

The above lists are different in order and purpose, and should be studied
and compared. Reuben, the firstborn, heads most of them but Judah heads
others, being the kingly and leading tribe (Numbers 2:3; Numbers 10:14;
Numbers 34:19; 1 Chron. 2:3; Rev. 7:5). Simeon and Reuben head a
divided list (Deut. 27:12-13). Dan heads the list in Ezekiel 48, because his
division of land in the Millennium will be the farthest to the north, the place
where most of the tribe of Dan eventually settled. Ezekiel 48 deals with the
eternal division of the land of the thirteen tribes of Israel under their
Messiah.

    came from the two sons of Gershon (Numbers 3:34 with Numbers 3:22).

From the above and the following chapter we see that the work of the
Levites was very hard labor in all the journeys from Sinai to Canaan
throughout the forty years. In the tabernacle alone there were no less than
23,408 pounds (nearly 12 tons) of metal to move from place to place (▪
Exodus 38:24-31, notes), besides the curtains, board walls, skin coverings,
and other things which made a great weight. In addition to this the Levites
had their own household goods, tents, and personal belongings to take care
of. To what extent the people carried things is not known. There were some
wagons and pack animals, for at least six covered wagons were dedicated to
the Levites, two wagons being given to the Gershonites and four wagons to
the Merarites, because they had the heavy metals to carry. None were given
to the Kohathites because they were to carry the furniture upon their
shoulders (Numbers 7:1-9. See Genesis 42:26; Genesis 45:17-19,27;
Genesis 50:9).

a [Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, ...]

                Fifteen Commands—the Law of Jealousy
1. Tell Israel that if a wife commits adultery and it be kept secret and there
   is no witness against her, or if the spirit of jealousy come upon her
   husband, whether she is guilty or not, then the man shall bring her to the
   priest with a meat offering (Numbers 5:12-15).

2. The priest shall bring her near, and set her before the Lord (Numbers
   5:16).

3. He shall take holy water in an earthen vessel and put dust in it (Numbers
   5:17).

4. He shall uncover the woman's head, put the meat offering in her hands
   and have the bitter water in his own hand (Numbers 5:18).

5. He shall charge her by an oath saying: If you are not guilty you are free
   from the bitter water that causes a curse; but if you are guilty the Lord
   make you a curse among your people, make your thigh to rot, and your
   belly to swell (Numbers 5:19-22).

6. The woman shall say, Amen, amen (Numbers 5:22).

7. The priest shall write these curses in a book and shall blot them out with
   the bitter water (Numbers 5:23).

8. He shall cause the woman to drink the water and it shall enter her and
   become bitter (Numbers 5:24). See Numbers 5:26 and point 10, below.

9. He shall take the jealousy offering, the meat offering, out of her hands
   and wave it before the Lord and offer it upon the altar (Numbers 5:25).

10. He shall take a handful of the meat offering, even the memorial of it,
   and burn it upon the altar, and afterward cause her to drink of the water
   (Numbers 5:26).

11. If she is guilty she shall be a curse among her people (Numbers 5:27).

12. If she is not guilty she shall be free, and shall conceive seed (Numbers
   5:28).
13. You shall execute this law upon a woman accused of adultery to
   determine her guilt or innocence (Numbers 5:29-30).

14. By these means shall it be determined whether her husband is guilty of
   false accusation (Numbers 5:31).

15. If she is found guilty she shall bear her inquity.

This was a just law, for it protected the innocent wife from the insane
jealousy of her husband, and manifested her innocence to all. It also
protected the husband from a guilty wife and allowed him to know the
truth. There is no record of this law ever being used. Perhaps, if guilty, she
would confess before going through such an ordeal; willingness to go
through it manifested innocence.

b [separate] Hebrew: palaÊ¼ (HSN-6381), to separate or distinguish; not
    the same as the other word for separate in this verse, the Hebrew: nazar
    (HSN-5144) (see note below).

c [Nazarite] Hebrew: nazir (HSN-5139), from the Hebrew: nazar (HSN-
    5144), to hold aloof; abstain from defilement (translated "separate" in
    Numbers 6:2-6; Leviticus 15:31; Leviticus 22:2; Ezekiel 14:7; Hosea
    9:10; Zech. 7:3; and consecrate in Numbers 6:12). Nazir is the only word
    for Nazarite in the Old Testament (Numbers 6:2,13,18-21; Judges 13:5,7;
    Judges 16:17; Lament. 4:7; Amos 2:11-12). It means a separated or
    consecrated person. The Rechabites (Jeremiah 35), Essenes, Anchorites,
    Hermits, Monks, and other monastic orders all borrowed from the
    Nazarite idea.

Nazarene in Matthew 2:23 has no connection with Nazarite; it simply
means an inhabitant of Nazareth, a place whose name bore reproach (John
1:46). Nazarene is used in Acts 24:5 of a follower of Jesus of Nazareth.
Christ was not a Nazarite, for He drank of the fruit of the vine and touched
the dead, which Nazarites were forbidden to do (Matthew 9:25; Matthew
11:19; Matthew 26:29; Mark 14:25; Luke 7:14,34; Luke 22:18). Whether
He cut His hair or not is not stated, but His consecration was greater for He
was sanctified when sent into the world (John 10:36), and depended on the
Spirit's anointing to distinguish Himself as separated to God rather than the
outward show of abstinence from grapes and refusal to cut His hair or touch
the dead (John 3:2,34; John 14:12).

a [when the days of his separation are fulfilled ...]

1. When the days of a Nazarite's vow are completed, he shall be brought to

2. He shall offer his offering to God:

    (1) A yearling male lamb ($80) for for a burnt offering (Numbers 6:14)

    (3) A ram ($125) for a peace offering

    (4) A basket of unleavened bread (Numbers 6:15)

    (5) Unleavened cakes mingled with oil

    (6) Unleavened wafers anointed with oil (Numbers 6:15)

    (7) Meat offering

temporarily, or for their whole life, as decided by the individual.

b [fulfilled] Nazarite vows were for various lengths of time. Only a few

    law of the Nazarite applied to them. It seems from Acts 21:23-27 that Paul

a [each prince of his day] The twelve offerings of the princes were exactly
    alike. They were actually gifts from the tribes as a whole, not from the
    princes personally. This indicated that all the tribes were equally indebted
    to God, so all should testify of their obligation and share alike in
    expressing thanksgiving. This prevented jealousy and competition in
    giving. Thus, the sin of emulation was nipped in the bud (Galatians 5:20).
    The vessels were all sacrificial, and the animals were all clean, fit for
    sacrifice. Everything was intended to show the gratitude and worship of
    the nation.

b [make an atonement]

                     Levites Make an Atonement
The Levites were to carry on the work of the tabernacle, performing the
services needed to keep Israel free from sin, sickness, and hell. All
atonement for Israel was made to this end, that God might be in their midst.
The priests were to make proper atonement for the nation as a whole, and
for the sins of each individual. Sickness and plagues were connected with
sin and rebellion, and freedom from plagues is connected with atonement
(Numbers 8:19). Certain plagues were stopped when atonement was made
(Numbers 16:46-47; Numbers 25:13; 2 Samuel 24:18-25). Others were
stopped in answer to prayer (Numbers 11:2; Numbers 12:13; Genesis 20).
God had promised to heal sickness as Israel obeyed, and to keep them in
perfect health as they continued to obey (Exodus 15:26; Leviticus 26; Deut.
28). Because He healed everyone, there was not a feeble one among them
(Psalm 105:37; Psalm 107:20). The means of healing and health were
included in the Mosaic covenant, and a special covenant was also made
with them (Exodus 15:26). Such physical provision was continued in all the
writings of Israel's prophets and inspired men (Psalm 91; Psalm 103:1-4;
Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 58). God sent Jesus to them and the Gentiles later, to
confirm and carry on the same program (Matthew 4:23-24; Matthew 8:1-
17; Mark 16:15-20; John 10:10; John 14:1-15; Acts 10:38). Later the
apostles confirmed and carried on the program (Acts 3:6,16; Acts 4:12;
Acts 5:15-16; Acts 15:4,12; Romans 15:17-19,29; 2 Cor. 1:6-7; 2 Cor. 12:1-
11; James 5:14-16; 1 Peter 2:24).

                 Eleven Commands—Blowing Trumpets
1. Make two trumpets of silver; of a single piece you shall make each one.

2. Use them for calling assemblies, for war, for journeying, and for making
   camps (Numbers 10:2-10).
3. When both are blown all Israel shall assemble at the door of the outer
   court (Numbers 10:3).

4. When one is used, then the princes of Israel shall gather (Numbers 10:4).

5. When you blow an alarm the three camps on the east (Judah, Issachar,
   Zebulun) shall go forward (Numbers 10:5; Numbers 2:3-9).

6. When you blow the second time, the three camps on the south (Reuben,
   Simeon, Gad) shall take their journey (Numbers 10:6; Numbers 2:10-
   16).

7. When you blow for a general assembly it shall not be a sound of alarm
   (Numbers 10:7).

8. The priest shall blow the trumpets (Numbers 10:8).

9. This shall be an ordinance to you forever in your generations.

10. If you go to war, then you shall blow an alarm with the trumpets
   (Numbers 10:9).

11. In the day of gladness, in your solemn days and in the beginnings of
   your months, you shall blow with your trumpets over your burnt
   offerings, and over your peace offerings as a memorial to the Lord
   (Numbers 10:10).

    purposes (Joshua 6:4). In Solomon's time there were 120 priests with
    trumpets (2 Chron. 5:12).

a [blow an alarm] Blowing long on both trumpets called the whole
    assembly together (Numbers 10:3). A long blast on one trumpet called
    only the princes together (Numbers 10:4). An alarm was probably staccato
    tones, to clearly distinguish it (cp. 1 Cor. 14:8). The first alarm caused the
    camps on the east to move; the second caused those on the south to move
    (Numbers 10:6); the third and fourth caused those on the north and west to
    move. These last two camps are not mentioned here, but the Septuagint
    mentions them. Thus, there was order and discipline in the Israelite
    camps. That they were well regulated and trained to respond quickly to
    their duties is understandable, for Moses was once a great military man of
    Egypt. See notes, ▪ Exodus 2:10.
