a [some uncleanness in her]

                              Reason for Divorce
Hebrew: Ê½erwah (HSN-6172), translated "uncleanness" (Deut. 24:1);
"shame" (Isaiah 20:4); and "nakedness" (Genesis 9:22-23; Genesis 42:9,12;
Exodus 20:26; Exodus 28:42; Leviticus 18:6-19; Leviticus 20:11-21; 1
Samuel 20:30; Isaiah 47:3; Lament. 1:8; Ezekiel 16:8,36-37; Ezekiel 22:10;
Ezekiel 23:10,18,29; Hosea 2:9). It comes from Ê½arah (HSN-6168),
which means to make bare; empty; destitute; discover; make naked;
uncover. The idea here is that of discovering or uncovering something in the
wife that was not known before to the husband. Exactly what uncleanness
included here is not known. Judging from how the word is translated it
would be something of the nature of shame, disappointment, and extreme
dislike. If the uncleanness refers to moral sin, as in Deut. 22:13-21, the
earlier law demanded the death penalty. Perhaps Moses saw that by carrying
out the letter of such a law there would be frequent executions due to
extremely lax morals among Israelites. He thus modified the law by
permitting a wife to clear herself with a solemn oath in some cases
(Numbers 5:11-31), and in other cases allowing the husband to divorce his
wife privately without bringing her to trial (Deut. 24:1-4; Matthew 1:19).

The various translations are as follows: Young: "nakedness of anything";
Rotherham: "some matter of shame"; the Peshitta: "some evidence of open
prostitution"; Berkeley: "something improper in her"; Moffatt: "found her
immodest in some way"; the Septuagint: "found something unseemly in
her"; Fenton: "found repulsive qualities in her." All this seems to indicate a
serious moral sin.

Whatever the intended thought, it is clear that divorce was not commanded
here, but permitted because of the hardness of hearts (Deut. 24:1; Matthew
19:8); that both divorced parties were free to remarry (Deut. 24:2); that the
first husband could not take the wife a second time, for that was an
abomination to God (Deut. 24:3-4).

Such things must be understood in the light of several factors: that a wife
became the actual property of the husband and he became her lord and
master (Exodus 21:7-11; 2 Cor. 11:3; Ephes. 5:22-33; Col. 3:18; 1 Peter
3:5-7); that easy divorces were a common thing in those days among all
nations; that Israel had been influenced greatly by such nations and was in
the habit of getting divorces for the most frivolous excuses; and that Moses
simply tolerated certain practices because of the hardness of the hearts of
Israel. Hence, this law limiting divorce to "uncleanness" was needed.

The rival schools of Hillel and Shammai in the days of Christ interpreted
this "uncleanness" different ways. Shammai held that it referred only to
moral and criminal sins of adultery; but Hillel contended that it referred to
anything disliked by the husband, even though it was something trivial
(notes, ▪ Matthew 5:31-32; note, ▪ Matthew 19:3; notes, ▪ Mark 10:1-9).
Christ sanctioned the teaching of Shammai, interpreting the uncleanness as
fornication, (porneia (GSN-4202), (Matthew 5:32; Matthew 19:9). See
notes, ▪ Matthew 5:31-32 for definitions of divorce, fornication, etc. For
wording of an ancient Jewish divorce decree, see note, ▪ Mark 10:4.

According to the Gospels (Matthew 5:31-32; Matthew 19:1-9; Mark 10:1-8;
Luke 16:18), Moses wrote the law on divorce because of "hardness of the
heart" of the people. Except for fornication, one must not divorce his wife
(Matthew 5:31; note, ▪ Matthew 19:9). Except for fornication, if one puts
away his wife he causes her to commit adultry (Matthew 5:32; Matthew
19:9). Except for fornication dissolving a marriage, one who marries a
divorced woman commits adultery. All hardness-of-heart divorces for any
and every cause are wrong, and only those with a scriptural reason for
divorce have the right to remarry. The man and woman who divorce
without scriptural grounds cause sin by forcing each other to marry
someone else. Paul gives one more scriptural reason for divorce—willful
desertion because of Christ and the gospel (2 Cor. 7:12-15).

b [then let him write her a bill of divorcement] Three commands—
 marriage and divorce:

1. If you take a wife, and she finds no favor in your eyes because of some
    uncleanness, you may write a bill of divorcement, put it into her hand
    and send her out of your house.

2. She may go and be another man's wife (Deut. 24:2).

3. If the second husband hates her and writes her a bill of divorcement, or if
    he dies, the former husband may not remarry her, for she is defiled
     (Deut. 24:4).

c [him] It appears that only the man had the authority concerning divorce.
    By New Testament times, however, a woman had such authority under
    certain circumstances.

b [raiment]

                     Pledging the Outer Garment
The outer garment of a poor man was usually the best he had to offer as a
pledge. Therefore, this law was for his benefit—so he would not suffer the
cold at night. The garment was shapeless, like a sack with head and arm
openings (Exodus 12:34). It was usually of wool and hair of varying
degrees of fineness, some entirely black and others completely white, often
marked with two broad stripes. It was used as a wrap by day and a covering
at night. Thus, it was so important, especially at night, that both here and in
Deut. 24:1 and Exodus 22:26 it is forbidden to be kept from the owner's use
as a pledge (cp. Job 24:7-8). The outer garment is called a "cloak"
(Matthew 5:40); "garment" (Matthew 14:36); "raiment" (Matthew 27:31);
and "vesture" (Rev. 19:13). Most places in the N.T. where "garment" is
mentioned refer to this outer garb (Matthew 21:7-8; Matthew 24:18; John
13:4,12; Acts 7:38; Acts 22:20-23).

                  Five Commands—Perpetual Families
1. If a married brother dies childless, the living brother shall go in to his
    brother's wife and raise up children for him.

2. The firstborn from such a union shall succeed in the name of the dead
   brother that his name be not blotted out of Israel (Deut. 25:6).

    wife shall take her case before the elders of his city for justice (Deut.
    25:7).

   children for his brother (Deut. 25:8).

5. If he persists in not fulfilling his obligation according to the law, then the
    brother's wife shall approach him in the presence of the elders, loose his
     shoe from his foot, spit in his face, and say that such disgrace rightly
     belongs to the man who will not build up his brother's house. His name
     in Israel shall be called: The house of him that hath his shoe loosed
     (Deut. 25:9-10).

   21:20-24). Since then (70 A.D.), Israel has been scattered among the
   nations and only recently have they had a homeland where they've
   partially regathered in fulfillment of prophecy. See Israel.

a [rejoiced over you to do you good]

                           Two Rejoicings of God
1. Rejoicing to do good to Israel when they were in obedience.

2. Rejoicing to destroy them when they were in stubborn and willful
   rebellion.

This latter rejoicing seems contrary to the nature of God's love and grace as
stated in many passages, but when viewed in the light of all Scripture it
becomes understandable. Because of the hard-hearted, hard-headed, willful
rebellion of Israel, God was forced to curse them and wash His hands of
them for a time. He was thus able to relieve Himself and give them up to
their own ways. God was also forced to do this to the Gentile world, as
recorded in Romans 1:18-32, and He reveals that He will take the same
attitude toward all rebels (Proverbs 1:22-31).
                               Backsliding
The theory that God will not punish, judge, and condemn His people when
they backslide and persist in sin and rebellion has no foundation in any
attribute, act, promise, prophecy, covenant, or revelation of God. He has
been just and good to all in all ages, blessing men when they obey and
cursing the same men when they disobey. He is completely impartial;
nothing can cause Him to act contrary His nature as He has revealed it. God
has given hundreds of warnings for men not to backslide lest they die in
their sin and rebellion and suffer the fate of all sinners. He has given many
examples of angels, demons, and men who have acutally suffered and will
yet suffer such destiny. See Twenty-one Examples of Beings Fallen from
Grace and 210 Plain Laws and Warnings.

Man's Part in His Destiny:

There are many simple statements in Scripture revealing man's part in his
own damnation or salvation. It is not God's will for anyone to perish, but for
all to come to repentance (John 3:16; 1 Tim. 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9; Rev. 22:17). If
people will not meet God's terms, they will be lost (Mark 16:16; John 3:3,5;
Proverbs 1:24-31); and if any turn away from the Lord after salvation, and
persist in rebellion until death, He is not responsible. The fact that all are
not going to be saved proves that man does have a part in the matter. In fact,
if any man fails to be saved, it is his own fault, not God's fault.

c [plucked] Hebrew: nacach (HSN-5255), to tear away; destroy; pluck; and
 root up. It was translated "pluck" (Deut. 28:63; Psalm 52:5; cp. Jeremiah
 12:14-17; Jeremiah 18:7; Jeremiah 24:6; Jeremiah 31:28,40; Jeremiah
 42:10; Jeremiah 45:4; Ezekiel 19:12; Daniel 11:4; Micah 5:14), "rooted
 out" (Proverbs 2:22), and "destroy" (Proverbs 15:25). It is true that no
 man, demon, angel, or any other power can pluck a true believer—one
 who hears the Lord's voice and follows Him—from the hands of God
 (notes, ▪ John 10:28-29); but it is also true that if one is ungodly, God
 Himself will do such plucking. See Backsliding.

Two examples of plucking up:

1. Nations (Deut. 28:63; 2 Chron. 7:19-22; Jeremiah 12:14-17; Jeremiah
   31:28)
2. King Jehoiakin (Jeremiah 22:24)

d [off the land] Being plucked "off the land" was to be the final judgment
    for their backslidings. The salvation of their souls was involved here, for
    if they were not godly enough to remain in the land, they were not godly
    enough to be received in heaven. The sins for which God plucked up the
    nations of Canaan were eternal death-penalty sins—sins that caused them
    to be damned eternally. Israel was warned of the same results, if they
    committed the same sins (Deut. 28:58-68; Deut. 18:9-12; Deut. 20:18;
    Leviticus 18:27-30).

                            Man's Responsibility
On the surface, this verse suggests that God was responsible for the people
not having proper faculties, but it literally means they did not use their
faculties properly and the grace that He gave them so that they might know
Him better. Therefore, they were not wise, loving, and obedient as they
should be. If they had had eyes eager to see, and ears eager to hear the Word
of God, and hearts eager to obey it, they would have been commended.
However, by not using their own created faculties the right way, it proved
they had grieved God and hardened themselves against the Holy Spirit and
the means of grace. God hated this (Deut. 29:4; cp. Deut. 5:29). The same
complaint was made by Isaiah and quoted in Matthew 13:14-16, which
further explains this verse. See Isaiah 6:9-10. Pharaoh is an outstanding
example of one who, through his refusal to hear and obey, hardened himself
when God gave him the opportunity to be broken and obedient.

a [The LORD will not spare him] God's Vow to Apostates:

God promises not to have mercy upon the backslider whose heart turns
away from Him and becomes apostate (Deut. 29:18-20; Jeremiah 13:14;
Jeremiah 21:7; Ezekiel 7:4,9; Ezekiel 8:18; Ezekiel 9:10; Romans 11:21).
God did not spare Israel (Romans 11:21; Jude 1:5), or the antediluvians and
fallen angels (2 Peter 2:4-5), so we cannot expect Him to spare other
apostates. See Backsliding.

Six Marks of Apostates:

1. Turning away from God in the heart (Deut. 29:18)

2. Idolatry

3. A zeal to lead others away from God and thus become a root of gall and
   bitterness to them
4. Pride and presumption which cause one to laugh at sin and make light of
   evil (Deut. 29:19)

5. Walking after the imaginations of the heart

6. Living a life of self-gratification and sensual lusts

Six Judgments of God upon Apostates:

1. They will receive no mercy (Deut. 29:20; Hebrews 10:26-29).

2. His fierce anger will be against them.

3. He will lay upon them all the curses written in this book.

4. He will blot out their names from under heaven.

5. He will separate them from the righteous to be punished (Deut. 29:21; 2
   Peter 2:9-10)

6. He will make them examples to coming generations of His wrath (Deut.
   29:22-28)

This passage speaks of the return of the Lord God of Israel and could refer

                    Four Uses of the Word "Rock"
1. Rock is a symbol of God:

   (1) The stable and strong One (Deut. 32:4; Isaiah 17:10)

   (2) The Rock of salvation (Deut. 32:15; Psalm 89:26; Psalm 95:1)

   (8) None like Him (2 Samuel 22:32)

   (1) A Rock of offense (Isaiah 8:14; Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8)

b [corrupted]

                               Israel Corrupted
Hebrew: shachath (HSN-7843), to decay; ruin; batter; cast off; corrupt;
destroy; lose; mar; perish; become utterly waste and good for nothing. Not
only did God declare that Israel would corrupt themselves from the time of
Moses' death until the last days (Deut. 4:25; Deut. 31:29), but He also
accused them of already corrupting themselves (Deut. 32:5; Deut. 9:12;
Exodus 32:7). Israel became increasingly corrupt before God through the
periods of the judges (Judges 2:19), the kings (2 Chron. 27:2; Isaiah 1:4;
Jeremiah 6:28; Ezekiel 16:47; Ezekiel 28:17; Hosea 9:9; Zeph. 3:7) and the
captivities (Neh. 1:7; Malachi 2:8). The Hebrew: shachath (HSN-7843) is
used in all these passages. The same idea is found in the N.T. where the
apostles warn that Christians can also become corrupt and lose their souls
(2 Cor. 7:2; 2 Cor. 11:3; Galatians 6:8; Ephes. 4:22; 2 Peter 1:4; 2 Peter
2:12,19-22; Jude 1:10).

c [spot]

                        The Marks of Idolaters
This may refer to the ancient practice of idolaters who inscribed on their
arms and foreheads some straight, oval, or circular sign of their particular
deity. In India the priest would make the mark with paint, with sawdust and
oil, or with dried cow dung and tumeric. In many cases, the marks were
renewed daily (cp. Job 11:15; Job 22:26; Job 31:7). On the other hand, it
may refer to the fact that people blemished with sin do not belong to God.
The Septuagint reads: "They have sinned! Blemished children are not His."

The Peshitta has: "They are not His children because of blemish."
Rotherham: "They have broken faith with Him to be no son of His." Fenton:
"Corrupt, you have not His Son's form,—You wayward and fickle race!"

    has eternally known every detail of thought and life for all free moral
    agents, even before their existence. Such is not necessary to understand
    the omniscience of God (see note a, ▪ Genesis 6:5). Scripture often records
    Him seeing and knowing things when they happen, thus limiting Himself
    for some purpose in His dealings with His subjects.

c [abhorred them] God can and does abhor backsliders as described in

    (Deut. 32:20-22). Other O.T. scriptures call saved people "sons" (Isaiah
    43:6; Isaiah 45:11; Hosea 1:10).

                 Seven Proofs taht He Is the Only God
1. He is the only One that can kill and make alive (Deut. 32:39).

2. He is the only One that can wound and heal.

3. He is the only One that is all powerful—none can deliver out of His
   hand.

4. He is the only One that can truly claim to be alive (Deut. 32:40).

    blessing all the tribes some have supposed that he is referred to along with

Date and Place: Written about 1645 B.C. in the plains of Moab by Jordan
near Jericho, just before the entrance into Canaan (Deut. 1:5; Deut. 34:1-
12).

Author: Moses, the lawgiver and leader of Israel.

Proof of Authorship: See Sixteen Proofs that Moses Wrote the Pentateuch.

Theme: The name of the book means Second Law, because it records the
repetition of the Ten Commandments (Deut. 5). It contains the parting
counsels of Moses to Israel in view of their entrance into Canaan; a
summary of the wilderness wanderings; many new laws that needed to be
added to those given some forty years before; many warnings in view of the
possibility of sin; prophecies concerning the future of Israel; and the
Palestinian covenant (Deut. 11:13-32; Deut. 27:1-30:20)

Statistics: 5th book of the Bible; 34 chapters; 959 verses; 28,355 words; 33
questions; 690 verses of history; 230 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 37 verses
of unfulfilled prophecy. Deuteronomy has 33 seperate messages from God
(Deut. 1:6,34,42; Deut. 2:2,9,17,31; Deut. 3:2,26; Deut. 4:10,12,14; Deut.
5:4,28,30; Deut. 6:1; Deut. 9:12,13,23; Deut. 10:1,11; Deut. 11:13; Deut.
12:1; Deut. 17:14; Deut. 18:15,17; Deut. 27:1; Deut. 29:1; Deut. 30:1; Deut.
31:14,16; Deut. 32:48; Deut. 34:4); 519 commands; 47 promises; and 497
predictions.

b [Jordan]

                              The Jordan River
Many events took place on the Jordan river. Lot chose the plain of Jordan
(Genesis 13:10-11). Jacob crossed the river twice (Genesis 32:10). Israel
camped on it at the end of the forty years (Numbers 22:1). Here is where
the book of Deuteronomy was uttered and written (notes, ▪ Deut. 1:1), and
where Joshua received his first instructions (Joshua 1:2). The river was
dried up by a miracle three times:

1. By Joshua (Joshua 3:1-4:23; Joshua 5:1)
2. By Elijah (2 Kings 2:7-8)

3. By Elisha (2 Kings 2:13-14)

Here battles were fought (Judges 3:28; Judges 12:5); Naaman was cleansed
from leprosy (2 Kings 5:10-14); and Christianity had its beginning
(Matthew 3:1-17; Mark 1:5-9; Luke 4:1; John 1:28; John 3:26; John 10:40).

Jordan has its source in the convergence of several rivers in the upper plain
of Lake Huleh in the Anti-Lebanon mountains. The Jordan itself emerges
from the southern tip of Lake Huleh, about 10 miles north of the Sea of
Galilee, and makes its final stop in the Dead Sea. The total length of the
river is about 200 miles, though its distance (as the crow flies) is only about
80 miles. Widths of the Jordan river vary from 60 to 100 feet, with depths
ranging from 3 to 10 feet.

At the base of Lake Huleh the Jordan is about 230 feet above sea level. By
the time it reaches the Dead Sea it has dropped to 1,290 feet below sea
level. Thus, the river is aptly named Jordan which means "descender."
Combined with the variations in width and depth, the steep descent
produces at least 27 series of rapids, making the Jordan a significant natural
barrier for east-to-west travel throughout Palestine.

The Jordan valley is about 4 to 10 miles wide. The river overflows its banks
in March and April, and it was in that state when Israel crossed it (Joshua
3:15; 1 Chron. 12:15).

b [two men to spy secretly]

                        Two Spies instead of Twelve
Joshua himself was one of the twelve spies sent from Kadesh (Numbers
13), and one of the only two men who did not rebel. Now, only two spies
were sent—secretly instead of publicly. This was to prevent negative
reports from spreading and causing panic, if the findings of the spies were
unfavorable. Joshua, while confident in God, used all natural means to
assure success. He did so by faith, or there would have been no works
(James 2:19-26). Like any good commander, he wanted complete
intelligence on the site—approaches, weaknesses of the city, defenses and
resources of the inhabitants, etc. Joshua realized later that this was
unnecessary, for nothing learned was used in the fall of Jericho which was
brought about by supernatural power (Joshua 6:1-27).

c [Jericho]

                                  Jericho
The name means "the moon" or "new moon," so called because of the
crescent-like plain in which it stood, formed by an amphitheatre of hills
surrounding it. Some think the name is derived from ruwach (HSN-7307),
meaning "smell" or "fragrance," referring to the many balsam and palm
trees in the city (Deut. 34:3).

One of the oldest cities in the Holy Land, Jericho was located about 18 or
20 miles from Jerusalem and about 4 miles from Jordan. Nothing is said of
the city except to mention its existence (west of Jordan) in 12 references up
to this point (Numbers 22:1; Numbers 26:3,63; Numbers 31:12; Numbers
33:48,50; Numbers 34:15; Numbers 35:1; Numbers 36:13; Deut. 32:49;
Deut. 34:1-3). It is named 29 times in Joshua and only 22 other times in the
rest of Scripture. Its fall and the curse upon the man who would rebuild it
are recorded in Joshua 6 and Hebrews 11:30. It was rebuilt by Heil (1 Kings
16:34). Elijah and Elisha both passed it when they made Jordan dry (2
Kings 2:4-18). Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, was captured there (2
Kings 25:5; Jeremiah 39:5; Jeremiah 52:8). Several interesting events took
place at Jericho during the ministry of Jesus (Matthew 20:29; Mark 10:46;
Luke 10:30; Luke 18:35; Luke 19:1). Under the Romans it was a royal
residence. Herod the Great died there. It was destroyed and rebuilt after this
several times.

            The Contract between Rahab and the Spies
1. The eightfold plea of Rahab:

  (1) I know the Lord has given you the land (Joshua 2:9).

  (2) Your terror has fallen upon us.

  (3) All Canaanites faint because of fear of you.

  (4) They have heard how the Lord dried up the Red Sea for you when
     you left Egypt (Joshua 2:10; Exodus 14-15).

  (5) They have heard what you did to the kings of the Amorites, Sihon
     and Og (Joshua 2:10; Numbers 21:21-35).

  (6) As soon as we heard those things, our hearts melted and there was no
     more courage in any man (Joshua 2:11).

  (7) We recognized that Jehovah your 'Elohiym is 'Elohiym in heaven
     above and in earth beneath.

  (8) Swear to me by Jehovah, since I have shown you kindness, that you
     will show kindness to my father's house and will protect my father,
     mother, brothers, sisters, and all that they have, and deliver us from
     death (Joshua 2:12-13).

2. The twofold pledge of spies:

  (1) Our life for yours, if you do not reveal our business (Joshua 2:14).

  (2) When God has given us the land, we will deal kindly and truly with
     you.

3. Carrying out the contract by Rahab:

  (1) She let them down by a cord through a window to the ground (Joshua
     2:15).
    (2) She instructed them to escape pursuers by hiding in the mountain
       three days, allowing men to return before going on the way (Joshua
       2:16).

4. The fourfold pledge of the spies:

    (1) We will be blameless of the oath if you do not have the scarlet cord
       in the window by which you let us down (Joshua 2:17-18).

    (2) Be sure your father, mother, brothers, sisters, and all their households
       are in your house when we overthrow the city (Joshua 2:18).

    (3) If one goes out of the house and is killed, we shall not be responsible,
       but if one who stays in is killed we shall be responsible (Joshua 2:19).

    (4) If you reveal our business, then we are free from our oath to you
       (Joshua 2:20).

5. Rahab's acceptance of the contract:

    (1) As you have said, so be it (Joshua 2:21).

    (2) She sent them away to make good their escape (Joshua 2:21-24).

    (3) She bound the scarlet cord in the window (Joshua 2:21).

6. Carrying out the contract by Israel:

    (1) Joshua saved Rahab the harlot alive, and her father's house, and all
       that she had (Joshua 6:25).

    (2) She dwelled in Israel to that day, because she hid the spies (Joshua
       6:25; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25).

a [till they were whole]

                            Divine Protection
From the natural standpoint it would take circumcised adults about three
weeks to get completely well. Of course, God may have healed them
miraculously. He promised to be their healer (Exodus 15:26; Exodus
23:23), and He was in Moses' day (Psalm 105:37; Psalm 107:20). However,
if they were not healed, then they were temporarily handicapped by their
pain. This is why the Shechemites were such easy victims for the few sons
of Jacob (Genesis 34:25). Yet Israel was not attacked while they were
vulnerable. This can only be explained by the fear of God being upon the
Canaanites.

Joshua, an able general, knew their danger; but he also knew that God could
not err, and that it was his duty to obey. Therefore, in the very teeth of his
enemies, he reduced the major part of his army to a state of helplessness,
simply trusting the protection of God who gave him orders. His confidence
was not misplaced, for God did not let one enemy rise up against the
Israelites during this time. Notice also that the command was not given
while the nation was in safety on the east side of the Jordan river. God
wanted to teach them another lesson of absolute dependence on Him for
success through His power and wisdom. For this same reason, He had them
cross Jordan when it was FLOODED instead of waiting until it could be
forded.

Hebrew: cherem (HSN-2764), "devoted to destruction" (see note, ▪
Leviticus 27:28). It was the devotion of any idolatrous object—person, city,
or thing—to utter destruction. When such a curse was pronounced on a city,
it meant that all the people, animals, and treasures that would ordinarily be
taken were to be completely burned in the fire or consecrated to the
sanctuary (Joshua 6:19,24). Joshua pronounced this ban on Jericho, a great
and wealthy city, evidently by divine decree, and the severity of the doom
that came to all violaters is illustrated in the punishment of Achan in Joshua
7. This curse was justified, not only because its inhabitants were part of a
people who had filled up their cup of iniquity (Genesis 15:16), but by the
fact that fighting men from many surrounding peoples were in Jericho
helping to defend it against Israel (Joshua 24:11). Its destruction would
serve to paralyze further resistance to Israel on the part of other Canaanite
cities when they saw the mighty power of God in the miracle of the walls
falling down flat.

                           The Power of One Sin
One sin brought all the nation to defeat and caused God to stop His
blessing. One sin is what caused Adam and the whole race to be under the
present curse (Genesis 2:19; Romans 5:12-21). One sin brings the same
result as committing all sins (James 2:9-10). Any one of the death-penalty
sins of Mark 7:19-21; Romans 1:21-32; 1 Cor. 6:9-11; Galatians 5:19-21;
Col. 3:5-10 will damn the soul of any person, regardless of his claims to
salvation, for there is no partiality with God. Grace, love, mercy, and
salvation from God do not license one to sin or free him from responsibility.
Sin has its deadly effect on all alike—in every generation, in every place
and among all races.
God was the leader of Israel and for Him to lead a people tainted with sin to
victory would be a stain upon His character. Hence, the demand for each
person to be clean and obedient to the law and will of God. The method
used in detecting the exact sin and the person who committed it brought
fear to all Israel and helped curb such practices during the rest of the war
(Joshua 7:10-15).

b [neither will I be with you any more, except ye destroy the accursed
    from among you] God promised not to be with Israel any more unless
    this sin was cleansed from the whole camp. He promises the same to all
    people in every age, regardless of law or grace. See Backsliding.

                     The Simplicity of Sanctification
We cannot over-emphasize the utter simplicity of sanctification. It is made
clear in every passage where the subject is found. It does not mean one
thing in one scripture or in one particular age and another thing in another.
It does not have one meaning for Israel and another for the church, one
meaning under law and another under grace. Wherever it is found
sanctification means a setting apart from a profane or secular use to a sacred
and holy use. Holy, sanctified, born again, converted, redeemed, saved, and
purified people can and must be continually set apart to obedience as they
walk in the light (1 John 1:7). How could Joshua sanctify the people, and
how could the people sanctify themselves, as commanded here? By setting
themselves apart for the revelation of God, in the same way that Israel
sanctified or set themselves apart to receive the law in Exodus 19:10-23.
See Sanctification.

a [Gibeon]

                                   Gibeon
Gibeon was a city about 7 miles from Bethel and 8 miles northwest of
Jerusalem. Being about 10 miles from Ai and about 18 west of Gilgal, the
inhabitants likely thought they would be next on Joshua's list of places to
conquer. Gibeon was the head of four towns, the others being Chephirah,
Beeroth, and Kirjath-jearim—all occupied by Hivites (Joshua 9:7,17;
Joshua 11:19), called Amorites (2 Samuel 21:2), the word being a general
term for the Canaanite nations. These four towns apparently had a
republican form of government.
Gibeon was an important city. It lay at the head of the pass of Beth-horon,
opposite the pass of Ai, and on the main route from Jerusalem and the lower
Jordan valley to Joppa and the Mediterranean Sea. Gibeon fell within the lot
of Benjamin (Joshua 18:25), and was one of the cities of the priests (Joshua
21:17). Several important events took place here: the slaughter of
Gibeonites by Saul (2 Samuel 21); the contest between Saul and David's
servants (2 Samuel 2:12-24; 2 Samuel 3:30); the slaying of Amasa (2
Samuel 20:8-13); and the vision of Solomon (1 Kings 2:4-5; 1 Kings 9:2). It
was at Gibeon that the sun was commanded to stand still (Joshua 10:12).
The sanctuary was located here for a long time (1 Kings 3:4-5; 1 Kings 8:4;
1 Kings 9:2; 1 Chron. 21:29; 2 Chron. 1:3,13). At Gibeon Joshua became
victor over five kings of Canaan, giving him possession of the southern half
of Palestine (Joshua 10). In another great battle (of Merom) he gained
victory over the northern part (Joshua 11-12), thus conquering most of
Palestine in two campaigns.

                  Six Mistakes of Joshua and Israel
1. They ate with the Gibeonites. According to ancient custom, eating
   together was a token of unalterable friendship, and those who ate salt
   together were bound to a perpetual covenant. So deeply rooted was this
   custom that intended robbery has been abandoned when a robber has
   accidently eaten salt while getting his plunder. Likewise, men have been
   freed from captivity by getting their captors to eat salt with them.

2. They did not ask for God's counsel. Without consulting God by the Urim
   and Thummim, they believed these men and made a covenant with them.
   Though He did not punish them for making the covenant, He later
   punished Israel for breaking it (2 Samuel 21:1-9). God expects people to
   keep their word, even when they vow to their own hurt (Psalm 15:4). He
   let Israel make this mistake without intervening, and He later used it to
   destroy His enemies (Joshua 11:18-20).

3. Joshua made peace with the Gibeonites (Joshua 9:15).
4. He made a league with them.

5. He let them live.

6. The princes of Israel swore to them, thus making the covenant binding on
   all Israel. Such contracting was forbidden by law (Exodus 23:32; Exodus
   34:13-17; Exodus 33:51-56; Deut. 7:1-2; Deut. 20:16).

                         The King of Jerusalem
This is the first time the word "king" is found in Scripture in connection
with Jerusalem, but it is used 86 times with other cities, before this. Once in
the N.T., Melchizedek is called "king of Salem," which was the ancient
name of Jerusalem (Hebrews 7:1-3; Genesis 14:18; Psalm 76:2). The word
Adonizedek (Joshua 10:1) means "lord of righteousness"; it is equivalent to
"king of righteousness," used of Melchizedek. These were the official
names of the kings of Jerusalem.

This is also the first time that Jerusalem is mentioned in Scripture. It means
city of peace, or foundation of peace. It is one of the ironies of history that
the city with such a name has seen so little peace, and that for its possession
rivers of blood have been shed. It was originally also called "Jebus" (Judges
19:10-11; 1 Chron. 4:5; 2 Samuel 5:6-9), the old name of "Jerus." It is
called "Jebusi" (Judges 18:16,28); "Ariel" (Isaiah 29:1); "the city of
righteousness" (Isaiah 1:26); and "holy city" (Isaiah 48:2; Isaiah 52:1; Neh.
11:1). David captured the city from the Jebusites and made it the capital of
united Israel (2 Samuel 5:6-9). It remained the capital until the division of
the kingdom about 1,000 B.C. Jerusalem then continued to be the capital of
Judah until 606 B.C. when it was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar. It became
the capital of Israel again about 546 B.C. and remained so until the nation
and city were destroyed by the Romans in 70 A.D. Jerusalem has undergone
no less than 28 sieges from Joshua's time to the present, 10 sieges beginning
from Joshua to Nebuchadnezzar (Judges 1:8; 2 Samuel 5:6-10; 1 Kings
14:25; 2 Kings 18:13-19:37; 2 Chron. 21:16-17; 2 Chron. 28:5-15; 2 Chron.
36:1-2). In the period between the close of the O.T. to 70 A.D. it was
besieged 10 times. Since then it has been besieged 8 times to 1917 A.D., 9
times if we consider the recent war between the Jews and Arabs (1967).
Jerusalem has a future as the capital of Israel and of the Antichrist (Ezekiel
37; Daniel 9:27-11:40-45; 2 Thes. 2:3-4; Rev. 11:1-11), and as the eternal
capital in the reign of Jesus Christ (Isaiah 2; Ezekiel 48; Joel 3; Amos 9:9-
15; Obadiah 15-21; Micah 4; Zech. 14).

a [And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed]

                     Eight Scientific and Biblical Facts
1. This was a genuine miracle. The sun and moon either stopped their
   influences on the earth, or stood still (see notes a through b, ▪ Joshua
   10:12).

2. It is not the only miracle involving the sun:

   (1) Historically: The earth was totally dark for an indefinite period
      (Genesis 1:2); there was darkness in Egypt for three full days (Exodus
      10:21-23); the shadow of the sun went back ten degrees on the sun
      dial of Ahaz (2 Kings 20:11; Isaiah 38:8); the sun went down at noon
      and the earth was darkened when Israel fell to Babylon (Amos 8:9);
      and there was darkness for three hours when Christ was crucified
      (Luke 23:44-45).

   (2) Prophetically: The sun will be darkened in the sixth seal (Rev. 6:12-
      17), the fourth trumpet (Rev. 8:12), the fifth trumpet (Rev. 9:2), the
      fifth vial (Rev. 16:10), and at the second advent of Christ and
      Armagedddon (Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7; Joel 2:10,31; Joel 3:15;
      Matthew 24:29-31).

3. The rising and setting of the sun is man's expression for the earth turning
   on its axis so that only part of it is toward the sun at a given time. The
   earth's rotation makes it appear that the sun is actually moving around
   this globe. The sun does travel through the heavens, making its own
   prescribed circuit, as do all stars and planets. See The Solar System.

4. It is in God's power to stop the movements of all or part of the solar
    system, if He sees fit to do so to further His purpose. As the Sovereign
    Creator of the laws of nature, He may suspend those laws anytime or
    anywhere He pleases.

5. It is believed that the command for the sun to stand still was given about
    the time of its setting for several reasons:

   (1) The sun was over Gibeon at the time (Joshua 10:12). Looking back
      from the east where Joshua and his men were pursuing, it could be
      seen setting in the sky over Gibeon.
   (2) The moon was coming up over the valley of Ajalon (Joshua 10:12)
      and could not have been seen with the naked eye in the afternoon sun.

   (3) The statement that the sun "hasted not to go about a whole day"
      indicates that it was setting at the time the command was given
      (Joshua 10:13).

   (4) If it had been in the middle of the day, Joshua would not have known
      whether he and his people could avenge themselves before the day
      was over because he would have had six hours or more left in which
      to fight.

6. Joshua spoke to the sun and moon, not the earth, for they are the
    influences causing tides and seasons and day and night and must
    influence the rotation of the earth (Genesis 1:14-18).

7. The earth's rotation could suddenly stop without noticeable change for its
   inhabitants other than the appearance of the heavens, so what is recorded
   in Joshua 10:12-14 could have happened without being disastrous to the
   earth and its peoples.

8. Greece, Egypt, China, and Mexico have records of a long day (or night)
   corresponding to the time of Joshua. By counting the equinoxes,
   eclipses, and transits backward from our day to his, and counting them
   from the prime date of creation (re-creation) on to Joshua's time, a whole
   day is missing. Mathematically, such a conclusion is unavoidable.

a [Hebron]

                                 Hebron
Hebron was about 38 miles south of Jerusalem, in the Judah portion of the
land (Joshua 10:3-5,23,36-39; Joshua 12:10; Joshua 14:13-15). One of the
most ancient and important cities of southern Palestine, it was said to have
been founded before Zoan in Egypt (Numbers 13:22). Its ancient name was
Kirjath-arba (Judges 1:10), and it was called Arba for the father of Anak
who founded one of the mighty races of giants (Joshua 14:12; Joshua
15:14). Abram dwelled here for many years after coming into Canaan
(Genesis 13:18), and from here he rescued Lot (Genesis 14). Here is where
his name was changed to Abraham (Genesis 17:5), where God and two
angels came to visit him, and where Isaac was finally announced (Genesis
18). Hebron is where Sarah died (Genesis 23), Isaac and Jacob spent most
of their lives (Genesis 35:27; Genesis 37:14), and the patriarchs were buried
(Genesis 49:30; Genesis 50:13). Jacob and his family went to Egypt from
here (Genesis 46:1), and the spies got their grapes near here (Numbers
13:22). Hebron became one of the Levite cities (Joshua 21:10) and a city of
refuge (Joshua 20:7). David was received with kindness at this place; later
he was anointed king and reigned over seven years here (1 Samuel 30:31; 2
Samuel 5:3-5). It is where six of his sons were born (2 Samuel 3:2), where
Abner was slain (2 Samuel 3:27), and Absalom rebelled (2 Samuel 15:7).
The city was fortified by Rehoboam (2 Chron. 11:10). Jews from the
captivity settled here (Neh. 11:25). The Maccabees recovered it from Edom
in the period after the close of the O.T. (1 Macc. 5:65). The Romans burned
it in their war against the Jews in 70 A.D. Because of its history, it was
respected by the Crusaders, and has retained importance during the Muslim
period because of its past relationship with Abraham. There were two men
in Scripture called "Hebron"—a Levite (Exodus 6:18; Numbers 3:19,27; 1
Chron. 6:2,18; 1 Chron. 23:12,19) and a descendant of Caleb (1 Chron.
2:42-43).

                                   Debir
Debir was about 7 miles south of Hebron. It was conquered by Joshua near
the end of his southern campaign (Joshua 10:3,38-39; Joshua 11:21; Joshua
12:13; Joshua 13:26). In Joshua 15:15-17; Judges 1:11-13 we have the
account of Othniel capturing Debir and winning a wife. It is called Kirjath-
sannah (Joshua 15:49), which is perhaps a corruption of Kirjath-sepher of
Joshua 15:15-16; Judges 1:11-12. It was one time a city of giants, of the
Anakim tribe (Joshua 11:21). Debir became a Levitical city (Joshua 21:15;
1 Chron. 6:58). It must have been a sacred city of the pagans, as its name
would indicate, for the Hebrew: debiyr (HSN-1687) is used in 1 Kings 6:5
to denote the holy of holies (oracle). There were two other towns called
Debir—one between Judah and Benhamin (Joshua 15:7), which must have
been east of Jerusalem on the Jericho road, and one on the border of Gad
near Mahanaim (Joshua 13:26) which may be the Lodebar of 1 Samuel 9:4.

             Eightfold Description of Unconquered Lands
1. All the borders of the Philistines—from Sihor, the border of Egypt, to
   Ekron, the north part of Philistia (Joshua 13:2-3).

2. All of Geshuri. An insignificant Aramaean kingdom, Geshur was located
   east of Bashan and north toward Syria (Joshua 12:5; Joshua 13:1-13;
   Deut. 3:14; 2 Samuel 15:8; 1 Chron. 2:23). The people once occupied
   the land of Philistia, but were driven out by the Caphtorims and
   Philistines (Genesis 10:14; Deut. 2:23; 1 Chron. 1:12; Jeremiah 47:4;
   Amos 9:7). Some remained in the south of Canaan (1 Samuel 27:8).
   Perhaps both branches are referred to here as being unconquered (Joshua
   13:2). David married the daughter of the king of Geshur, who became
   the mother of Absalom and Tamar (2 Samuel 3:3; 2 Samuel 13:1). It was
   to Geshur that Absalom fled (2 Samuel 13:37; 2 Samuel 14:23).
3. The Avites (Joshua 13:3). These were a branch of the giants who were
   disposessed by the Caphtorims (Deut. 2:23; cp. 2 Kings 17:31).

4. All the land of the Canaanites from the south going north to Mearah near
   Sidon in Phoenicia and east to Aphek in Syria (Joshua 13:4; note, ▪
   Joshua 12:18). It is true that Joshua defeated all the major cities and the
   organized opposition against him, but many sections and people were
   left in the promised land which should have been totally destroyed. God
   said these would be thorns for Israel to test and prove them to see if they
   would be obedient (Joshua 23:13; Numbers 33:55-56; Judges 2:3).

5. All the land of the Giblites—the inhabitants of Gebal in north Palestine
   (Joshua 13:5; Psalm 83:7; Ezekiel 27:9).

6. All of Lebanon east from Baal-gad under Mount Hermon and to Hamath
   (Joshua 13:5).

7. All the inhabitants of the hill country in north Palestine from Lebanon to
     Misrephoth-maim (Joshua 13:6; note d, ▪ Joshua 11:8).

8. All the Sidonians—inhabitants of Phoenicia in general (Joshua 13:6).
   The Sidonians were never expelled; they will be under Israel in the
   Millennium (Ezekiel 48). They were friends of David and Solomon.

b [five lords of the Philistines]
                   The Five Lords of the Philistines
1. Lord of Gazathites—inhabitants of Gaza which was the most southern
   city of Philistia. It was reached by Joshua but he did not conquer it
   (Joshua 10:41; Joshua 11:22). It was later taken by Judah (Judges 1:18)
   and given to that tribe (Joshua 15:47), but was regained by the
   Philistines and was ever afterward considered their city until the
   Assyrians took it about 720 B.C. Gaza is mentioned in the period of the
   judges and kings as one of the chief enemies of Israel (Judges 6:4;
   Judges 16:1,21; 1 Samuel 6:17; 2 Kings 18:8; 1 Chron. 7:28). It was
   doomed by the prophets (Jeremiah 47:1,5; Amos 1:6-7; Zeph. 2:4; Zech.
   9:5. See Acts 8:26.

2. Lord of Ashdothites—inhabitants of Ashdod (Joshua 13:3; Joshua
   11:22). Ashdod was also given to Judah (Joshua 15:46-47), but was
   regained by the Philistines. It was a bitter enemy of Israel (1 Samuel 5:1-
   7; 1 Samuel 6:17; 2 Chron. 26:6), and was also doomed by the prophets
   (Isaiah 20:1; Jeremiah 25:20; Amos 1:8; Amos 3:9; Zeph. 2:4; Zech. 9:6.

3. Lord of Eshkalonites—inhabitants of Askelon, another city allotted to
   Judah but retaken. It remained a Philistine city to fight Israel many times
   (Judges 1:18; 1 Samuel 6:17; 2 Samuel 1:20).

4. Lord of Gittites—inhabitants of Gath, the fourth Philistine city not taken
   by Joshua, but allotted to Judah (Joshua 13:22). It was first conquered by
   David (1 Chron. 18:1). Gath was the town of Goliath and other giants (1
   Samuel 17:4; 2 Samuel 21:18-22). David came here twice in his flight
   from Saul (1 Samuel 21:10; 1 Samuel 27:2-4). It is mentioned more in
   Scripture than any other of the five cities of the Philistines (1 Samuel
   5:8; 1 Samuel 6:17; 1 Samuel 7:14; 1 Samuel 17:4,23,52; 1 Samuel
   21:10-12; 1 Samuel 27:2-11; 2 Samuel 1:20; 2 Samuel 15:18; 2 Samuel
   21:20-22; 1 Kings 2:39-41; 2 Kings 2:17; 1 Chron. 7:21; 1 Chron. 8:13;
   1 Chron. 18:1; 1 Chron. 20:6-8; 2 Chron. 11:8; 2 Chron. 26:6; Amos 6:2;
   Micah 1:10). Many Gittites were great friends of David and hundreds
   served him (2 Samuel 6:10-11; 2 Samuel 15:19-22; 2 Samuel 18:2; 2
   Samuel 21:19).
5. Lord of Ekronites—inhabitants of Ekron, the fifth Philistine city allotted
   to Judah. It was regained and remained an enemy of Israel (Joshua 13:3;
   Joshua 15:11,45-47; Joshua 19:43; Judges 1:18; 1 Samuel 5:10; 1
   Samuel 6:16-17; 1 Samuel 7:14; 1 Samuel 17:52; 2 Kings 1:2-6,16).
   Ekron was also doomed by the prophets (Jeremiah 25:20; Amos 1:8;
   Zeph. 2:4; Zech. 9:6-7).

                            Reuben's Inheritance
1. The tribe received land according to the number of families (Joshua
   13:15).

2. Their general borders were from Aroer on the bank of the river Arnon
   (Joshua 13:9,16) on the south (which was the north border of Moab),
   from the city in the middle of the valley of Arnon, and from the whole
   plain of Medeba northward to Mahanaim (Joshua 13:30), and from the
   Dead Sea and the Jordan river on the west to the Ammonite kingdom on
   the east (Joshua 13:16-23).

3. Fifteen named cities:

  (1) Aroer on the bank of Arnon, the north border of Moab (Joshua
      13:9,16; note, ▪ Joshua 12:2).

  (2) Medeba, a city infamous for its idolatry, and located southwest of
      Heshbon (Joshua 13:9,16; Numbers 21:30; 1 Chron. 19:7; Isaiah
      15:2).

  (3) Heshbon, the capital of Sihon (Joshua 13:21; note, ▪ Numbers 21:26).

  (4) Dibon.

  (5) Bamoth-baal (only here, Joshua 13:17). It means the high places of
      Baal; altars to him had been erected there.

  (6) Beth-baal-meon (only here, Joshua 13:17). Called Baal-meon
      (Numbers 32:38; 1 Chron. 5:8; Ezekiel 25:9).

  (7) Jahaza (only here, Joshua 13:18). Called Jahaz (Numbers 21:23; Deut.
      2:32; Judges 11:20; Isaiah 15:4; Jeremiah 48:34), Jahazah (Joshua
      21:26; Jeremiah 48:21), and Jahzah (1 Chron. 6:78); it was given to
      Levites.

  (8) Kedemoth (Joshua 13:18; Joshua 21:37; Deut. 2:26; 1 Chron. 6:79).

  (9) Mephaath (Joshua 13:18; Joshua 21:37; 1 Chron. 6:79; Jeremiah
      48:21). It was located in the east part of the desert near Moab, and
       was given to Levites (Joshua 21:37).

    (10) Kirjahaim (Joshua 13:19; Numbers 32:37; 1 Chron. 6:76). It was
        near the border of Moab and originally inhabited by the Emims, a
        giant tribe. It was conquered first by the Moabites, then by the
        Amorites and finally by the Israelites who held it until the Babylonian
        captivity when it was regained by the Moabites.

    (11) Sibmah, well known for its vineyards (Joshua 13:19; Isaiah 16:8-9;
        Jeremiah 48:32).

    (12) Zareth-shahar, light of the dawn, or mount of the valley; perhaps
        because of being built on a hill where it caught the rays of the rising
        sun. Only here, Joshua 13:19.

    (13) Beth-peor, the house of Peor, located on the top of a mountain by the
        same name (Joshua 13:20; Deut. 3:29; Deut. 4:46; Deut. 34:6).

    (14) Ashdoth-pisgah (Joshua 13:20; Joshua 12:3; Deut. 3:17).

    (15) Beth-jeshimoth (Joshua 13:20; Joshua 12:3; Ezekiel 25:9). Called
        Beth-jesimoth (Numbers 33:39). See other lists of cities of this
        inheritance, notes, ▪ Numbers 32:3,34.

4. The unnamed city in the middle of the valley where Arnon flows (Joshua
   13:9,16).

   appears from this that the entire kingdom of Sihon was given to Reuben,
   although Gad also inherited part of it (Numbers 32). See Nine Cities of
   Sihon and Og, for a list of other cities in this territory.

1. Manasseh was given inheritance according to the number of families

2. The tribe's general borders were from Mahanaim north, including all of
   Bashan, the kingdom of Og, and the 60 towns of Jair, the west border
   being the Sea of Galilee and Jordan north of Galilee (Joshua 13:30-33).

3. Two named cities:

     (1) Ashtaroth, a city named after the supreme goddess of Canaan, the
        female counterpart of Baal. The name and cult came from Babylon
        where Istar or Ishtar represented the morning and evening stars
        (Judges 2:13; Judges 10:6; 1 Samuel 7:3-4; 1 Samuel 12:10; 1 Samuel
        31:10). Ashtaroth was the capital of Og, king of Bashan (Joshua
        13:12,31; Joshua 9:10; Joshua 12:4; Judges 1:4).

     (2) Edrei, the place where Og was defeated (Joshua 13:12,31; Joshua
        12:4; Joshua 19:37; Numbers 21:33; Deut. 1:4; Deut. 3:1,10).

4. Sixty towns of Jair (Joshua 13:30). Originally, 23 cities were taken by
   Jair (1 Chron. 2:22); then the number was increased to 30 (Judges 10:4),
   and finally it grew to 60 (1 Chron. 2:23). They are called Havoth-Jair
   (Numbers 32:41; Judges 10:4). These 60 towns were all located on the
   east of Jordan; and they made a great inheritance for Manasseh.

a [Kenezite]

                               Kenezites
The word "Kenezite" must not be confused with "Kenites" of Genesis
15:19; Numbers 24:21-22; Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11-17; Judges 5:24; 1
Samuel 15:6; 1 Samuel 27:10; 1 Samuel 30:29; 1 Chron. 2:55; and
"Kenizzites" of Genesis 15:19. It seems that Kenaz was a family name
among Edomites who came from Isaac through Esau (Genesis 36:11,15,42),
and among Israelites in the tribe of Judah (Joshua 14:6,14; Joshua 15:17;
Judges 1:13; Judges 3:9-11; 1 Chron. 4:13-15). The word "Kenezite" in
Joshua 14:4,14; Numbers 32:12 is equivalent to "son of Kenaz" (Joshua
15:17), head of the father's house which came from Kenaz; that is, a
subdivision of the Judahite family of Hezron (1 Chron. 2:42). Caleb, the
brother of Jerahmeel and father of Achzah (1 Chron. 2:42,49), was the same
person as Caleb the descendant of Hezron (1 Chron. 2:18). The Kenaz
(father of Jephunneh, the father of Caleb) of Joshua 14:14 was a descendant
of Hezron, the son of Pharez, the son of Judah (1 Chron. 2:5,18,25); hence,
it was not the name of a tribe, but of a person; and, as we may see from 1
Chron. 4:15, one of Caleb's sons was named Kenaz, the name being
repeated in the family. The sons of Judah that came with Caleb (Joshua
14:6) were members of the family that took the name Kenaz for their family
name, Caleb being the head of this particular family of Judah.

a [the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah]

                          Inheritance by Prophecy
God had prophetically spoken through Jacob (Genesis 49) and Moses
(Deut. 33), indicating that certain portions were to be allotted to certain
tribes. Now the actual lot was being cast to confirm the previous
predictions. All this not only guaranteed divine inspiration in the selection
of each portion, but also assured that all jealousy arising from any source
would be unfounded. Each tribe was placed by divine lot in the exact place
predicted by Jacob 243 years before and by Moses some 5 years before. It
was thus evident that God was directing in both the predictions and the lot
for the tribes. See Jacob's Prophecy of the Tribes, and notes on Moses'
prophecy in ▪ Deut. 33:6-29.

b [by their families] The inheritance of Judah was according to the number
 of families.

c [border of Edom the wilderness of Zin southward was the utter most
 part of the south coast]

                            Borders of Judah
1. Southern border—Judah occupied the most southerly part of the land of
   Canaan. The southern border extended from the lower end of the Dead
   Sea on south by Edom and the wilderness of Sin to Maaleha-crabbim, to
   Zin to Kadesh-barnea, to Hezron to Adar, to Karkaa, to Azmon, to Sihon
   or the river of Egypt and on to the Mediterranean Sea (Joshua 15:1-4).

2. Eastern border—the Dead Sea (Joshua 15:5).

3. Northern border—from the bay of the Dead Sea where the Jordan
   empties into the sea to Beth-hogla, to Beth-arabah, to the stone of Bohan
   to Debir to Adummim to En-shemesh, by the valley of the son of
   Hinnom, to the south of Jerusalem, to the top of the mountain that lies
   before the valley of the son of Hinnom westward, to the end of the valley
   of the giants, to the fountain of water of Nephtoah, to the cities of Mount
   Ephron, to Baalah or Kirjath-jearim and westward, to Mount Seir and
   along the north of Mount Jearim or Cesalon, to Beth-shemesh, to
   Timnah, to the north side of Ekron, to Shicron, to Mount Baalah to
   Jabneel, and to the Mediterranean Sea (Joshua 15:5-11).
4. Western border—the Mediterranean Sea (Joshua 15:12).

a [twenty and nine] The difference in the total number here and the actual
    names listed could be due to the fact that there were twenty-nine cities as
    stated and nine villages worthy of mention with them, making thirty-eight
    places named. Or, it could be that a copyist's error was the cause. Letters
    were used as numerals and a scribe could have mistaken some that were
    similar. Otherwise, it could be that compound names in the original were
    separated by the translators who thought they represented more than one
    place. This is understandable since the oldest original MSS were written
    in large capital letters, about an inch high, with no space between the
    letters and no punctuation. With such a list as here it would be difficult to
    separate the names and decide which should be single or compound
    words.

                                  Shiloh
Shiloh, a town in Ephraim where Israel assembled at the close of the five
years of war in Canaan, and where the tabernacle was set up for the first
time in conquered Canaan (Joshua 18:1-10; Joshua 19:51; Joshua 21:2;
Joshua 22:9-12). It was no doubt set up at Gilgal during the conquest. At
Shiloh the last seven tribes received their lots by a special commission
(Joshua 18:2-10). From here Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of
Manasseh went back to their own homes and the other tribes gathered to
make war against them because it was thought they were rebelling (Joshua
22:1-34). The tabernacle remained at Shiloh during the period of the judges
(Judges 18:31; Judges 21:12-21; 1 Samuel 1:3,9,24; 1 Samuel 2:14; 1
Samuel 3:21; 1 Samuel 4:3-12; 1 Kings 2:27; 1 Kings 14:2-4; Psalm 78:60;
Jeremiah 7:12-14). Here is where the maids were captured to be wives of
Benjamites (Judges 21:21); where Samuel's mother prayed for him, and
where he was brought as a young boy to serve God (1 Samuel 1:3-28).
From here the ark was captured by Philistines (1 Samuel 2:1-7:14).
Evidently, Shiloh was destroyed at this time (Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12-
14; Jeremiah 26:6-9). Its location was about 8 miles north of Bethel and
south of Shechem (Judges 21:19).

Jerusalem was a Jebusite city before David conquered it and made it the
capital of the united kingdom of Israel (2 Samuel 5:6-12). Here the most
extraordinary events of human history have taken place—events in which
God, angels, and men have played a part. Here is where the temples of
Israel have been and will again be located. Here is where Christ was
consecrated to God, where He was crucified and buried, where He arose
from the dead, and the place He will come to at the second advent (Zech.
14:1-5). At Jerusalem is where Christ will reign forever when He comes
(Isaiah 2:1-4; Ezekiel 43:7; Ezekiel 48:35; Joel 4:20; Zech. 14). The city
has undergone no less than twenty-eight sieges and two more are yet to
come (Zech. 14; Rev. 20:7-10). It was the center of Jewish life—political,
social, business, and religious. The gospel was first preached here by the
early church (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:4-8; Acts 2:14). Here the first
congregation of Christians was formed, the church saw its greatest victories
and had its greatest struggles to survive; here is where the first Christian
martyr laid down his life (Acts 2-12). Many prophecies are yet to be
fulfilled concerning Jerusalem as we shall see in the various books of the
prophets.

                           Zebulun's Inheritance
The beginning of this south border was Sarid, an unidentified place. It ran
westward to Maralah, to Dabbasheth, to the river that is before Jokneam in
Carmel (Joshua 12:22) which is on the Mediterranean Sea (Joshua 19:10-
11). From Sarid the boundary ran eastward to the border of Chisloth-tabor,
out to Daberath, to Japhia, on east to Gittah-hepher, to Neah (Joshua 19:12-
13). It is almost impossible to trace this border accurately in either direction
from Sarid, for most of these points are unknown except Jokneam on
Carmel which we know to be on the Mediterranean Sea (Joshua 12:22).
One thing is certain: Genesis 49:13 and Deut. 33:19 predict the portion of
Zebulun to be on the sea as a haven for ships; so regardless of what was
possessed at first, the tribe will finally have a coastline on the
Mediterranean and the Sea of Galilee. In the Millennium the allotment of
land will be on a different principle. Each of the twelve great portions will
run west from the Euphrates and the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean,
giving each tribe an outlet by water (Ezekiel 48).

    opposition to Jesus Christ and the apostles. "High priest" appears 24 times

    3:32).
                     Ten Facts about High Priests
1. Their office was by inheritance (Exodus 27:21; Exodus 28:43; Exodus
   29:9).

2. They were to be holy (Leviticus 21:6-7; Leviticus 22:9,16).

3. There were without any physical blemish (Leviticus 21:17-23).

4. They wore special garments (Exodus 28; Exodus 39:1-29; Leviticus
   6:10-11; Leviticus 8:13)

5. They were limited in the selection of a wife (Leviticus 21:7-15).

6. They were exempt from tax (Ezra 7:24).

7. Respect was due to them (Acts 23:5).

8. They had assistants (Numbers 3:32; Numbers 4:16; Numbers 31:6; 1
   Chron. 9:20; 2 Samuel 15:24).

9. They had to be consecrated (Exodus 29; Leviticus 6:24-30; Leviticus
   21:10; Psalm 133:2).

10. The duties of high priests:

   (1) To serve as overseer of sanctuary (Numbers 18:1-7).

   (2) To offer sacrifices (Hebrews 5:1; Hebrews 8:3).

   (3) To officiate in consecration of Levites and other priests (Numbers
       8:11-21).

   (4) To light lamps in sanctuary (Exodus 27:20; Exodus 30:8; Leviticus
       24:3-4; Numbers 8:3).

   (5) To burn incense (Exodus 30:7-8).

   (6) To place showbread on the table every sabbath (Leviticus 24:8).
     (7) To offer sacrifice for own sins (Leviticus 4:3-12).

     (8) To officiate in most holy place once a year (Exodus 30:10; Leviticus
         16; Hebrews 5:3).

     (9) To mediate between God and man (▪ Exodus 28:29-30, notes).

     (10) To judge and act in an offical capacity at many times (Numbers
         5:15; Numbers 27:18-21; Deut. 17:8-13).

                     SUMMARY OF JOSHUA
                            ____________________

Date and Place: Joshua's part of the book was perhaps written at Gilgal in
Canaan as the events transpired form 1646-1616 B.C. When and by whom
the postscript (Joshua 24:29-33) was written is not known, but Jewish
tradition says that Josh. Joshua 24:29-32 of the last chapter were added by
Eleazar and Joshua 24:33 was added by Phinehas.

Author: Joshua, except for the postscript and a few other verses. He was of
the tribe of Ephraim (Numbers 14:8,16), and became the leader of Israel
after Moses (Joshua 1:9-14; Joshua 24:13; Numbers 27:18-23; Deut. 1:38;
Deut. 3:21,28; Deut. 31:3-23; Deut. 34:9). He is mentioned in the Book of
Joshua 168 times. The name "Joshua" is found 216 times throughout
Scripture. In the Septuagint the name is "Jesus" which is retained in the
Greek N.T. (Acts 7:45; Hebrews 4:8). "Joshua" is also called "Jehoshua"
and "Oshea" (Numbers 13:8,16) and "Jehoshua" (1 Chron. 7:27). He was a
slave in Egypt. At his death, he was 110 years old, the same age that Joseph
was when he died (Joshua 24:29). He was thus about 40 years old at the
time of the exodus from Egypt.

Proof of Authorship: In every generation of Israel there were men called
scribes and recorders who kept up the national records of current events
(Exodus 17:14; Exodus 34:27; Numbers 5:23; Numbers 17:2-3; Deut.
17:18; Joshua 10:13; Judges 5:14; 2 Samuel 1:18; 2 Samuel 8:16-17; 2
Samuel 20:24-25; 1 Kings 4:3; 2 Kings 12:10; 2 Kings 18:18; 2 Kings 19:2;
etc.). There were also many prophets who wrote books recording national
events (Joshua 24:26; 1 Samuel 10:25; 1 Kings 11:41; 1 Kings 14:19,29; 1
Kings 15:7,23,31; 1 Kings 16:5,14,20,27; 1 Kings 23:39,45; 2 Kings 1:18; 2
Kings 8:23; 2 Kings 10:34; 2 Kings 12:19; 2 Kings 13:8,12; 2 Kings
14:6,15,18,28; 2 Kings 15:6,11,15,21,26,31,36; 2 Kings 16:19; 2 Kings
20:20; 2 Kings 21:17; 2 Kings 22:13; 2 Kings 23:3,21,24,28; 2 Kings 24:5;
1 Chron. 9:1; 1 Chron. 29:29; 2 Chron. 9:29; 2 Chron. 12:15; 2 Chron.
13:22; 2 Chron. 16:11; 2 Chron. 17:9; 2 Chron. 20:24; 2 Chron. 25:26; 2
Chron. 27:7; 2 Chron. 28:26; 2 Chron. 33:18-19; 2 Chron. 35:27; 2 Chron.
36:8). No doubt Joshua wrote all of the book bearing his name except the
postscript (Joshua 24:29-33); the story in Joshua 15:16-19 of Othniel (the
first judge of Israel after Joshua) getting a wife through conquest (Judges
1:1,10-15); and the story of Dan conquering Leshem or Laish (Joshua
19:47) which was not actually accomplished un til the death of Joshua
(Judges 18). Apart from these exceptions—records that could have been
added by Eleazar, Phinehas, Samuel, or any other prophet, scribe, or
recorder in Israel—we conclude that Joshua was the author. This seems
clear from Joshua 24:26. At the least, many references in the book indicate
that the events of Joshua were written by an eyewitness (Joshua 1:10-18;
Joshua 2:1; Joshua 3:1-17).

Theme: The book deals with the consummation of the redemption of Israel
out of Egypt, for redemption has two parts—out and into (Deut. 6:23). It
records the fulfillment of the prophecies of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and
Moses regarding the land of promise being given to Israel, and the conquest
and division of this land to them. Joshua may be divided into two equal
parts of 12 chapters each: Joshua 1-12 the conquest; Joshua 13-24 the
division of the land among the tribes, with Joshua 1:1-9 forming the
introduction and Joshua 24:29-33 the conclusion. The inspiration of the
book is confirmed by several quotations in the N.T. (compare Joshua 1:5
with Hebrews 13:5; Joshua 2:1-24 with James 2:25; Joshua 6:20 with
Hebrews 11:30; Joshua 6:23 with Hebrews 11:31; Joshua 14:1-2 with Acts
13:19; and Joshua 24:32 with Acts 7:16 and Hebrews 11:22).

Statistics: 6th book of the Bible; 24 chapters; 658 verses; 18,852 words;
624 verses of history; 42 verses of fulfilled prophecy; no unfulfilled

c [Judah] As a man,Judah played an important role in Israel, even during
    the lifetime of his father. His name means praise. He was the fourth son of
    Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:35). He saved Joseph from the pit in which
    the others had cast him to die (Genesis 37:20-27), and by persuading his
    brothers to sell him paved the way for the preservation of Israel. Judah
    was capable of confessing his sins (Genesis 38:26). He pledged himself to
    Jacob for the safe return of Benjamin (Genesis 43:3-14), and plead with
    Joseph to spare him (Genesis 44:18-34). Judah was the one through whom
    the Messiah was to come and rule (Genesis 49:10). His tribe led the others
    in their marches (Numbers 2:3; Numbers 10:14), and it was first in a
    number of other activities (Numbers 34:19; Joshua 15:1).

a [Gaza]

                                     Gaza
Gaza, meaning strong, was one of five Philistine cities allotted to Judah
(Judges 1:18; Judges 6:4; Joshua 10:41; Joshua 11:22; Joshua 15:47). It was
perhaps the oldest city of Philistia, located near the coast of the
Mediterranean about 40 miles south of Joppa, and on a hill rising 60 to 200
feet above the plain, with sand dunes between it and the sea 2.5 miles away.
The plain was fertile with many wells of water which made it an important
place on the border of the desert between Syria and Egypt.
Gaza is mentioned 19 times in Scripture, as far back as Genesis 10:19. It
was taken by the Philistines and remained their city until it was taken by
Sargon, king of Assyria, in his war with Egypt. Alexander the Great took it
after a two-month siege and destroyed it, putting all the men to death and
selling the women and children as slaves. The city was restored and later
taken by the Maccabees and later still by Alexander Jannaeus. The Romans
rebuilt it in 57 B.C.

Gaza is mentioned only once in the N.T. (Acts 8:26). In the second and
third centuries A.D. it became a center of Greek culture and commerce with
a strong pagan influence. Many martyrs died for Christ there. Gaza was
taken by the Arabs in A.D. 634 and has remained a Moslem city most of the
time since. In O.T. days it was the enemy of Israel (1 Samuel 6:17; 2 Kings
18:8; 1 Chron. 7:28). See Gaza in the prophetic books (Jeremiah 47:1-5;
Amos 1:6-7; Zeph. 2:4; Zech. 9:5).

b [Askelon] Askelon, another Philistine city taken by Judah, but not for
 long. Only here and 1 Samuel 6:17; 2 Samuel 1:20. Called Ashkelon,
 migration (Judges 14:19; Jeremiah 25:20; Jeremiah 47:5-7; Amos 1:8;
 Zeph. 2:4-7; Zech. 9:5).

c [Ekron] Ekron, the third Philistine city taken by Judah, but not for long
 (Joshua 13:3; Joshua 15:11,45-46; Joshua 19:43; 1 Samuel 5:10).

a [could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had

                            Failure of Judah
This reads as if God could not defeat the inhabitants of the valley because
they had chariots of iron, but this was not so because:

1. The first part of Judges 1:19, "And the Lord was with Judah," should end
   Judges 1:18, showing the reason for the success in conquering the eight
   cities of Judges 1:4-18. The remainder of Judges 1:19 refers to another
   time when Judah failed God and He consequently withdrew His support
   in the effort to drive the Canaanites out of the valley. If God had been
   with Judah in this effort they would have been victorious as in the
   conquests of Judges 1:4-18.

2. Some codices read in Judges 1:19, "did not" instead of "could not," thus
   revealing that Judah failed because they were afraid of the iron chariots
   in the lowlands, having only soldiers on foot. It shows distrust and lack
   of simple and firm reliance upon God and His promises—the only
   grounds for success. The other verses in this chapter expressing failure
   read "did not" or "neither did," proving Judges 1:19 to mean "did not"
   (Judges 1:21,27,28,29,30,31,33).

3. Various translations make the verse clearer. Rotherham says, "took
   possession of the hill country—but did not possess the inhabitants of the
     vale," not because God was powerless, but because they did not put forth
     the proper effort. The Septuagint has, "he (Judah) took possession of the
     mountain, for they were not enabled to drive out the inhabitants of the
     vale, because Rechab dissuaded them." Jonathan ben Uzziel reads, "they
     extirpated the inhabitants of the mountains; but afterwards, when they
     sinned, they were not able to extirpate the inhabitants of the plain
     country, because they had chariots of iron." When they sinned they were
     left to their own strength.

                              Failure of Asher
Asher failed to drive the Canaanites out of seven places (Joshua 19:24-31):

1. Accho, meaning sand-heated; a town on the Syrian border a few miles
   north of Carmel and north of the Haifa bay. It was an important
   stronghold in the times of Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia,
   Greece, Rome, and Syria, but is mentioned only this once in Scripture, as
   being too strong for Asher to overcome (Judges 1:31). During the
   Christian era it was a center of struggle between the Crusaders and
   Saracens and at one time was taken at the expense of 100,000 Crusaders
   and held for 100 years. It was the last Christian stronghold in Palestine in
   A.D. 1291. Since then it has undergone many sieges by the Egyptians,
   French, English, and Turks. It is now the modern city of Acre in Israel.
2. Zidon, fishing. Also called Sidon—a city of Phoenicia (note c, ▪ Joshua
   11:8).

3. Ahlab, fat or fruitful. A small town allotted to Asher.

4. Achzib, lying or disappointing. It was 9 miles north of Accho; it was
   strong and hard to conquer for a people who had no ships. The
   Phoenician cities helped one another in case of attack. Tyre and Zidon
   became very powerful and rich, more so than Accho. Achzib is now
   known as Ez-Zib; it appears in Assyrian inscriptions as Aksibi.

5. Helbah, an unknown town assigned to Asher but not occupied by them.

6. Aphik, another unknown town allotted to Asher, but not occupied by
   them. Called Aphek, strength (Joshua 12:18; Joshua 13:4; Joshua 19:30;
   1 Samuel 4:1; 1 Samuel 29:1; 1 Kings 20:26,30; 2 Kings 13:17). See
     note a, ▪ Joshua 12:18.

7. Rehob, broad; a town in Asher given to the Levites (Joshua 19:28-30;
   Joshua 21:31; 2 Samuel 10:8; 1 Chron. 6:75). Called Bethrehob (Judges
   18:28; 2 Samuel 10:6).

                         God Keeps Covenants
God has kept and always will keep His part of any covenant with any
people. Israel was not cursed with defeat, captivity, dispersion, and
judgment because God broke the covenant; they were to blame. He told
them plainly what He would do if they broke the covenant, so He could not
do otherwise (Leviticus 26; Deut. 28). Even yet, God promises that when
they repent and keep His covenant, He will restore them as in days of old
(Deut. 4:25-31; Deut. 30:1-10; Isaiah 11:10-16; Jeremiah 23:1-8; Jeremiah
30:1-31:40; Jeremiah 32:37-44; Jeremiah 33:3-26; Ezekiel 34:11-31;
Ezekiel 36:1-38; Ezekiel 37:1-28; Amos 9:9-15; Zeph. 3:8-20; Zech. 8:3-
8,20-23; Zech. 12:10-13:9; Zech. 14:14-21; Matthew 24:31; Romans 11:25-
29). God is as quick to accuse and judge when the time comes to do so, as
He is to bless. It is God who charges anyone who transgresses with sin, not
man (Romans 8:33-34; Romans 14:4; 1 Cor. 11:32). If, like Paul, we are
persuaded to let nothing separate us from God, we are secure (Romans
8:35-39); and if we practice Paul's method of keeping the body under
subjection we shall never be a castaway (2 Cor. 9:27); but if we go into sin
we shall die spiritually; and if we persist in sin, refusing to repent and live
righteously, we shall be cut off from God forever (Romans 6:16-23;
Romans 8:12-13; Romans 11:11-29; 2 Cor. 3:16-17; 2 Cor. 6:9-11;
Galatians 5:19-21; Galatians 6:7-8; Hebrews 6:4-9; Hebrews 10:26-29; 2
Peter 2:20-21). See Backsliding.

a [when Joshua had let the people go ...] These verses introduce the long
    record of apostasies and judgments listed in Judges. As long as Israel
    served God, He caused them to prosper; but when they forsook Him, He
    no longer blessed them. Instead He permitted defeat, servitude to their
    enemies, and various judgments to whip them into line again, seeking to
    save the nation from the destruction He had promised if they backslid and
    rebelled. Judges is a record of repeated sins, apostasy, judgment, with
    temporary repentance—as long as a leader was alive whom God raised up
    to deliver Israel from their enemies. This program went on for 520 years
    under judges, then continued for another 513 years under kings—until the
    nation was destroyed and taken into captivity (Judges 2:11-2 Chron. 36).

a [hot] Hebrew: charah (HSN-2734), to be hot or furious; to burn; be
    incensed. God is spoken of as becoming hot in anger ten times (Judges
    2:14; Judges 3:8; Judges 6:39; Judges 10:7; Exodus 22:24; Exodus 32:10-
    11,22; Deut. 9:19; Psalm 6:1; Psalm 38:1). Four reasons for this:

1. Oppressing widows, orphans, and strangers (Exodus 22:21-24)

2. Stubbornness and idolatry (Judges 2:11-15; Judges 3:7-8; Judges 10:6-
   18; Exodus 32:8-11; Deut. 9:19-22)

3. Forsaking and forgetting Him (Judges 2:12; Judges 3:7)

4. Sin (Psalm 6:1; Psalm 38:1-5)
b [delivered them into the hands of spoilers] This is the beginning of
    many defeats of Israel under judges, kings, and even during the restoration
    from captivity. See Victories, Civil Wars, and Defeats of Israel.

c [sold] Hebrew: makar (HSN-4376), to sell a daughter in marriage or
    slavery; to surrender or give over. This was God's way of saying that He
    gave Israel over to their enemies to punish them for backsliding (Judges
    3:8; Judges 4:2; Judges 10:7; Deut. 28:68; Deut. 32:30; 1 Samuel 12:9;
    Esther 7:4; Psalm 44:12). The word is also used of men selling or giving
    themselves over to do evil (1 Kings 21:20,35; 2 Kings 17:17; Isaiah 50:1;
    Isaiah 52:3), of selling slaves (Genesis 25:33; Genesis 37:28,36; Genesis
    45:4; Deut. 15:12; Psalm 105:17; Jeremiah 34:14), and selling
    merchandise (Deut. 14:21; Ruth 4:3; 2 Kings 4:7; Neh. 13:15,16; Proverbs
    31:24).

d [could not any longer stand before their enemies] Formerly, when
    Israel was obedient no man could stand before them (Deut. 7:27; Deut.
    11:25; Joshua 1:5; Joshua 10:8; Joshua 23:9), but now in disobedience
    they could not stand before any man (Leviticus 26:27).

                            A New Kind of War
How could an unarmed army of 10,000 defeat a well-armed one with 900
chariots of iron? The Vulgate gives an interesting translation of this verse:
"The Lord chose a new species of war, and himself subverted the gates of
the enemy." What was this new kind of war? In the first place a woman
gave the orders and directed the war by prophecy (Judges 4:6-14). Then,
God put it into the hearts of 10,000 unarmed men to have faith to overcome
a greater, well-armed company. This was a great miracle in itself, for later
under Gideon, there were only 300 who showed this kind of faith (Judges
7:5-25). Barak retired to Mount Tabor with the 10,000 men, and they were
attacked by Sisera's well-armed men. Suddenly Barak and his men rushed
upon them and God began to act, causing terror and confusion throughout
the Canaanite army who threw down their arms to flee. The routing was
instantaneous and complete, the Israelites picking up the arms of their
enemies and slaying them as they ran away. Even Sisera, no longer safe in a
chariot, fled on foot. The entire army was slain by men and the captain by a
woman. This was the new "species" of war that brought deliverance in
Israel.

                Ten Statements about the Ten Tribes
According to various versions the statements of Judges 5:14-17 are highly
poetical. They could be rendered as follows:

1. Ephraim moved into the valley whose root is in the mountains formerly
   possessed by Amalek. Deborah was from Ephraim, so naturally some
   from Ephraim followed her in this battle with the Canaanites.

2. Benjamin followed Ephraim among the people to war against Sisera.

3. Commanders came from Machir (eastern Manasseh).

4. From Zebulun came those who carry the pen of the writer (Septuagint,
   marshal's staff).

5. Issachar's princes rallied to Deborah (Judges 5:15).

6. Naphtali supported Barak, following close at his heels.

7. Reuben made great resolutions to help their brethren, but because of
   great deliberations between their factions they let opportunity slip
   (Judges 5:15-16).

8. Gad of the land of Gilead remained beyond Jordan (Judges 5:17).

9. Dan remained by his ships.

10. Asher remained by the seashore and clung to his bays.

The first four tribes—Reuben, Gad, Dan, and Asher, along with Judah and
Simeon who are not mentioned—failed to help their brethren in this
struggle with the Canaanites. The 10,000 men who fought came only from
Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali. From
some of these came but a few, the most being from Naphtali which was the
tribe of Barak (Judges 4:6), and Zebulun (Judges 5:18).

                  Eightfold Purpose of Deborah's Song
The song of Deborah seems to have been both religious and political:

1. To thank God for the recent victory over the Canaanites and the
   deliverance of Israel from twenty years of defeat and oppression (Judges
   5:1-8; Judges 4:3).

2. To celebrate the zeal and bravery of the rulers and people of certain tribes
   who had faith in God and had volunteered their services against a
     common foe (Judges 5:9-15,18-19).

3. To rebuke the unbelief and lukewarmness of certain tribes who stayed at
   home, betraying the public cause of the people of God (Judges 5:15-17).

4. To honor God for His supernatural part in the uneven struggle between
   two earthly foes (Judges 5:20-22).

5. To curse those who refused to take part in the battle (Judges 5:23).

6. To bless the woman who was bold enough to slay Sisera (Judges 5:24-
   27).

7. To show the disappointment and anguish of the mother of Sisera (Judges
   5:28-30).

8. To pronounce a blessing upon the people of God and a curse upon their
   enemies (Judges 5:31).

b [let all thine enemies perish] See Psalm 45:5; Psalm 60:12; Psalm 66:3;

    might] Twofold contrast:

1. Let God's enemies perish.

2. Let His friends shine forth in glory as the sun in all his might.

                           Gideon's Battle Plan
Never in history has there been a more seemingly foolish plan of battle.
Evidently, God gave Gideon these instructions and he was simply carrying
them out to the letter. He was content after four signs that God would give
the victory. The plan was simple:

1. Divide the 300 men into 3 companies.

2. Put a trumpet in the hand of every man, with an empty pitcher, and a
   lamp burning within the pitcher.

3. Surround the camp of the enemy and do exactly as the leader did. When
   he blew the trumpet all should do so, breaking the pitchers, holding the
   lamps in their left hands, and crying, "The sword of the Lord and of
   Gideon" (Judges 7:17-20).

Imagine 301 trumpets (counting Gideon's) blasting all at once when the
whole camp of the enemy was asleep, then waking to see 301 lamps
burning all around the camp, and hearing the breaking of pitchers and 301
loud voices crying, "The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon." This would be
startling in itself without the added confusion produced supernaturally by
the Lord. The Midianites, believing that a huge army had suddenly made an
attack, fled in all directions.

b [lamps] These lamps were torches, which would smoulder in a jar or
    pitcher, and burst into flame when taken out and waved.

                                Abimelech
Abimelech, father of a king; he was the son of Gideon through a concubine
living at Shechem (Judges 8:31). He was one of five men by this name
(Judges 9:1; Genesis 20 and Genesis 26; 1 Samuel 21:10-22:1; 1 Chron. 18
and 1 Chron. 24). Israel had declared that Gideon, his son, and his son's son
should reign over them (Judges 8:22). Thinking that he had as much right to
this as the other sons, Abimelech sought the support of his mother's people
in Shechem (Judges 9:2-3). He appealed to the city elders who naturally
desired their city to become great. They gave him blood money to hire
assassins to kill the seventy sons of Gideon. These evil men became
Abimelech's followers and killed all but Jotham (Judges 9:4-5), leaving no
rivalry from that source. The people of Shechem then made Abimelech
king. He reigned for three years before being fatally wounded by a woman
(Judges 9:6,22,53).
