a [Jephthah]

               Twenty-three Facts concerning Jephthah
1. He was born in Gilead by his father, Gilead, and a harlot.

2. He was a mighty man of valor.

3. His father's sons cast him out and refused to give him inheritance because
   he was illegitimate (Judges 11:2).

4. He fled from his brethren and dwelled in the land of Tob (Judges 11:3).

5. He became the leader of a band of worthless men who followed him in
   various adventures, during which he learned and perfected the art of war.

6. When war with Ammon was imminent the elders of Israel in Gilead sent
   for him to be captain of the army.
7. He reproved them for casting him out and then seeking his help when
   they were in distress (Judges 11:7).

8. He refused to return home to head the army in war if he could not be the
   head in time of peace (Judges 11:8-9).

9. He was promised headship of all Gilead, if he would come and be captain
   of the army in the war with Ammon (Judges 11:10).

10. He was made head over all Gilead by the people in Mizpeh (Judges
   11:11).

11. He sent messengers to the king of Ammon to avoid war if possible
   (Judges 11:12).

12. His people, Israel, were accused by the Ammonites' king of taking their
   land when coming up out of Egypt about 350 years before; Jephthah was
   told the land should be restored.

13. Jephthah denied the charge, stating the historical facts—that Israel did
   not take the land of Ammon or Moab, and they even went around Edom
   and Moab to avoid war (Judges 11:14-18).

14. He explained that Israel did not even intend to take the land of the
   Amorites, but were forced to fight them because they would not let the
   nation pass through to Canaan (Judges 11:19-22).

15. He informed the king of Ammon that the land Israel possessed did not
   belong to his people and they would not give it to them (Judges 11:23).

16. He told the king that Ammon should be satisfied with their possession
   as Moab had been with theirs, stating that Israel had not tried to enlarge
   their borders at the expense of Edom, Moab, or Ammon, and declaring
   that the Lord should judge between them if he was determined to make
   war (Judges 11:24-27).

17. His appeal had no effect (Judges 11:28).
18. The Spirit of God came upon Jephthah and he swiftly moved to fight
   Ammon (Judges 11:29).

19. He made a rash vow if God would only give him victory (Judges 11:30-
   31).

20. He defeated Ammon (Judges 11:32-33).

21. He fulfilled his vow (Judges 11:34-40).

22. He defeated Ephraim in a civil war and killed 42,000 men (Judges 12:1-
   6).

23. He judged Israel six years, then died and was buried in Gilead (Judges
   12:7).

a [vowed a vow unto the LORD]

                      Two Parts of Jephthah's Vow
1. Dedicate it to God, according to Leviticus 27

2. If suitable, offer it as a burnt sacrifice to Jehovah

According to the most accurate Hebrew scholars, this twofold vow reads: "I
will consecrate it to the Lord, or I will offer it for a burnt offering," meaning
that anything fit for a burnt offering should be made one, and anything fit
for the service of God should be consecrated to Him. Even if this translation
is incorrect, we must understand that such a thought is implied in the vow
since God would NOT accept a human sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; Leviticus
20:2-5), or any animal other than the ox, bullock, lamb, ram, goat, heifer,
pigeon, or turtledove. Therefore, the only thing Jephthah could do was offer
her to the Lord by a perpetual virginity (Judges 11:36-40).

The law of vows (Leviticus 27) provided that persons, beasts, and other
things could be offered to God for holy uses even though all could not be
used for burnt offerings. Furthermore, these could be redeemed with money,
if the vow was a simple one, and the amount given to the priests and
Levites (Leviticus 27:1-25). Other things (as the firstborn of clean animals,
all tithes, and anything dedicated to the Lord as a devoted thing) could not
be redeemed. Devoted things were to remain in the service of God
(Leviticus 27:26-29). It was this nature of vow that Jephthah made to Him,
so he devoted his daughter to God by perpetual virginity—this he was under
obligation to do (Judges 11:35).

                       Proud and Haughty Ephraim
The men of Ephraim always seemed to be proud and haughty, causing
division and strife in Israel.

Eight Strifes Caused by Ephraim:

1. He was the cause of misunderstanding even in the blessing of the sons of
   Joseph by Jacob (Genesis 48:3-22).
2. The tribe complained in the division of the land (Joshua 17:14-18).

3. They contended with Gideon because they were not called by him to
   fight the Midianites (Judges 8:1-3).

4. They contended with Jephthah because they were not considered by him
   in the war with Ammon. In fact, they declared war on him and Israel east
   of the Jordan over such a trivial thing and were defeated, losing 42,000
   men (Judges 12:1-6).

5. They joined others in the division of the kingdom in the days of David
   and Ishbosheth (2 Samuel 2:8-11).

6. They joined the revolt against David under Absalom (2 Samuel 17:26).

7. They revolted with ten tribes against David in the matter of jealousy over
   bringing him back (2 Samuel 19:43-20:26).

8. They were leaders in the final revolt against the house of David in the
   second and last division of the kingdom of Israel; Ephraim became the
   name of the northern kingdom of Israel as used in many scriptures (1
   Kings 12; Isaiah 7:2-17; Isaiah 11:13; Isaiah 28:1; Ezekiel 37:16-19;

                          Ancient Weddings
It was the custom for a proposal of marriage to come from the family of the
bridegroom, but occasionally this was reversed as in Exodus 2:21; Joshua
15:16-17; 1 Samuel 18:27. There is no evidence of a religious ceremony in
the early marriages. After making a contract for the dowry and any other
business matter, taking the bride to the groom's home was all that remained
to complete the marriage. Isaac simply brought Rebekah to his mother's tent
and they became man and wife (Genesis 24:67). In the case of plural wives
each had a separate tent (Genesis 31:33). Later, marriages were concluded
with festivities, and contracts usually stated a certain length of time
between the agreement and the actual marriage. The average time was
about one year (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:24-38,56-57). Feasts lasting
seven days were a part of some festivities (Judges 14:12-18; Genesis 29:22;
Esther 2:18; Matthew 22:1-14; Rev. 19:1-10). Marriage processions and
noisy demonstrations took place on such occasions (Jeremiah 7:34;
Jeremiah 16:9; Jeremiah 25:10; Jeremiah 33:11; ▪ Matthew 25:1-13, notes;
Rev. 18:23). In N.T. times it was customary for the bridegroom to have
male companions (Judges 14:11) and the bride to have a number of virgins
with her in the wedding festivities (▪ Matthew 25:1-13, notes).

Heading It is impossible to tell exactly when the events of Judges 17-21
    took place, but it seems clear that those of Judges 17-18 happened in
    Joshua's lifetime, for they are referred to in Joshua 19:47-48, soon after
    the division of the land. This would have to be the case if Joshua wrote the
    book by his name. This story is enlarged in Judges 17-18 as a further
    background and an introduction to the happenings of Judges 19-21, which
    seem to have been in the days of the early judges.

                     The Chronology of Judges 17-21
1. According to Joshua 19:40-48, the inheritance of Dan was too small for
   the whole tribe so some went and fought against Leshem and possessed
   it. It was also called Laish (Joshua 18:7,14,27,29), and afterwards called
   Dan after the name of the father of the tribe (Judges 16:29; Joshua
   19:47-48). The taking of Leshem by the Danites is dealt with more fully
   here than in Joshua 19:47.

2. The fact that Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua and the elders
   that outlived him, proves that the terrible moral depravity of Judges 19-
   21 could not have taken place while these men were alive (Joshua
   24:31).

3. In Judges 18:1 it is clear that at least Judges 17-18 refer to a time before
    all the tribe of Dan was fully settled in an inheritance. This would take
    us back to the days of Joshua and the time immediately following his
    death. At the very latest the events should be connected with Judges 1:34
    when all the tribes were becoming adjusted among their neighbors, from
    then to the first apostasy of Israel which made the institution of judges
    necessary (Judges 2:1-3:8).
4. When the events of Judges 19-21 took place, Phinehas was still alive
   (Judges 20:28), and, since he was the third high priest, and a grown man
   at the end of the wilderness wanderings (Numbers 25), the events of
   Judges 19-21 had to be early.

a [Jonathan] Jonathan was the grandson of Moses. His contemporary in
    the high priesthood was Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, mentioned in
    Judges 20:28. Manasseh had no son named Gershom, but Moses did. It is
    believed that Moses was altered to Manasseh in some copies, to preserve
    the honor and memory of the great lawgiver among Israelites. A simple
    suspension of the Hebrew letter nun (n) over the word Mosheh (Moses)
    would change it to Manasseh. Ancient authorities—both Jews and
    Gentiles—agree about this, as do many modern translators. Rotherham,
    Moffatt, Berkeley and others have: "son of Moses." Many commentators
    also agree. Moses' genealogy in 1 Chron. 23:14-16 has Shebuel as the son
    of Gershom. Shebuel, meaning "captive of God," is thought to be the
    name of Jonathan after his repentance (1 Chron. 26:24; also called
    Shubael, 1 Chron. 24:20).

b [he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan] The sons of Jonathan
    were idolatrous priests at Dan until the ark was taken by the Philistines in
    the last year of Eli's life (after which the ark was returned to Shiloh no
    more). Many think that because of this idolatry God does not name Dan in
    the list of the tribes saved during Daniel's 70th week (Rev. 7:1-8), but
    there is no proof for this. All the tribes were guilty of idolatry at various
    times during the more than 1,053 years between Joshua and the
    Babylonian captivity. In fact, this was the reason for the captivity of all
    Israel to Assyria and Babylon (Judges 2:11-15; 2 Kings 17:7-23; 2 Kings
    23:3-20). See Why Dan Not Sealed.

c [captivity of the land] This refers to the Philistines' capture of the ark
    and destruction of the tabernacle in the forty years of Eli (Judges 18:30-
    31; 1 Samuel 4; Psalm 78:60-64; Jeremiah 7:12; Jeremiah 26:6).

                   SUMMARY OF JUDGES
                          ____________________

Date and Place: Written in Palestine about 1126 B.C.

Author: From all indications, Samuel was the author; Jewish tradition
assigns authorship to him. Or, the book may have been written by Isaiah
(see note c, ▪ 2 Chron. 32:32).

Proof of Authorship: Facts regarding events of the book were perhaps
written by the men whose exploits are recorded (or by some scribe in the
tribe to which each judge belonged), then later collected and put in the
present form when the nation was united under a king. From the book itself
it is clear that it was written after Israel had kings, for twice the author
states he was writing of events and things happening in the days before
there was a king in Israel (Judges 19:1; Judges 21:25). The book further
reveals that it was written before the time of David, for the tabernacle was
at Shiloh where it was set in the days of Joshua (Judges 18:31; Judges
21:12,19-21). It remained there until the fortieth year of Eli when it was
destroyed (1 Samuel 4). It was heard of no more until David w as made
king and he brought the tabernacle to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6; 1 Chron.
21:29; 2 Chron. 1:3). In view of these facts, Samuel was the most likely
person to collect all the records of the judges and compile them into one
book.

Theme: The book is a record of Israel's failure during the rule of the judges.
It records 9 apostasies, 7 servitudes, 14 judges and their exploits (not
including those of Eli and Samuel, the 15th and 16th judges, which facts are
in 1 Sam.), and 5 civil wars. The events of Judges cover at least 440 years.
For a chronology, see Dispensation of Law.

Statistics: 7th book of the Bible; 21 chapters; 618 verses; 18,966 words;
585 verses of history; 33 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 92 questions; 23
messages from God (Judges 1:2; Judges 2:1,20; Judges 4:6; Judges
6:8,12,16,20,23,25; Judges 7:2,4,7,9; Judges 10:11; Judges
13:3,11,13,16,18; Judges 20:18,23,28); 71 commands; 26 predictions; and 5
promises.

Time of the Events of Ruth

One thing is clear—the events of Ruth took place in the early days of the
judges, because Ruth 4:21-22 states that Boaz was the son of Salmon who
married Rahab the harlot of Jericho (Matthew 1:5). If Salmon married
Rahab soon after the conquest of Jericho, the event would have to occur at
least during the first 50 to 75 years of the 520 years from Joshua to Saul
(for the chronology of this period, see Dispensation of Law). If Boaz was
born to Salmon late in life and Boaz himself married late in life, the events
would still have to take place in the first 100 years of the 520 years—during
the judgeship of Othniel perhaps (Judges 3:9-11), the 18 years of servitude
to Moab (Judges 3:12-14), or at the latest, during the time of Ehud (Judges
3:15-20). If this is true, we must acknowledge that not all the names of the
men in the genealogy of Christ were given at this point, because we have
only four names in the list from Salmon to the birth of David, and the lives
of four men would not cover that long a period, with the usual span of life
being what it was at that time. It would have required Salmon, Boaz, Obed,
and Jesse to have their children in this genealogy at the average age of 125
which is very unlikely. Bible scholars agree that not all the names of royal
genealogies were always given, nor were they necessary; so it seems wise
to recognize that some names have been omitted (Ruth 4:20-22; Matthew
1:4-6; Luke 3:31-32). See notes, ▪ Matthew 1:8,11.

Parched Corn (Grain)

Parched "corn" was prepared from grains of wheat which were not yet fully
ripe. They were roasted in a pan or iron plate, or sometimes the stalks of
wheat were tied in small bundles and the ears held in a blazing fire until
roasted. Roasted grain was eaten with or without bread. In Leviticus 23:14
it is classed with bread and green ears. In Leviticus 2:14 it is called green
ears of "corn" dried in the fire. It was a common article of food in Palestine
and Egypt. Jesse sent an ephah (five gallons, dry) to the army (1 Samuel
17:17). Abigail gave five measures of it to David's men as a present (1
Samuel 25:18). David was supplied with it in his flight from Absalom (2
Samuel 17:23).

Harvest Time in Israel

The harvests were the most important times of the year in Israel. Events
were reckoned from harvest times (Ruth 1:22; Ruth 2:23; Genesis 30:14;
Joshua 3:15; Judges 15:1; 1 Samuel 6:13; 2 Samuel 21:9; 2 Samuel 23:13).
The three great yearly gatherings of Israel took place at the time of the three
harvest seasons (Exodus 23:16; Exodus 34:21-22):

1. The feasts of the passover, firstfruits, and unleavened bread were held
   every April in connection with the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22; Ruth
   2:17,23; Leviticus 23:4-15).

2. The feast of Pentecost was held seven weeks later at the time of the
   wheat harvest (Exodus 34:22; Leviticus 23:15-22).

3. The feast of tabernacles was held at the end of the year at the time of the
   fruit harvest. The feast of trumpets and the day of atonement preceded
   that of tabernacles, so Israel could gather and remain for all three feasts,
   which were held in October (Leviticus 23:23-44).

Between the barley harvest in April and the wheat harvest in June, most of
the other grains were reaped. The grapes began to ripen in August, but the
gathering to make wine, molasses, and raisins was at the end of September.
Figs and other fruits were also gathered about this time. Then Israel was
ready to attend the last of the great annual feasts. Between the barley and
wheat harvests a few showers of rain fell, helping to ripen the wheat, but
from the wheat harvest to the fruit harvest there was no rain (2 Samuel
21:10; Jeremiah 5:24). The harvesters longed for cool weather during the
reaping season (Proverbs 25:13).

                    SUMMARY OF RUTH
                         ____________________

Date and Place: Written in Palestine in its original form, as a record in
Israel, between 1600-1500 B.C., but in its present form perhaps by Samuel
between 1163-1123 B.C., or by Isaiah 743-683 B.C. (see note at ▪ 2 Chron.
32:32).

Author: Perhaps Samuel or Isaiah, to show the ancestry of David.

Proof of Authorship: There is no definite proof of authorship for Ruth; it
is only supposed that the book was written by Samuel. It was put in its
present form after the rule of the judges (Ruth 1:1).

Theme: The Book of Ruth is a simple historical record of life in Israel
during the judges, illustrating the law of kinsman redemption, recording the
story of a Gentile woman in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, and updating the
genealogy of David—from Pharez to David.

Statistics: the 8th book of the Bible; 4 chapters; 85 verses; 2,575 words; 16
questions; 1st book of the Bible without a prophecy or any particular
message from God by a prophet to Israel; 30 commands and 2 promises.

                                    Temple
Hebrew: heykal (HSN-1964), a large public building, such as a palace or
temple. It is first used here. It is the same word used of Solomon's temple (1
Kings 6:3,5,17,33; 1 Kings 7:21,50; 2 Kings 18:16; 2 Kings 23:4; 2 Kings
24:13; 2 Chron. 3:17; 2 Chron. 4:7-8,22; 2 Chron. 26:16; 2 Chron. 27:2; 2
Chron. 29:16) and of Zerubbabel's temple (Ezra 3:6,10; Ezra 4:1; Neh.
6:10-11). It is used of the temple of the Lord in 41 places in the Psalms and
books of the prophets. Also translated palaces of kings 10 times (1 Kings
21:1; 2 Kings 20:18; Psalm 45:8,15; Psalm 144:12; Proverbs 30:28; Isaiah
13:22; Isaiah 39:7; Daniel 1:4; Nahum 2:6). It is translated temple referring
to the house of the Lord in the days of the judges before Solomon's day (1
Samuel 1:9; 1 Samuel 3:3; 2 Samuel 22:7).

It may be that Israel had built a more permanent house in connection with
the temporary tabernacle of Moses which was made of cloth walls and skin
coverings. It could have been a house for the high priest and others to live
in, for it seems Eli and Samuel lived in one to take care of the daily duties
of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 3:3,5-18). God Himself testified that He had not
dwelt in a permanent house, but in a tent and a tabernacle from the days of
Moses to David (2 Samuel 7:6-7; see 1 Chron. 15:1; 2 Chron. 1:4; Psalm
78:60). It is clear then that the tabernacle of Moses was called a temple of
the Lord (1 Samuel 1:9; 1 Samuel 3:3). See note on ▪ Rev. 11:2 for five past
and future temples of the Lord besides the heavenly temple of Rev. 3:12;
Rev. 7:15; Rev. 11:19; Rev. 14:15,17; Rev. 15:5-8; Rev. 16:1,17; Rev.
21:22. These and the tabernacle (called a temple) make seven temples of
Scripture. There are seven references in the N.T. about believers being the
temple of God, but this by no means does away with the fact of a literal
temple of God in heaven, as in the above scriptures (2 Cor. 3:9-17; 2 Cor.
6:19; 2 Cor. 6:16; Ephes. 2:20-21; Hebrews 3:6; 1 Peter 2:5; 1 Peter 4:17).

                             Hannah's Prayer
The Chaldee reads, "And Hannah prayed in the spirit of prophecy." This
expresses the true nature of the song and prayer. It deals with Hannah (1
Samuel 2:1); God's character and His seventeen acts (1 Samuel 2:2-10); and
warning (1 Samuel 2:3-5). It is poetic and prophetic and takes its place
along with the songs of Moses, Miriam, Deborah, David, Elizabeth, Mary
and other psalmists and prophets whose inspired utterances have been
recorded in the Bible. These songs each sprang forth from the individual's
personal experience, then widened to include the nature and acts of God,
and the glories of the coming kingdom of the Messiah and of God among
men in all eternity, making reference to things of the future. See Eight
Songs of Praise in Scripture.

b [My heart rejoiceth in the LORD ...] The 1st prophecy in 1 Samuel (1
    Samuel 2:1-10; 1 Samuel 2:1-8 fulfilled and being fulfilled among men; 1
    Samuel 2:9-10 future). Next, ▪ 1 Samuel 2:27.

   Samuel 2:6,9; Matthew 25:30; Jude 1:13)

7. Out of heaven shall the Lord thunder upon His enemies (1 Samuel 2:10;

1. My heart rejoices in the Lord

2. My horn is exalted in the Lord

c [horn is exalted in the LORD] Some say this refers to the long horns
 women used to wear on their heads to hold their veils. These were 6 to 30
 inches long and several inches wide at the base, tapering to a point. This
 can't be the reference though, in view of how the word is used elsewhere.
 Here Hannah's horn was exalted.
                           Horns in Scripture
Five Exalted Horns of Scripture:

1. Hannah's (1 Samuel 2:1)

2. Messiah's (1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 89:24)

3. Israel's (Psalm 89:17; Psalm 148:14)

4. Horn of an unknown psalmist (Psalm 92:10)

5. Horn of righteous (Psalm 75:10; Psalm 112:9)

Ten Examples, Debased Horns of Scripture:

1. Job's horn defiled (Job 16:15)

2. Horn of Moab cut off (Jeremiah 48:25)

3. Horn of Israel cut off (Lament. 2:3)

4. Horns of Gentiles cast out (Zech. 1:18-21)

5. Horns of Judah scattered (Zech. 1:21)

6. The three of ten horns that fell (Daniel 7:20-24)

7. Little horn destroyed (Daniel 7:11,21-27)

8. The two horns broken off (Daniel 8:7)

9. Great horn broken off (Daniel 8:21-22)

10. The ten horns overcome (Rev. 17:12-14)

Ten Victorious Horns of Scripture:

1. David's horn to bud (Psalm 132:17)
2. Horn of Israel to bud (Ezekiel 29:21)

3. Zion's horn like iron (Micah 4:13)

4. Horn of salvation raised up (2 Samuel 22:3; Psalm 18:2; Luke 1:69)

5. Horns of Joseph push the people to the ends of the earth (Deut. 33:17)

6. Horns of God coming out of His hand (Habakkuk 3:4-16) to drive
   asunder the nations

7. Little horns subduing and plucking up three others (Daniel 7:8,24)

8. Great horn broke two horns (Daniel 8:7)

9. Horns of Gentiles scattered Judah

10. The horn of David (Messiah) shall overcome all nations and bud in the
   earth (1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 89:24; Psalm 132:17-18; Rev. 17:12-14;
   Rev. 19:11-21)

From all these facts it is clear that a horn in figurative statements refers to
power, authorty, and kingship. Here Hannah was merely ascribing
exaltation to her King and Messiah because He had overcome His enemies
and brought salvation or deliverance to Israel (1 Samuel 2:1,10).

                               Man of God
God always has His man when one is needed to go on some special mission
for Him. He can and does move in every crisis of human history to warn,
rebuke, judge, and otherwise intervene in the affairs of men. Moses was the
first to be called "man of God" (Deut. 33:1; Psalm 90, title). It was a term
among the common people for a prophet who was a spokesman for God
(Exodus 4:16; Exodus 7:1). The term is found 78 times in Scripture.

Six Qualifications of a Man of God:

1. Know Scriptures (2 Tim. 3:15-17)

2. Be perfect (2 Tim. 3:17)

3. Be throughly furnished unto all good works (2 Tim. 3:17)

4. Inspired by the Holy Spirit (2 Tim. 3:16-17; Neh. 9:30; Numbers 11:16-
    29)

5. God making Himself known to him (Numbers 12:6; Ezekiel 3:17;
   Jeremiah 15:19)

6. Qualified to act in God's stead as if God Himself were acting. In fact, on
   some occasions, God Himself was called "man of God" (Judges 13:6,8-
   22)

Twelve Persons Called "Man of God":

1. Moses (Deut. 33:1; Joshua 14:6; 1 Chron. 23:14; 2 Chron. 30:16; Ezra
   3:2; Psalm 90, title)

2. God (Judges 13:6,8-22)

3. An unknown prophet (1 Samuel 2:27)

4. Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6-10)

                               God's Promise
God did promise that the priesthood should continue in the family of Aaron
forever (Exodus 29:9; Exodus 40:15; Numbers 25:10-13). It appears that
the promise was absolute but, like all other such promises, it was
conditioned by obedience; the family of Eli reaped for disobedience. Many
times God has plainly stated the conditions of blessing and cursing, and
these apply to all men alike—including priests (Leviticus 26; Deut. 28).
God cannot and will not bless any man who backslides and lives in sin
contrary to the covenants made with Him. God is as obligated to curse those
who sin as He is to bless those who do not; this is true under both law and
grace. See Backsliding.

b [but now the LORD saith] God's plan for an everlasting priesthood
 changed (1 Samuel 2:30,35).

                     Ten Examples of "But Now"
1. We remember the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic, but
   now our soul is dried away (Numbers 11:5-6)

2. I promised you an everlasting priesthood, but now be it far from Me to do
    this (1 Samuel 2:30)

3. I sent you without purse, scrip, and shoes, but now take them (Luke
    22:35-36)

4. You were free from righteousness, but now you are free from sin
   (Romans 6:20-22)

5. The law had you bound, but now you are delivered from it (Romans 7:1-
   6)

6. You were afar from God, but now in Christ you are made near (Ephes.
   2:12-13)

7. You were in darkness, but now are you light in the Lord (Ephes. 5:8)

8. You walked one time in sins, but now you put off all these (Col. 3:7-10)

9. You were not a people of God, but now are the people of God (1 Peter
   2:10)
10. You had not obtained mercy, but now you have (1 Peter 2:10)

See 17 other "but now's" in Scripture (2 Kings 3:15; Job 4:5; Job 16:7; Job
35:15; John 8:40; Romans 3:21; Romans 16:26; 2 Cor. 12:20; 2 Cor. 8:22; 2
Cor. 12:6; Galatians 4:9; Phil. 2:12).

                                   Vision
The Hebrew: chazown (HSN-2377) occurs 35 times, always translated
"vision" (1 Samuel 3:1; 1 Chron. 17:15; 2 Chron. 32:32; Psalm 89:19;
Proverbs 29:18; Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 29:7; Jeremiah 14:14; Jeremiah 23:16;
Lament. 2:9; Ezekiel 7:13,26; Ezekiel 12:22-27; Ezekiel 13:16; Daniel
1:17; Daniel 8:1-2,13,15-17,26; Daniel 9:21,24; Daniel 10:14; Daniel
11:14; Hosea 12:10; Obadiah 1:1; Micah 3:6; Nahum 1:1; Habakkuk 2:2-3;
cp. Daniel 2:19,28; Daniel 4:5,9-10,13; Daniel 7:1-2,7,13,15 where chezev
(HSN-2376) means the same as chazown (HSN-2377)).
God often used vision or mental pictures to impart revelation to men.
Objects were seen as in a dream, whether men were asleep (Isaiah 29:7;
Daniel 2:19,28; Daniel 4:9; Daniel 7:1-2,7,13; Daniel 8:18), in a trance with
their eyes open (Numbers 24:4,16; Acts 10:10; Acts 11:5; Acts 22:17), in
deep meditation (Jeremiah 23:16), in prayer (Daniel 9:21-24; Daniel 10:2-
21), or in the course of duty while awake (Matthew 17:1-9; Luke 1:22;
Luke 24:23; Acts 9:10-12; Acts 10:3,17-19; Acts 12:9; Rev. 1:10; Rev. 4:1-
2; Isaiah 6; Ezekiel 1:1; Ezekiel 8:3; Ezekiel 40:2; Ezekiel 43:3). Whether
one was asleep or awake when he saw a vision, the image or picture came
to the mind, and the message of God was always clear. Whatever was
predicted always happened or will yet happen in accordance with the
vision. Both visions and dreams are referred to as means of revelation from
God (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). See Dreams and Twenty-one Men Who Had
Visions From God.

                         All Israel Knew Samuel
All Israel was conscious of the fact that Samuel was God's chosen leader in
place of Eli and the priests. Never did a priest of Eli's house rule in Israel
again as judge or king. All in his family were either under Samuel, the last
judge, or under kings until the house of Eli was destroyed (1 Kings 2:26-
27). Israel turned to Samuel instead of anyone left of the house of Eli (1
Samuel 1:20; 1 Samuel 7:1-17). To say that Samuel was the first of the
prophets and the last of the judges is only half true; for, whereas there was
no other judge after him, there were other prophets before him (1 Samuel
2:27; Genesis 20:7; Exodus 7:1; Deut. 18:18; Deut. 34:10; Judges 6:8; Acts
3:21). His own mother was a prophetess, and so was Miriam as well as
Deborah (1 Samuel 2:1-10; Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4).

                            Locations of the Ark
We never read of the worship of God at Shiloh after the capture of the ark,
and it was never returned to Shiloh. It remained in Kirjath-jearim for twenty
years (1 Samuel 7:1-2). It is mentioned once in the record of Saul's reign (1
Samuel 14:18). In David's reign it was brought to Jerusalem from Gibeah (2
Samuel 6; 1 Chron. 6:31; 1 Chron. 13:1-14; 1 Chron. 15:1-29; 1 Chron.
16:1-37; 1 Chron. 17:1; 2 Chron. 1:4). The tabernacle was also in Jerusalem
at that time (2 Samuel 7:2; 2 Samuel 11:11). The ark was taken with David
in his flight from Absalom and then brought again to Jerusalem (2 Samuel
15:24-29). Solomon brought it into the temple after its completion (1 Kings
8; 1 Chron. 22:19; 1 Chron. 28:2,18; 2 Chron. 5:1-10; 2 Chron. 6:11,41; 2
Chron. 8:11; 2 Chron. 35:3). The ark remained there until the Babylonian
captivity, at which time Jeremiah is thought to have hidden it in a cave
where it was supposed to remain, it is said, until the coming of the Messiah
(Jeremiah 3:16; 2 Macc. 2:1-7).

b [Hophni and Phinehas, were slain] A fulfillment of 1 Samuel 2:31-34.

                            Shortened Lifespan
The span of life has shortened much since the Antediluvian Age when men
lived to be almost 1,000 years old (Genesis 5; Genesis 9:29). Immediately
following the flood they lived 500 to 600 years (Genesis 11:10-17); then
200 to 230 years (Genesis 11:18-23). Later the span dropped to 140 to 205
years (Genesis 11:24-32; Genesis 25:7,17; Genesis 35:28; Genesis 47:28;
Job 42:16); and then to 110 to 120 years (Genesis 50:26; Deut. 34:7; Joshua
24:29). Finally, the average ages dropped to between 80 and 100 (1 Samuel
4:15; Luke 2:37). Now, with modern, fast-paced lifestyles, lifespans are
even lower.

                 Eight Miracles Because of the Ark
1. The overthrow of Dagon. God evidently sent an angel who toppled
   Dagon from his pedestal onto his face before the ark of the Lord as if in

Heading [Beginning of Israel under kings]

    Harmony of 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, 1 Kings and 2 Kings, and
                  1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles
For a better understanding of 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, 1 Kings and 2 Kings,
and 1 Chron. and 2 Chron., there are 115 harmonies of events noted in the
headings of the text in these books. Like the four Gospels—Matthew, Mark,
Luke, and John—they can and should be harmonized. The books of
Chronicles (originally one book) are entirely independent of the books of
Samuel and Kings. Bible critics often create their own difficulties, and have
done so with these books by assuming that they should be alike; because
they are not it is supposed there are descrepancies. Samuel and Kings give
the events from the human, historical, and chronological standpoint as
viewed by the natural man. Chronicles, on the other hand, gives the Divine,
moral, and spiritual viewpoint—things viewed by God without regard to
chronology which is sometimes ignored to emphasize the moral, religious,
and spiritual causes or consequences of the historical facts. Samuel and
Kings give the complete history of both kingdoms of Israel, while
Chronicles gives only the history as it relates to the house of David and the
ruling tribe of Judah, as being founded on God's covenant with David and
his seed. See Notes on Chronicles.

                           God Rejected by Israel
Samuel, like all men of God, went immediately to Him in prayer. The Lord
told him to do as the people had requested, saying, "they have not rejected
you, but Me" (1 Samuel 8:6-8). God recognized that these were a stubborn
people determined to have what they set their hearts on, and that being
rejected as their King was not as bad as being forsaken by them to serve
other gods—a sin they had been committing since leaving Egypt (1 Samuel
8:8). God further instructed Samuel to protest their choice and make it plain
to them that this would increase their burdens, being more costly than the
present theocracy which was a simple form of government requiring only
faith and dependence on God (1 Samuel 8:9-18). Regardless of this, Israel
was determined to have their king (1 Samuel 8:19-22).

What could be more clear! Saul was a partaker of the Holy Spirit and
genuinely converted, born again, redeemed, and made a new creature at this
time.

Five Spiritual Blessings of Saul:

1. The Spirit of God came upon him (1 Samuel 10:6,10-13; 1 Samuel 11:6)

2. He prophesied (1 Samuel 10:6,10-13)

3. He was turned to another man (1 Samuel 10:6)

4. God was with him (1 Samuel 10:7)

5. God gave him another heart (1 Samuel 10:9)

Fifteen Steps in Saul's Downfall:

1. He intruded into the priest's office (1 Samuel 13:8-10)
2. He made excuse for his sin of breaking the commandment of God (1
   Samuel 13:11-12)

3. Again broke the commandment of God which called for the destruction

4. Lied to Samuel about obeying God in destroying the Amalekites (1
   Samuel 15:13-20)

6. Became exalted, not staying small in his own sight (1 Samuel 15:17)

a [Nahash the Ammonite]

                          Nahash the Ammonite
Nahash means serpent. There are three in Scripture: an Ammonite king (1
Samuel 11:1-2; 1 Samuel 12:12); another Ammonite king (2 Samuel 10:2; 2
Samuel 17:27; 1 Chron. 19:1-2); and the mother of David and Abigail (2
Samuel 17:25 with 1 Chron. 2:13-17).
Nahash was a very proud and haughty man, a bitter enemy of Israel who
wanted the land back which Sihon and Og had taken from his people, the
Ammonites, before Israel came out of Egypt (Numbers 21:21-35; Deut.
2:19,37; Deut. 3:11,16; Joshua 12:2; Joshua 13:10,25; Judges 3:13). The
Ammonites had helped oppress Israel in the sixth servitude for eighteen
years and were then defeated by Jephthah (Judges 10-11). Feeling strong
enough to take vengeance now, they imposed terms of putting out the right
eyes of all the Jabesh-gileadites as a perpetual reproach against Israel (1
Samuel 11:2-3). Messengers were sent to Saul telling of their fate. When he
heard the terms the Spirit of God came upon him, and he assured the men of
Jabesh they would have immediate help. He took a yoke of oxen, cut them
in pieces, and warned Israel that this would be the fate of their oxen if they
did not come at once to help him against the Ammonites (1 Samuel 11:4-7).
He acted in his own name and that of Samuel who also went with the army
in this war (1 Samuel 11:12-15). The fear of God fell upon Israel, so
330,000 men of Israel came with one accord to do their duty. They fought
under Saul against Ammon and God gave them complete victory (1 Samuel
11:8-11).

b [thrust out all your right eyes] Putting out their right eyes rendered
    them permanently useless as soldiers. The right eye was used to look at
    the enemy over the shield. Israel would have been easy to conquer had
    such injury come to their soldiers, and the enemy would have reproached
    them and made slaves out of them all their days.

a [renew the kingdom]

                         The Kingdom Renewed
Saul had not been anointed before all Israel when he was chosen king (1
Samuel 10:24-27), only privately by Samuel (1 Samuel 10:1). Now Samuel
took the occasion of victory and the pride of all Israel in their king to anoint
him in public. This is what is really meant by renewing the kingdom at
Gilgal. Josephus says that Saul was anointed a second time at this
convocation. Here we read that "they made Saul king before the Lord" (1
Samuel 11:15); that is, they fully accepted him as their king, and Samuel
anointed him in the presence of all the people, offering peace offerings and
holding a great feast in honor of him (1 Samuel 11:14-15). The Septuagint
reads, "Samuel anointed Saul to be king, before the Lord." The second
anointing is plainly implied in the term "made Saul king." David was
anointed to be king three times:

1. In a private family gathering (1 Samuel 16:1-13)

2. When he was made king of Judah by the elders (2 Samuel 2:4)

3. When he was made king over all Israel (2 Samuel 5:3)

been faithful to tell of the goodness as well as the failures of men. This
proves it has been divinely inspired, for no man would record his own
deeds of failure and evil without being inspired by God to do so.

a [no smith found throughout all the land of Israel]

                             No Smith Found
The Philistines had taken all the smiths from Israel lest they arm themselves
with swords and spears. All the Israelites had were files; they even had to
go to Philistia to get their farm tools repaired. It can be seen from this what
lack of preparation Israel experienced when trying to fight such a large and
well-equipped army (see note b, ▪ 1 Samuel 13:15). Not even the few
hundred with Saul and Jonathan had swords or spears, none except the two
leaders (1 Samuel 13:19-23). Under these circumstances it seemed
absolutely impossible for Israel ever to be a free and victorious people
again. They wouldn't have been except for God who supernaturally helped
them and gave the victory (1 Samuel 13:12-46). It's not hard to see why
Saul's army hid themselves in dens, caves, and other places. Even with
bows, arrows, and slings to throw stones they couldn't hope to win, looking
at things from the natural viewpoint. How Israel got in this condition under
Samuel is not stated; they had defeated the Philistines over twenty years
earlier (1 Samuel 7:1-14). Perhaps Philistia began to retake Israel little by
little without opposition, until Israel was destitute. Israel should have been
well equipped after defeating the Ammonites and taking all their weapons
(1 Samuel 11:1-15)—unless the events of 1 Samuel 13:1-14:52 were before
the war with the Ammonites, which is entirely possible. If so, then Israel
got military equipment from the defeated Philistines to fight the Ammonites
with later.

a [pomegranate tree]

                              Pomegranates
The pomegranate tree or shrub grows ten to fifteen feet tall. Its oval leaves
fall in winter, and it has brilliant scarlet blossoms in the spring. Its fruit,
which is ripe in September, is apple-shaped and yellowish brown with a
blush of red. The rind is hard and the fruit consists of hundreds of juicy
white and purplish seeds packed together with white partitions like an
orange. The juice was used in ancient times as a syrup for flavoring drinks,
and also made into wine (Song 8:2). The rind was used for medicine and for
tanning hides, particularly in the making of genuine Morocco leather. Both
the orchard in bloom and the opened fruit were considered beautiful (Song
4:3,13; Song 6:7; Song 7:12). The tree grows wild in Palestine, Syria,
Persia, Arabia, Egypt, and parts of Europe and Africa. It is referred to in
Scripture 31 times. Pomegranates were alternated with gold bells on the
bottom of the priest's garment (Exodus 28:33-34; Exodus 39:24-25). Hiram
worked metal pomegranates into the temple art work (1 Kings 7:18-20,42; 2
Kings 25:17; 2 Chron. 3:16; 2 Chron. 4:13; Jeremiah 52:22-23).
Pomegranate fruit was brought back from Canaan by the spies (Numbers
13:23). It is mentioned along with other fruits of that land in a number of
places (Numbers 20:5; Deut. 8:8; Joel 1:12; Habakkuk 2:19).

This was in direct disobedience to the command of 1 Samuel 15:1-3.

                              Saul Inexcusable
The commandment was so clear that there was no excuse for Saul or the
people to violate it through covetousness—sparing all that was good and
destroying only that which was vile and refuse (1 Samuel 15:8-9). God
indicted Saul for his sin of turning back from following Him and in refusing
to obey His commandments (1 Samuel 15:10-11). Saul lied to Samuel
saying, "I have performed the commandment of the Lord" (1 Samuel 15:12-
13). When confronted by Samuel as to what was meant by the sheep
bleating and the cattle lowing if he had obeyed God's commandment, Saul
excused himself and blamed the people for sparing the best of the stock to
use as sacrifices to the Lord (1 Samuel 15:14-15).

The last time before this that Samuel rebuked Saul, it was for disobedience,
at which time he was rejected as king; and at that time Samuel himself was
accused of being to blame, for not showing up on time as he had promised
(1 Samuel 13:1-15). Here again Samuel announced the sin of Saul, but Saul
again maintained that he had obeyed the voice of the Lord—that he did
destroy all the Amalekites except the king, and that the people were to
blame for saving the best of the stock (1 Samuel 15:16-21). Once again
Samuel announced the rejection of Saul as king (1 Samuel 15:22-23).

After all this Saul acknowledged he had sinned, the reason being that he
feared the people and obeyed their voice (1 Samuel 15:24). He begged for
pardon, asking Samuel to turn again to him so he could worship the Lord,
but Samuel refused and still another time announced his rejection as king (1
Samuel 15:25-26). When Samuel turned to go away Saul laid hold of his
mantle and it tore (1 Samuel 15:27). Samuel then told Saul the Lord had
torn the kingdom from him that day, giving it to his neighbor; and assured
him that God would not change His mind in the matter (1 Samuel 15:28-
29). Saul again repented, begging Samuel at least to honor him before the
elders and let him worship the Lord once more. Samuel relented this much
and permitted Saul to worship (1 Samuel 15:30-31), then commanded that
Agag be killed before he left (1 Samuel 15:32-33). Samuel went home
mourning for Saul, and did not come back to him as long as he lived (1
Samuel 15:34-35).

 prophecy of Balaam which suggests an Agag was a mighty king in the
 earth (Numbers 24:7,20). Another Agag is mentioned here as the leader of
 the people who had been Israel's first enemy after leaving Egypt (1
 Samuel 15:8-9,20,32-33; Exodus 17:8-16; Deut. 25:17-19).

c [every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly] Two
 things Saul did destroy:
1. The common people of Amalek (1 Samuel 15:8)

2. Everything vile and worthless (1 Samuel 15:9)

d [vile and refuse] This means all the stock that was worthless and all the
    goods that weren't fit to save. A selfish and covetous man like Saul would
    save only the beautiful and useful things.

                        God's Choice of David
God had evidently directed Samuel to have each of Jesse's sons pass before
him, speaking in his ear in each case to say this was not the right one (1
Samuel 16:7-10; 1 Samuel 9:15). When none were chosen Samuel knew
something was wrong, because he had been directed to anoint one of Jesse's
family as king. Upon inquiring he learned of another son who had been too
busy to come to the feast. He was young and perhaps smaller than the
others, but he was chosen by God who was looking on the heart and not the
outward appearance. The Lord saw in him a man after His own heart (1
Samuel 13:14; 1 Samuel 16:7). David was the youngest of Jesse's eight
sons. He became a mighty man of valor (1 Samuel 16:18). He is referred to
many times as a mighty warrior and able to do more than many others in
combat. He killed a lion and a bear even as a youth (1 Samuel 17:34-36).
His own mighty men acknowledged that he was worth 10,000 of them in
war (2 Samuel 18:3). As to physical appearance, in youth he is described as
ruddy, of a beautiful countenance, and good to look at (1 Samuel 16:13). He
had the true qualities of a king, but compared to his grown-up brothers he
was not even counted important enough to be urged to attend the feast (1
Samuel 16:7-11).

b [the Spirit of the LORD]

                           Transfer of Spirits
In contrast with the Spirit of the Lord coming upon David from that day
forward (1 Samuel 16:13), the same Holy Spirit departed from Saul, and an
evil spirit troubled him (1 Samuel 16:14). This is evidence again that one
who returns to sin may lose the Holy Spirit. Saul lost Him after having Him
on his life for several years (1 Samuel 10:6,9-13; 1 Samuel 11:6; 1 Samuel
13:1). David believed such was possible, for he prayed for God not to take
the Spirit from him (Psalm 51:11). Lucifer, fallen angels, demons, Adam
and Eve, and many others are examples of sin causing one to lose what he
has been given by the Lord. See Twenty-one Examples of Beings Fallen
From Grace and Backsliding.

c [departed from Saul]

                  Holy Spirit Departing From Saul
Not only the Holy Spirit, but God Himself had also departed from Saul (1
Samuel 18:12). The same was true of Samson—God departed from him
(Judges 16:20).
Six Divine Things Can Depart From Man:

1. God Himself (1 Samuel 18:12; 1 Samuel 28:15-16; Judges 16:20; Hosea
   9:12)

2. The Holy Spirit (1 Samuel 16:14; Psalm 51:11)

3. God's glory (1 Samuel 4:21-22; Ezekiel 10:18)

4. God's Word (Deut. 4:9; Proverbs 3:21; Proverbs 4:21; ▪ Hebrews 2:1,
   notes)

5. God's soul (Jeremiah 6:8; Hebrews 10:38-39)

6. God's mercy (2 Samuel 7:15)

Five Divine Things Man Can Depart From:

1. God Himself (Jeremiah 17:5,13; Isaiah 59:13; Hosea 1:2; Hebrews 3:12)

2. God's Word (Proverbs 5:7)

3. Following the Lord (2 Chron. 34:33)

4. The way of the Lord (Malachi 2:8)

5. The faith (1 Tim. 4:1)

d [evil spirit from the LORD]

                            Evil Spirit From God
Evil spirits come from God only in the sense of being permitted by Him to
trouble those who are backslidden and persist in sin and rebellion (1 Samuel
16:14; 1 Kings 22:21-24; 2 Chron. 18:20-23). The idea is that God does not
protect such a person from spirits as He otherwise would if he yielded to
Him. God gave Saul over to an evil spirit as punishment for his sins and
self-will. Naturally, when the Holy Spirit left him he was open to an evil
spirit of torment from Satan.

                               Order of Events
Since 1 Samuel 16:14-23 comes chronologically between 1 Samuel 19:9
and 1 Samuel 19:10 (see True Chronological Events), this 1 Samuel 17:15
must refer to David helping his three brothers to the army with their
equipment and returning to his father again. This seems clear from the fact
that it says, "the three eldest followed Saul (went to be in Saul's army). But
David (who helped them get to the valley of Elah with their camp
equipment and weapons) went and returned from Saul to feed his father's
sheep at Bethlehem" (1 Samuel 17:14-15). Some days later, after Israel was
mobilized, and at the end of about forty more days, David was sent back to
the army to see how his brothers were faring and to take them provisions. It
was then that he found Goliath defying the army of God and of Israel (1
Samuel 17:16-29).

Some versions suggest David went back and forth from Saul's army and his
father's home to herd the sheep. He could have done so to supply his
brothers on several occasions during the time the army was being mobilized
and during the forty days Goliath was defying them. On the fortieth day
when the army seemed to be in commotion, perhaps getting ready to attack
the Philistines, David, who had come to see his brothers, found out what
Goliath was doing and saying (1 Samuel 17:14-28). He then offered to fight
the giant if no other man in Israel would do so (1 Samuel 17:30-37). He had
not yet met Saul but did so when he made this offer (1 Samuel 17:30-40).
While he went to face Goliath Saul asked Abner who he really was (1
Samuel 17:41-56). These facts should harmonize the seeming discrepancies
of David being with Saul to play for him (1 Samuel 16:14-23), of his
leaving the camp of Saul to go home (1 Samuel 17:14-15), and of Saul
being ignorant of ever meeting David before (1 Samuel 17:30-58).

                 Four Pieces of a Shepherd's Equipment
1. A club. Usually made of oak two to three feet long with a knob on one
   end about the size of an orange and a loop attached to the other end
   which enabled him to carry it over his arm or on his girdle. Hebrew:
   shebet (HSN-7626), a rod or club (Exodus 21:20; Leviticus 27:32; 2
   Samuel 23:21; 1 Chron. 11:23; Psalm 2:9; Psalm 23:4).
2. A staff or crook about six feet long and generally made of a peeled vine
   branch. It was used for climbing, walking, slashing twigs and leaves,
   rescuing sheep fallen into a pit, and for strafing lingering or fighting
   goats. Hebrew: maqqel (HSN-4731), a staff (1 Samuel 17:40; Genesis
   32:10; Exodus 12:11; Numbers 22:27; Hosea 4:12; Zech. 11:10,14), and
   rod (Jeremiah 1:11; Jeremiah 48:17). About the same as Hebrew: matteh,
   a staff (Genesis 38:18,25; Isaiah 10:5,16,24; Isaiah 14:5; Isaiah 28:27;
   Jeremiah 48:17) and rod (Exodus 4:2,4,17,20; Exodus 7:9-20; Exodus
   8:5,16-17; Exodus 9:23; Exodus 10:13; Exodus 14:16; Exodus 17:5,9;
   Numbers 17:2-10; Numbers 20:8-11; 1 Samuel 14:27,43).

3. A bag or scrip made of leather and thrown over the shoulder to carry
   provisions (1 Samuel 17:40; Matthew 10:10; Mark 6:8; Luke 9:3; Luke
   10:4; Luke 22:35-36).

4. A sling. It was made of leather, plaited work of wool, rushes, hair, or
   sinews with a wider middle piece (about two inches wide) to hold the
   stone. Stones were collected from dry river beds or brooks and kept in
   the shepherd's bag. In one end of the sling there was a loop which was
   placed over the thumb in order to hold it when the stone was thrown.
   The sling was used by the shepherds to keep wild beasts away from the
   flock and to keep the sheep from straying. Stones could be thrown with
   such velocity they could pierce a helmet or a shield (1 Samuel 17:40,50;
   1 Samuel 25:29; Proverbs 26:8; Jeremiah 10:18; Zech. 9:15). Men of the
   tribe of Benjamin could sling stones "at an hair breadth, and not miss"
   (Judges 20:16).

                             Boast of Goliath
The Philistine drew near to David, hiding behind the large shield carried by
a man before him, not knowing what he was to face. When he looked from
behind the protecting shield he was full of wrath a mere boy should be sent
against him. He hurled slander at David and cursed him by his gods,
promising to give his flesh to the birds and beasts (1 Samuel 17:41-44).
Such a boy without armor and weapons of warfare made the vain giant
careless in his defense, so he came at the opponent to tear him in pieces
with his hands.

Two-fold Boast of Goliath (1 Samuel 17:43-44):

1. Am I a dog, that you come to me with staves? There could be no stronger
   statement of contempt (2 Kings 8:13; Matthew 15:26); and since David
   was coming against him with a club, which was used on dogs, it made
   him blind with rage that helped cause his own downfall.

2. Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the fowls of the air, and the
   beasts of the field.

                           David and Jonathan
David and Jonathan became close friends from this time on. Jonathan was
possibly forty years old when he met David and fifty-five when he died
with Saul (1 Samuel 31:1-13). Ishbosheth, the youngest son of Saul, was
forty when he began to reign (2 Samuel 2:10). The love of Jonathan and
David was like that of father and son, and as true brothers in the same
nation—not the depraved, unnatural, homosexual and demonic love which
some have sought to attach to this story (based on 1 Samuel 18:1; 2 Samuel
1:26). Theirs was a genuine affection which was pure and normal, as it
should be with all men.

                            Custom of Women
It was the custom for women to express their delight in victory by songs,
music, and dancing in the presence of the conquerors (1 Samuel 18:6;
Exodus 15:20; Judges 11:24). This encouraged the seed of jealousy that
caused the many sins of Saul and the sufferings of David whom they
wanted to honor. Many times an innocent thing becomes a deadly poison
which causes untold heartache and destruction. This was something Saul
could not overlook. He wanted to be the hero and could have been if he had
killed the giant; but he did not even attempt it. Saul reasoned the people
might as well give David the kingdom. Then a jealous demon took hold of
him from that time forward (1 Samuel 18:8-9). This is further proof that
happenings of 1 Samuel 16:14-23 were after all the events of 1 Samuel 17.

a [Jonathan spake good of David unto Saul his father]

                  Eightfold Plea of Jonathan for David
1. Spoke good of David unto Saul (1 Samuel 19:4)

2. He said, Let not the king sin against his servant David

3. David has not sinned against you

4. His works have always been very good toward you

5. He took his life in his own hands and slew the giant (1 Samuel 19:5)

6. The Lord wrought a great victory and salvation in Israel, through him

7. You yourself saw it and rejoiced

8. Why then will you sin against innocent blood, to slay without a cause?

This is one of the most appealing pleas for righteousness from a son to a
father on record. It struck right at the root of the matter and covered every
general principle involved between the two men. It cleared David of any
wrongdoing and indicted Saul of extreme selfishness and jealousy before
God and man. It cleared the injustice regarding an innocent, blameless,
faithful man. It showed what a godly man will do for God and his country,
being an example for all to follow. It was a most touching defense of a
friend, a man of God, and a true patriot who had risked his life for the good
of his people and saved them in a desperate crisis.

b [company of the prophets]

                          Schools of the Prophets
Hebrew: lahaqah (HSN-3862), to gather; an assembly; a company. From
this assembly of the prophets we get the idea of the school of the prophets.
It seems that men who desired to be prophets gathered together to learn the
ways of God and to be trained in divine matters.

No doubt they sought God and were anointed with the Holy Spirit as in
other periods. Certain men in every age have been spiritually minded and
hungry for the Lord. There were such gatherings from Samuel's day on (1
Samuel 19:20,24; 1 Samuel 10:5-12; 1 Kings 18:4,13; 1 Kings 19:1,10,14).
Those who gathered in Elijah and Elisha's day were called the "sons of the
prophets" (1 Kings 20:35,41; 2 Kings 2:2-7,15; 2 Kings 4:1,38; 2 Kings
5:22; 2 Kings 6:1; 2 Kings 9:1). They were the special servants of God (1
Kings 17:13,23; 1 Kings 21:10; 1 Kings 24:2; 2 Chron. 20:20; 2 Chron.
24:19; 2 Chron. 29:25; 2 Chron. 36:16; Ezra 9:11; Neh. 9:26-32; Isaiah
29:10); and they were the preachers of their day (Neh. 6:7; Neh. 9:26;
Amos 2:11; Acts 3:21; 2 Cor. 14:3,24-32).

Here Samuel stood among them as their appointed leader or president of the
school (1 Samuel 19:20). Elijah and Elisha were heads of the prophets in
their time (2 Kings 2:2-7,15; 2 Kings 6:1). In such gatherings there seemed
to be a general spirit of prophecy that would come upon all present. At
least, this is what happened here. Three companies of Saul's soldiers had the
Spirit come upon them when they came among the prophets (1 Samuel
19:20-21). Then when Saul—the backslider from whom the Spirit had been
taken away—came among them, the Spirit was upon him again for the time
being (1 Samuel 19:22-24).

c [exceeded]

                              David's Distress
David's distress in leaving his true friend Jonathan, the loss of his wife and
home with all its comforts, the loss of his relatives, friends, and beloved
people of Israel, his country and inheritance, and above all the altars of God
—all this would naturally cause him to weep excessively. David was not a
mere boy anymore; he was a man of war, as brave and powerful as the best;
but he was crushed at the injustice shown to him (1 Samuel 20:41). He set
an example of godliness that cannot be surpassed and became a pattern here
for all others to imitate. He could have killed Saul, organized an army of
true followers in Israel, divided the kingdom and split the whole nation; but
he neither sought power, personal gain, nor vengeance in the least degree.
He did not linger to recruit sympathizers. He simply left everything to the
providence of God to work out in His time and way.

                                David's Fear
David had a right to be afraid, not realizing what attitude they would have
after knowing that the killer of their giant champion of Gath, and the man
who had caused their defeat more than once, was in their hands. David
should have had faith though, and recognized that God had chosen him to
be the king of Israel, and that He would therefore see to it that he fulfilled
his calling in spite of Saul and the Philistines. Instead, he took things in his
own hands and decided to act insane, thinking they would then turn him
loose to go where he pleased (1 Samuel 21:12-13). The strategy was a
success, for Achish rejected him (1 Samuel 21:14-15). David composed
Psalm 56 on this occasion.

a [cave Adullam]

                          The Cave of Adullam
The cave of Adullam was a large one near the city of Adullam in Judah—
about 12 miles southwest of Bethlehem and about 20 or more miles from
Nob, a place about 2 miles north of Jerusalem (1 Samuel 22:1; Joshua
12:15; Joshua 15:35; 2 Samuel 23:13; 1 Chron. 11:15; 2 Chron. 11:7; Neh.
1:30; Micah 1:15; cp. Genesis 38:1,12,20). Here is where David gathered
his mighty men who helped him in his adventures with Saul and others, and
who also helped him get the kingdom of Judah after the death of Saul. At
first, 400 men gathered to him and he became their leader (1 Samuel 22:1-
2); then others came until there were about 600 (1 Samuel 23:13; 1 Samuel
27:2; 1 Samuel 30:9). Psalm 57 was written on this occasion.

b [went down thither to him]

                       Four Classes Joined David
1. His brethren and his father's house

2. Everyone that was in distress

3. Everyone that was in debt
4. Everyone that was discontented

It wasn't just the blood ties that caused his father's house to go down to him,
but because they were all in danger of being killed by Saul who was
determined to slay David and thus get rid of his rival from the house of
Jesse. If any in the gathering thought it was a good chance to take
vengeance on Saul, to rob and plunder, and get gain, they were
disappointed, for David never misused his power; he always made it count
for good and in defense of his people.

Abiathar, excellent father. The son of Ahimelech and twelfth high priest in
Israel (1 Samuel 22:20-23; 1 Samuel 23:6-9; 1 Samuel 30:7; 1 Kings
1:7,19,25,42; 1 Chron. 27:34; Mark 2:26). He was joint priest with Zadok
who was with Saul's party (2 Samuel 8:17; 2 Samuel 15:24-36; 2 Samuel
17:15; 2 Samuel 19:11; 2 Samuel 20:25; 1 Chron. 15:11). He had a son who
was also joint priest with Zadok for a while (1 Chron. 18:16; 1 Chron.
24:6). Solomon deposed Ahimelech because he espoused his brother' cause
to become king; and Zadok became sole high priest (1 Kings 1:7-42; 1
Kings 2:22-25). Thus, the prophecy to Eli of the cutting off of his house as
priests was fulfilled (l Sam. 2:31), for Abiathar was the last of his line to be
sole high priest. Eli and Abiathar were of the house of Ithamar and Zadok
was of the house of Eleazar. By this act of Saul he caused the transfer of
Urim and Thummim to David (1 Samuel 23:2,4,6,9-12).

                             Men of Principle
Both Jonathan and David were men of principle, with qualities of
faithfulness and unselfishness in all their dealings with fellowmen. Jonathan
was the rare type who was willing to recognize the will of God and be
content in the second place to a superior (1 Samuel 23:17). David was the
rare type to refuse to hurt others even if it would bring him prosperity. He
had the legal and customary right, the divine permission, and actual
opportunities to kill his enemy, Saul, so that he could live free from the life
of an outcast. By doing so he could have regained his home, his family
inheritance, and had the respect of his fellowmen, as well as the kingship
and other worthwhile things; but he would not violate the principle of
refusing to harm any man who had at one time been anointed and used by
God. The only regrettable part of the whole story is that if he had killed
Saul when he had him in his hands, Jonathan no doubt would have been
spared from death in battle with the Philistines, and he and David would
have had a wonderful record of exploits and unity in government between
what was now the two ever widening factions of Israel.

                                   Engedi
Engedi, the fountain of the kid, was a city on the western shore of the Dead
Sea, about the middle section. Originally called Hazezon-tamar it was the
home of Amorites in the days of Abraham (Genesis 14:7); also Hazazon-
tamar (2 Chron. 20:2). The fountain which comes out of the mountainside
about 400 feet above the sea is still called Ain-jidy, from which the city
took its name. Near it are the ruins of several buildings. The old city site
was on the level ground at the seashore, which is still strewn with ruins.
The wilderness of Engedi included the wild and rugged mountain regions
extending from the city toward Hebron, Tekoa, and Bethlehem. It was and
still is the home of wild goats. In every ravine are immense caverns in
which David and his men could have hidden from Saul (1 Samuel 23:29; 1
Samuel 24:1-2). Some could have held all 600 of David's men (1 Samuel
24:3). The cave of Khrureitun at the upper end of the wilderness would hold
as many as 3,000. One great hall alone is said to be 45 by 120 feet, with an
arched roof. Such caves are to be found throughout the East, especially
where limestone abounds.

                         Saul's Acknowledgement
Saul acknowledged the justice and mercy of David as well as his own fault
and guilt, and begged mercy and kindness to his own house when David
would become king. He seems to have been a man of strong emotions,
capable of grateful expressions when normal, and uncontrollable temper
and wickedness when overcome by his depraved disposition and under the
influence of a demon that had come into his life instead of the Holy Spirit
(1 Samuel 24:16-22; 1 Samuel 16:13-23). Saul's change here was only
shortlived, and his clear and sane acknowlegement and admiration of the
character and conduct of the one he dreaded was transient. Nevertheless,
God used these circumstances for a temporary escape for David. Psalm 142
was composed on this occasion.

                      David's First Act of Judgment
This was the first act of judgment by David upon anyone who had insulted
and mistreated him among his own people. He did not seek judgment upon
Saul or Doeg, or the cities of Keilah and Ziph who had all betrayed him; but

undoubtedly had many men with him at the feast he was making, and went
to administer the punishment. He left 200 men at the camp with the women
and children (1 Samuel 25:13).

                                    Figs
The word fig is used 66 times in both testaments—41 times in the O.T. and
25 times in the N.T. The first mention is when Adam and Eve sewed fig
leaves together to make aprons for their nakedness (Genesis 3:7). Fig trees
abounded in Palestine, and figs are mentioned as one of the fruits of Canaan
(Numbers 13:23; Numbers 20:5; Deut. 8:8; Judges 9:10-11). The expression
"sitting under a fig tree" is one of security and peace (1 Kings 4:25; Micah
4:4). Some species of fig trees had leaves 4 or 5 ft. long and 3 ft. wide, and
the shade was greatly valued (1 Kings 4:25; 2 Kings 18:31; Isaiah 36:16;
Micah 4:4; Zech. 3:10; John 1:48). Fig trees grow in Egypt as well as
Palestine (Psalm 105:33), some said to be 10 to 25 ft. high. The various fig
trees altogether bear about ten months out of the year and are of three kinds:

1. The early fig (Song 2:13; Hosea 9:10). The fruit is ripe toward the end of
   June; it is the most beautiful and delicious kind (Jeremiah 24:1-8).

2. The summer fig. This fruit begins to appear in June about the time the
   early fig is ripe and comes to maturity in August; it lasts a long time and
   may be preserved.

3. The winter fig appears in August about the time the summer fig is ripe
   and reaches the ripening stage toward the latter part of October and
   November. If the winter is not too severe this fruit can still be plucked
   toward spring.

Figs which were used as food the year round were said to possess medicinal
properties (2 Kings 20:7; 1 Chron. 12:40; Isaiah 38:21). The putting forth of
the fig tree was one of the earliest signs of summer (Song 2:13; Matthew
24:31-32; Luke 21:29); failure to produce fruit was a calamity (Jeremiah
5:17; Jeremiah 8:13; Joel 1:7,12; Habakkuk 3:17-18). A favorite way to
preserve the fruit was to press the figs into large cakes and dry them to be
eaten when needed (1 Samuel 25:18; 1 Samuel 30:12; 1 Chron. 12:40;
Isaiah 38:21. See Proverbs 27:18; Song 2:13; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 36:16;
Jeremiah 5:17; Jeremiah 8:13; Jeremiah 29:17; Hosea 2:12; Hosea 9:10;
Joel 1:7,12; Joel 2:22; Amos 4:9; Nahum 3:12; Habakkuk 3:17; Haggai
2:19; Zech. 3:10; Matthew 7:16; Luke 6:44; Luke 13:6-7; James 3:12; Rev.
6:13).

                        Twenty Qualities of Abigail
1. She was a woman of good understanding (clever and wise, 1 Samuel
   25:3).

2. She was beautiful, but not proud or self-exalted (1 Samuel 25:3).

3. She was humble and godly—unspoiled regardless of her riches (1
   Samuel 25:2,6,23-35).

4. She appreciated anything others did to aid her household in any degree (1
   Samuel 25:14-19).

5. She was reasonable, listened to her servants, and sought to protect her
   unworthy husband as well as all her household from danger (1 Samuel
   25:14-35).
6. She was quick to act in time of danger to protect her own (1 Samuel
   25:17-19).

7. She didn't nag her husband for his mean disposition, but patiently lived
   with him, tolerating the abuse which she no doubt received from such a
   man (1 Samuel 25:3,19,36).

8. She was generous, seeking to help meet the needs of others (1 Samuel
   25:18).

9. She was independent enough to act without the consent of her husband
   when it was for his good and the good of others concerned (1 Samuel
   25:19,36).

10. She was bold and businesslike in meeting the problems of life; did not
   become panic-striken (1 Samuel 25:17-35).

11. She was brave and willing to face danger which might involve her own
   life and certainly that of others. Alone she faced an entire army that was
   coming to destroy her household (1 Samuel 25:19-35).

12. She was gracious, and pliable when it was necessary (1 Samuel 25:23-
   35).

13. She was willing to take blame and be personally responsible for the acts
   and sins of another whom she sought to reconcile to the one offended (1
   Samuel 25:24-25,28).

14. She was courteous in her dealings with an enemy who had already
   passed the death sentence on all men of her household (1 Samuel 25:23-
   35).

15. She had wisdom enough to recognize the kind of disposition her
   husband had, yet at the same time she loved him and tried to save him
   from harm (1 Samuel 25:25).

16. She was diplomatic in her approach and appeal to the enemy of her
   household, turning his wrath to mercy (1 Samuel 25:26-35).
17. She had faith in God and recognized His plan in Israel concerning the
   one who sought to do her harm (1 Samuel 25:28-35).

18. She was zealous to keep even an enemy spotless in life and conduct (1
   Samuel 25:28-31).

19. She wisely kept from her husband the report of the great danger he had
   been in until he was sober and sensible enough to discuss it (1 Samuel
   25:36-38).

20. She was willing to forgive the wrongs intended against her and her
   house, and soon afterward accepted the very man as a husband who was
   responsible for these plans of evil (1 Samuel 25:39-42)

                    Nine Proofs This Was Not Samuel
1. God would not answer Saul either by dreams and visions, Urim and
   Thummim, or by prophets, for He had departed from him and had taken
   the Holy Spirit away from him because of sin (1 Samuel 28:6,15-16; 1
   Samuel 15:26; 1 Samuel 16:13-23; 1 Chron. 10:13-14). If God had
   refused to answer him by legitimate means, He certainly would not
   answer contrary to Scripture (Luke 16:26). If He would not answer by
   the Holy Spirit, He certainly would not answer by a demon seeking to
   imitate Samuel (1 Samuel 28:7-19; 1 Chron. 10:13-14).

2. It is clearly stated that Saul sought information from demons, not from
    God who refused to answer him. He specifically wanted a witch that had
    a familiar spirit, to inquire of her (1 Samuel 28:7). His request was for
    her to divine by the familiar spirit (1 Samuel 28:8).

3. The Bible plainly teaches that communication with the dead can be
   demons imitating departed loved ones (1 Samuel 28:7-19; Deut. 18:11; 1
   Chron. 10:13-14; Isaiah 8:19).

4. It is commanded in many scriptures not to traffic with demons or seek
    communication with the dead (note, ▪ Luke 12:29); therefore, God would
    not allow Samuel to communicate through a witch.

5. The seeming appearance of Samuel to the witch was simply the familiar
   spirit imitating and impersonating him (1 Chron. 10:13-14). When it
   appeared that Samuel was speaking to Saul, it was the demon speaking;
   it would know about both Samuel and Saul and their past relationship.
   Such a demon could also make predictions (Deut. 13:1-3). Isaiah warned
   later that those who sought the dead were deceived by familiar spirits
   (Isaiah 8:19).

6. The demon practically revealed his identity when he said that Saul and
   his sons would be with him tomorrow. Saul went to the torment
   compartment of sheol or hades, whereas Samuel went to the comfort side
   of the underworld of departed spirits. See Where Are the Dead? and
   Hell.

7. There is no record of God seeking to intercept the communication of
   demons and men. Saul inquired of a demon and was answered by one.
   When God gives answers His messages come only through the Holy
   Spirit in different ways, but never through unlawful or unscriptural ways,
   as here. The case of Balaam is sometimes mentioned as proof that God
     intercepts messages of Satan and utters His own through the same
     channel, but this is not true. Balaam was a true prophet as long as he was
     used by God. See Thirty-five Biblical Facts About Balaam.

8. It is stated in 1 Chron. 10:13-14 that Saul died for his previous sins and
    also for sinning against the Word of the Lord (which forbade witches and
    traffic with demons, and for asking counsel of one that had a familiar
    spirit) and not inquiring of the Lord (on this occasion). Thus, it was from
    a familiar spirit, and not Samuel, that he obtained his information.

9. Jesus taught that it is impossible for the dead to communicate with living
    persons on earth, and all scriptures on the subject of the state of the dead,
    and on heaven and hell, completely confirm His teaching. There was an
    impassible gulf between the compartments so that they could not go
    from one place to the other, nor go back to the earth (Luke 16:26-31).
    The only case of any person leaving his place of confinement between
    death and resurrection is the case of Moses whom God brought up for a
    purpose, on the mount of transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-8). We must
    bear in mind though, that this was an act of God and not a demonized
    witch or wizard. Hence, we conclude that 1 Samuel 28:7-19 is the record
    of a demon impersonation.

c [for he had eaten no bread all the day, nor all the night] Saul had
    fasted all day and night up to this point, which was perhaps near midnight,
    for they came and went back by night (1 Samuel 28:8,25). This proves
    that fasting in itself does not bring an answer from God.

                   SUMMARY OF 1 SAMUEL
                            ____________________

Date and Place: The records which make up 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel were
written by Samuel, David, Nathan, and Gad from 1204-1035 B.C. in
Palestine, but were perhaps finally made into one book by Isaiah the
prophet, about 743-683 B.C. He seems to have been the author of Judges,
Ruth, 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, 1 Kings and 2 Kings, and 1 Chron. and 2
Chron. in their final form, according to the note on ▪ 2 Chron. 32:32.

Author: Samuel, David, Nathan, and Gad no doubt kept the original
records from which Isaiah compiled the book about 743-683 B.C.

Proof of authorship: It is necessary to treat the two books as one because,
in the Hebrew canon and early editions of the Hebrew text, the two were
one. The division came with the Septuagint translators about 289-294 B.C.
and this has been followed in all editions since then. Samuel perhaps wrote
1 Samuel 1-24; David, Nathan, and Gad, 1 Samuel 25-2 Samuel 24 (1
Samuel 10:25; 1 Chron. 29:29). There is a reference to the book of Jasher in
2 Samuel 1:18, which may have also been used in the final writing of the
book by Isaiah, who wrote the history of the kings of Judah and Israel (▪ 2
Chron. 32:32, note).

Theme: 1 Samuel presents the life history of Samuel; the last of the days of
the judges; the moral failure of the priesthood under Eli; the moral failure of
the judges under Samuel; the beginning and failure of the monarchy under
Saul; the anointing and trying experiences of David; and the end of Saul.

Purpose: The original book, now divided into 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, was
written to record the history of Israel under the judges; to show the change
in the government of Israel from a system of judges to kings; and to record
the background of the people through whom the Messiah would come.

Statistics: 9th book of the Bible; 31 chapters; 810 verses; 25,049 words;
157 questions; 50 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 1 verse of unfulfilled
prophecy; 29 distinct messages from God (1 Samuel 2:27; 1 Samuel
3:4,6,8,10; 1 Samuel 8:7,22; 1 Samuel 9:15,17; 1 Samuel 10:1,18,22; 1
Samuel 13:11; 1 Samuel 15:2,11,18; 1 Samuel 16:1,2,7,8,9,10,12; 1 Samuel
22:5; 1 Samuel 23:2,4,11,12; 1 Samuel 30:8); 4 promises; 117 commands;
and 57 predictions.

                               Hebrew Crowns
We know very little about the kind and shapes of crowns the Hebrew kings
wore. The Hebrew: nezer (HSN-5145) (translated crown here) means
something set apart in the dedication of a priest or king; hence it came to be
used of the headpiece which signified one's office (2 Samuel 1:10; 2 Kings
11:12; 2 Chron. 23:11; Psalm 89:39; Psalm 132:18; Proverbs 27:24; Zech.
9:16). The same word is used of the crown of the high priest in Exodus
29:6; Exodus 39:30; Leviticus 8:9; Leviticus 21:12. Only in Zech. 9:16 do
we have the idea of precious stones being set in the crown. The high priest's
crown was made of gold (Exodus 25:11,24-25; Exodus 30:3-4; Exodus
37:2,11-12,26-27) as were others (Esther 8:15; Psalm 21:3; Rev. 14:14).
Kings of Israel were anointed and were called the Lord's anointed in the
same sense that the high priest was the anointed of God (2 Samuel 1:14,16;
1 Samuel 12:3-5; Psalm 2:2; Habakkuk 3:13).

a [lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son]
                          David's Lamentation
This lamantation is really a martial ode and one of the first and finest odes
in the O.T. David's own sufferings are forgotten while his fervent love and
deep grief for Saul and Jonathan are expressed. There is no bitter exultation
over the death of his greatest enemy, Saul. The song is about the mighty
warrior, the anointed of the Lord, the delight of his people, and the father of
his beloved friend.

It was customary in the East to give quaint and even farfetched titles to odes
and treatises. The Hebrew title of this ode is Qesheth, the bow. This idea is
expressed in English by omitting "the use of" from 2 Samuel 1:18. These
italicized words are supplied by translators. The original reads, "Also he
bade them teach the children of Judah The bow." The title is given because
of the occasion of the Philistine archers (1 Samuel 31:3) and the bow of
Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:22). The tribe of Benjamin was noted for the use of
the bow (1 Chron. 8:40; 1 Chron. 12:2; 2 Chron. 14:8; 2 Chron. 17:17).
David could hardly forget the bow of Jonathan which sent the arrow used as
a sign for his departure from his own home and country (1 Samuel 20:36).
It was the time when the covenant was made and eternal affection was
expressed between them, which David calls wonderful, passing the love of
women in 2 Samuel 1:26.
