                          The Anglo-Saxon Theory
In general, the erroneous Anglo-Saxon theory (also called the British-Israel
theory) teaches the following:

1. That the British and American people are the ten lost tribes of Israel

2. That Britain is Ephraim and America is Manasseh

3. That all the promises made to Israel are now being fulfilled with Britain
   and America and never will be fulfilled with Jews

4. That the royal family of England are the true legal heirs of the throne of
   David through Zedekiah's daughter, and that the throne of England is the
   throne of David. See David's Eternal House, Kingdom, and Throne

5. That the Coronation Stone of England was the original Jacob's pillow
6. That there is vital distinction between Israel and the Jews; that they are
   not the same kind of people and never will be; and that each has a
   different destiny

7. That the terms Israel, Judah, Jews, the house of Israel, and the house of
   Judah are never used interchangeably in Scripture

8. That the Israel of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and other prophets had no tribe of
   Judah in it

9. That Jews descended from the tribe of Judah only

10. That it is erroneous to call Jews of today Israel; and the house of Israel
   is not Jewish

11. That ten tribes were lost and whoever they are, they are not Jews

12. That not once in the Bible does the term Israel refer to Jews exclusively,
   for although Jews may be a part of Israel, Israelites are not Jews

13. That the returning exiles from Babylon under Ezra and Nehemiah were
   Jews only, and not Israel

14. That Israel left their own land when taken into captivity by the
   Assyrians; that they never were to return and never did; and that Israel
   then began to abide many days without a king (Hosea 3:4)

15. That the Jews of the N.T. were only from Judah, Benjamin, and Levi

16. That the ten tribes were to remain lost as to identity until the very last
   days in which we live

17. That Christ is not coming to a nonexistent throne, but to one that exists
   now

18. That David's throne was to be transferred from Judah to the ten tribes

19. That because Israel lost the sabbath, the sign which identified them as
   Israel, they utterly lost their identity and their national name, becoming
   known as Gentiles

20. That Israel was to have a new land of promise northwest of Palestine—
   on islands—from where they would move no more

21. That Israel was to be punished for 2,520 years, from 721 B.C. to A.D.
   1800, and then be identified and blessed above all other people on earth

22. That because the Anglo-Saxons are so great, powerful, and rich, they
   must be the ten tribes or the whole house of Israel

         Eighty-two Proofs that Jews and Israel the Same
1. There is no special significance to the term Israel when used in contrast
   or in apposition with other names, other than the fact that it conveys the
   idea of the majority of the nation of Israel as compared with a smaller
   body of the same nation. In no case does it mean the two parts of the
   same nation are two different kinds of people.

   (1) Israel is used in apposition to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of
      Manasseh (Joshua 22:11-34).

   (2) Israel is used in apposition to Benjamin (Judges 20:1-21:6). It is the
      term used of Benjamin in 2 Samuel 2:25-28.

   (3) Israel is used in apposition to Judah, but only from the time of
      David's being chosen—from the tribe of Judah—as king over all
      Israel (1 Samuel 16:1-13; 1 Samuel 17:52; 1 Samuel 18:16).
      Naturally, from this time on Judah would be emphasized as the ruling
      tribe in fulfillment of prophecy (Genesis 49:10), because now it was
      known more fully that the Messiah was to come through this tribe,
      making Judah the eternal head of all the other tribes in God's program
      (2 Samuel 7:1-29; 1 Chron. 5:2; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 9:6-7; Matthew
      1:1-17; Luke 3:23-38; Luke 7:14; Rev. 5:5). Hence, before the
      division of Israel into two kingdoms, during this division for 260
      years (from Rehoboam to the captivity of the northern kingdom to
      Assyria), and after the return from captivity and the uniting of all the
      tribes again as a single nation under Ezra, Nehemiah, and the prophets
      to the first coming of Christ—this distinction of Judah over any one
      or all the other tribes was made. But this certainly could not make the
      tribe of Judah any less Israel or a part of all twelve tribes in the
      fulfillment of God's covenants and promises which were made to all
      Israel, not to ten tribes only. In fact, the promises of an eternal
      Davidic kingdom were made to Judah in particular, so if any tribes
      were ever to be cut off it wouldn't be Judah (2 Samuel 7:1-29; Psalm
      89:4-5,20-37). If we make two different peoples with two different
      destinies out of Israel and Judah because the terms are used in
      apposition, then to be consistent we must do likewise with Israel,
      Benjamin, Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh listed in
      previous points. However, if we did this, we would be destroying part
      of the ten tribes as well as Judah and Benjamin as having a part in the
      plan of God.

2. It was Ephraim that departed from Judah which was the ruling tribe, not
    Judah that departed from Ephraim (Isaiah 7:17). So if anyone was to be
    cut off for departure from God's plan it would be Ephraim, not Judah.

3. The promises of a Davidic throne were based based on obedience; it was
   to be cut off until the second coming of Christ if the royal line went into
   sin. Then at the second coming Judah and all Israel ase to become one
   nation again under the Messiah in Palestine—not in the British Isles (2
   Samuel 7:10-16,24-29). Nothing is said here or in any other passage
   about this Israel of the Davidic covenant consisting of the tribe of Judah
   only, or meaning the ten tribes exclusive of Judah and Benjamin; nor is
   there a statement anywhere in Scripture that even hints that the throne or
   kingdom would be taken from Judah and given to the ten tribes. On the
   contrary, the scepter is not to depart from Judah until Shiloh comes
   (Genesis 49:10); then the Messiah from Judah will reign over the house
   of Judah and the other tribes eternally. David understood that his throne
   would be cut off temporarily if his descendants sinned (1 Kings 2:4);
   Solomon and all Israel understood it this way (1 Kings 9:3-9); and this is
   exactly what happened when Solomon sinned (1 Kings 11:11-13,30-38).
   The books of Kings and Chronicles are full of records of God cutting off
   many kings because they went into sin. This continued until God found
   it necessary to cut off both houses of Israel (2 Kings 17:4-23; 2 Kings
   23:27; 2 Kings 24:1-25:30; 2 Chron. 36). Failure to find the throne of
   David in generations past until now is no failure on God's part, nor does
   it prove the Bible untrue; it only proves that God will not bless any
   people who continue to sin to the point that God has to curse them. Such
   was true of all the tribes of Israel, not Judah only; so God would not
   curse Judah only and not the other tribes since all were guilty of the
   same sins. On the other hand, the British Empire and America have been
   as guilty of sin and departure from God as all the tribes; so why should
   God bless these and curse others for the same thing—disobedience and
   rebellion? We see no reason, therefore, to believe that the throne of
   David is the British throne.

4. David's kingdom and throne were postponed from the time of the
   Babylonian captivity, with such to continue until the second coming of
   Christ (Hosea 3:4-5; Acts 15:13-18). There has been no such throne from
   then until now. It was said to Jeconiah, the last ruler of David's line to be
   king in Judah, that no man of his seed would ever rule again on David's
   throne or rule in Jerusalem over Judah; so there could not have been a
   succession of Israelite kings and queens from his day to the present
   queen of England. None could have been a legal heir to the throne of
   David; no man can ever again be a legal heir to that throne until Messiah
   comes. Even He is not the literal seed of Jeconiah or of the royal line of
   David, for Christ inherited the throne rights through Joseph, the husband
   of Mary (note, ▪ Matthew 1:6). He came through Nathan, son of David,
   not Solomon—the kingly line.

5. David's throne will be reestablished after the church age, for we read:
   "And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written, after this
   (after taking out of the Gentiles a people for His name) I will return, and
   will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down (not which
   is built up and kept up by the kings of England); and I will build again
   the ruins thereof, and I will set it up" (Acts 15:15-16; Amos 9:11-15).

6. David's throne will be restored at the regathering of Israel and the second
   coming of Christ. He cannot sit on David's throne until He does come
   (Isaiah 9:6-7; Isaiah 16:5; Luke 1:32-33; Rev. 11:15; Rev. 20:4-6).
7. David's throne will be restored to Judah when the time comes—not to
   another tribe of Israel or to Anglo-Saxons who never were descendants
   of Israel, but rather plain Gentiles from Japheth (Genesis 49:10; Amos
   9:11-12; Acts 15:13-18). The British, Irish, Welsh, German,
   Scandinavian, and other Anglo-Saxon people descended from Japheth—
   not from Shem, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. See Sons of Japheth.

8. Jerusalem—not London, Washington, or some other Gentile city—will
    be the capital of the restored kingdom of the twelve tribes when Messiah
    comes (Isaiah 2:1-4; Isaiah 44:26; Isaiah 52:7-9; Isaiah 62:6-12; Isaiah
    65:18-25; Isaiah 66:19-20; Jeremiah 3:17; Ezekiel 48; Joel 3:16-20;
    Micah 4; Zech. 12:2-11; Zech. 13:1; Zech. 14:1-21). No Gentile city in
    the British Isles or America is ever once mentioned in Scripture, but
    Jerusalem is named 814 times.

9. It seems there should be at least some hint in Scripture of events as
    important as changing the throne rights from Judah to an Israel which
    has no Judah in it, changing the capital of Israel from Jerusalem to
    London, and and the changing of the promises and covenant made in
    particular to David and Judah to another distinct people which has no
    tribe of Judah whatsoever. But such is not the case, for Judah and
    Jerusalem are the subject of the prophets, not Israel and Jerusalem
    excluding Judah. The term "Judah and Jerusalem" is used 31 times
    whereas "Israel and Jerusalem" is not found once. "Judah, Israel, and
    Jerusalem" is found only once (Zech. 1:19), referring to the scattering
    and restoration of all the tribes of Israel to Jerusalem, their capital. There
    is not one hint anywhere in Scripture of God cutting off Judah from the
    promises and covenants, and no suggestion that there is an Israel which
    does not have a tribe of Judah in it to enjoy these blessing along with
    other tribes.

10. Not one scripture ever says that God would give Israel a land other than
   the original land of promise to all the twelve tribes. They will never be
   moved from this, for it was given to Abraham and his seed to be the land
   of the twelve tribes forever. The land is specifically stated to be Canaan
   and that of surrounding nations with boundary lines clearly marked from
   the Mediterranean on the west to the Euphrates on the east, and from
  Hamath on the north to the Indian Ocean on the south (Genesis 13:14-
  17; Genesis 15:18-21; Genesis 17:8; Genesis 26:3-4; Genesis 28:4;
  Genesis 35:12; Ezekiel 48).

11. It is in the original promised land that all the twelve tribes will be
   gathered again to make an eternal nation under the Messiah (Deut. 30:1-
   10; Isaiah 11:10-16; Isaiah 60:8-22; Isaiah 66:19-21; Jeremiah 16:14-21;
   Jeremiah 23:3-8; Jeremiah 30:1-24; Jeremiah 31:18-40; Jeremiah 32:7-
   44; Jeremiah 33:6-26; Jeremiah 50:19-20; Ezekiel 11:17-21; Ezekiel
   20:33-44; Ezekiel 28:26-28; Ezekiel 34:11-31; Ezekiel 36:1-38; Ezekiel
   37:1-28).

12. Both the house of Israel and the house of Judah were to be gathered
   again the second time and assemble in their own land the outcasts of
   Israel and the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth—to
   be united together again in victory over their enemies (Isaiah 11:10-15),
   not to envy each other. The first dispersion was in the Assyrian and
   Babylonian captivities (2 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 25). After the
   Babylonian captivity the first gathering of Israel and Judah was under
   Ezra and Nehemiah. If both are to be gathered again it proves that some
   of all the twelve tribes were gathered this first time under Ezra and
   Nehemiah, not some from Judah only, as we shall see below. There was
   no other gathering of any of Israel in history. The second dispersion of
   Israel was at the destruction of Jerusalem, A.D. 70. The second gathering
   is now under way and will continue until the second coming of Christ
   when all Israel will be gathered (Isaiah 66:19-21; Matthew 24:29-31). If
   Britain and America were made up of some lost tribes, it would require
   the people of these countries to move to Palestine, which would be
   contrary to the teachings of Anglo-Israelism. All scriptures (under point
   11, above) plainly state that all Israel was dispersed among the nations,
   not only Judah; therefore, all must be regathered a second time the way
   they were the first time under Ezra and Nehemiah.

13. Both houses of Israel were to become one nation in the same land of
   promise after this second regathering (Ezekiel 37:22), and they were to
   be under their Messiah forever (Psalm 2; Isaiah 2:1-4; Isaiah 9:6-7;
   Isaiah 52:7; Ezekiel 37:28; Ezekiel 43:7; Ezekiel 48:35; Daniel 2:44-45;
   Daniel 7:13-14,22,27 Zech. 14:1-5,9,16-21; Luke 1:32-33; Acts 15:13-
   18; Rev. 11:15; Rev. 20:1-10).

14. David will be resurrected in the latter days to reign as king over both
   houses of Israel, as he did before while alive on earth (Jeremiah 30:9;
   Jeremiah 33:17; Ezekiel 34:23-24; Ezekiel 37:24-25; Hosea 3:4-5).

15. The twelve apostles will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes
   of Israel under David and their Messiah (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:28-
   30). All twelve tribes must be back in Palestine when this happens, so
   we must limit Israel to the Jews of today who are already beginning to
   return to Palestine. We aren't to suppose that the Anglo-Saxon peoples of
   Europe and the Americans are included, for they will never go from their
   countries as a regathered people in Palestine.

16. The gathering of both houses of Israel is to be in the latter days (Deut.
   4:25-31; Jeremiah 30:22-31:14). Both houses are to go through the great
   tribulation of the future, the last three and a half years of Daniel's
   seventieth week (called the time of Jacob's trouble); both are to be saved
   out of it, and then be ruled by David and Messiah (Jeremiah 30:3-10;
   Daniel 7:27; Rev. 10:1-18:21).

17. All the families of Israel (not Judah only) will be gathered at the same
   time to Zion (Jeremiah 31:1-14).

18. A new covenant will be made with both houses of Israel (Jeremiah
   31:27-40; Jeremiah 33:7). Anglo-Israelitism cuts off Judah from all the

   with Anglo-Saxons, declaring that the Israel of the prophets has no tribe

19. Both houses of Israel will be the people of God from this final
   regathering forever (Jeremiah 32:37-44).

20. There will be a great real estate boom in Judah, Jerusalem, and all other
   cities of Israel after this regathering (Jeremiah 32:44). Judah and

   cities of England and America.
21. Israel is mentioned as being blessed with a part of Judah's blessings, not

22. Judah shall be saved and Jerusalem made safe in the days of the
   Messiah, but nothing is said of an Israel being a separate people in a land

23. The Davidic covenant was made with all Israel, but particularly with

25. Both houses will be converted to God at the same time in their own

   36:16-37:28; Zech. 12:10-13:1; Romans 11:25-28).

26. God said He had not forsaken Judah anymore than He had the rest of
   Israel (Jeremiah 50:5; Romans 11).

27. The house of Israel (including Judah) will be brought back to Palestine

28. Israel now (including Judah) is fulfilling the many days without a king,

   nation comes to repentance, God will continue His covenants with them,

29. All twelve tribes were to be dispersed or scattered among the nations

30. The whole house of Israel will be jealous for God in the day of their

32. In the Millennium and the New Earth the promised land will be divided

33. All Israel (including Judah) must be planted in their own land again

34. God was to give up all Israel (not just Judah) until the future time of

   Romans 11:25-28).

35. God will yet inherit Judah in the Holy Land, and choose Jerusalem as
   the capital of all Israel forever (Zech. 2:11-13; Zech. 8:3-8,23; Zech.
   10:6-12; Zech. 12:1-14:21; Malachi 4:5-6). London will never fulfill
   this.

36. The curses of God upon Israel for sin were promised to all the tribes
   alike (Leviticus 26; Deut. 28), and all are partaking of them alike among

   scattered and cursed) could not be fulfilling such predictions, but rather

37. The Messiah was to be Judah's King, the rest of Israel being blessed

38. There is no doctrine in Scripture teaching their identity. The only sense

   and being estranged from God. The lost sheep of the house of Israel in
   Matthew 10:5-6; Matthew 15:24 were definitely Jews, as can be seen by
   the fact that Christ ministered only to Jews in Judea, Samaria, Galilee,

39. It is Judah that is mentioned as the Israel that will fight on the side of

40. The reason the term "Judah and Israel" is used so often from David's

(8) Christ promised that the twelve apostles would sit on twelve thrones
    judging the twelve tribes of Israel when He comes again to set up the
    kingdom of Israel (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:29-30). Paul spoke of all
    twelve tribes in his day as having hope in the resurrection (Acts
    26:7). James spoke of the twelve tribes scattered abroad and wrote to
    them (James 1:1). How could he write to ten tribes who were lost and
    unknown at the time? There will be twelve thousand from each of the
    twelve tribes sealed in the future tribulation in Palestine, so they will
    be back in their own land at that time or this could not be true (Rev.
    7:1-8). The twelve tribes will be restored in Palestine during the
    Millennium, for Ezekiel names them as inheriting twelve portions of
    the land of promise at that time (Ezekiel 47:13-29). The names of
    twelve tribes will be on the earthly city Jerusalem in the Millennium
    (Ezekiel 48:30-35). They will also be on the heavenly New
    Jerusalem (Rev. 21:12). Since Anglo-Saxons are not going back to
    Palestine and they plainly declare they are not supposed to go back,
    then they are not of the twelve tribes of Israel.
(9) Jesus plainly taught that the kingdom of God was in the hands of the
    Jews during His day (Matthew 21:33-46). It was to be taken from
    them and given to another nation (people)—the Gentiles—as Paul
    declares (Acts 13:46-49; Romans 11:13-29; cp. Acts 15:13-18).

(10) Matthew calls the Jews who helped crucify Christ the children of
    Israel (Matthew 27:9; Matthew 28:15; John 18:12-39; John 19:7-40).
    They are also called men of Israel, all the house of Israel, elders of
    Israel, all the people of Israel (Acts 2:22,36; Acts 3:12; Acts 4:8-10;
    Acts 5:21).

(11) John the Baptist was to turn many of the children of Israel to God
    (Luke 1:16), but all he ever went to were Jews. He was to minister to
    Israel, but he ministered only to Jews (Matthew 3:1,5; John 1:19).

(12) Simeon waited for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), but the
    Jews got the consolation (Luke 2:26-32; Matthew 10:5; John 1:11).

(13) Christ was to be the glory of Thy people Israel (Luke 2:32), but He
    only went to the Jews (John 11:11; Romans 1:16).

(14) Christ was set for the fall and rising of many in Israel (Luke 2:34),
    but this was fulfilled only with Jews (Matthew 21:42-44; Matthew
    23:37-39).

(15) Christ was to be made manifest to Israel (John 1:31), but it was to
    Jews only that He was manifested (John 1:11,29).

(16) Christ was called King of Israel (John 1:49; John 12:13); and He
    was King of the Jews (Matthew 2:2; Matthew 27:11).

(17) Nicodemus was master in Israel, but ruler of the Jews (John 3:1,10).

(18) Disciples wanted to know whether Christ was now going to restore
    the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:7). When it does happen it will be to
    Judah and the house of David (Isaiah 9:6-7; Zech. 14; Luke 1:32-33;
    Acts 15:13-18).
(19) The senate of the children of Israel is mentioned in Acts 5:21, but it
    was the senate of the Jews, called elders of the Jews (Luke 7:3; John
    3:1).

(20) Paul was chosen to bear the name of Christ before the children of
    Israel (Acts 9:15). This he did not do if Jews were not the Israel of
    his day, for he went to Jews in various places of the Roman Empire.
    No reference is made of him going to ten lost tribes. His first
    sermons were to Jews and his first persecution was from them (Acts
    9:22-23). In fact, the first gospel sermon by any apostle was to Jews
    only, called "men of Israel" (Acts 2:5,10,14,22) and "all the house of
    Israel" (Acts 2:36). Paul's first missionary trip was to Jews (Acts
    13:5,42-45). They rejected his preaching and he became bold enough
    to declare that if they did not want the gospel he would take it to the
    Gentiles—not to some so-called lost tribes of Israel (Acts 13:46-50).
    He continued preaching however, in the synagogues of the Jews
    (Acts 14:1-5,13; Acts 16:3,20; Acts 17:1,5,10,13,17; Acts 18:4-
    5,12,14,19,28; Acts 19:10-17,33; Acts 20:21; Acts 21:11,20-21,27;
    Acts 22:12,30; Acts 24:5,9,18; Acts 26:2-7,21; Acts 28:17,19,29;
    Romans 3:9,29; Romans 9:24; 1 Cor. 9:20; 1 Cor. 10:32; 1 Cor.
    12:13; Galatians 2:13-15). The Jews were his persecutors (Acts
    20:9,19; Acts 21:11-27; Acts 23:12-30; Acts 24:5-9,18,27; Acts
    25:2-24; Acts 26:2-21; 2 Cor. 11:24).

(21) Jesus was sent to Israel (Acts 10:36), but He went to Jews (John
    1:11; John 5:1-11:54)

(22) Paul called all the Jews he preached to "men of Israel" and "this
    people of Israel" (Acts 13:5,16,17). He declared to these Jews that
    God had fulfilled His promise in sending a Savior to Israel and that
    John the Baptist had preached repentance to all the people of Israel
    (Acts 13:23-24).

(23) The Jews from Asia visiting the temple in Jerusalem saw Paul with
    all the other Jews and cried out, "Men of Israel, help." They caught
    Paul and started to kill him, but he was rescued (Acts 21:27-28).
(24) Paul, in appealing to the Jews at Rome (Acts 28:17-19), told them
    that he was bound in chains because of the hope of Israel (Acts
    28:20). This would be no way to win Jews if they thought he was
    referring to an unknown and lost people and not to them.

(25) The Judah of Isaiah 1:1,9 is called Israel in Romans 9:27-33; but
    these people were the Jews of the N.T. (Romans 3:9,29; Romans
    9:24).

(26) Paul speaks of Jews and Israel as being the same and sets forth their
    rejection by God because of sin, and the acceptance of the Gentiles
    (not the so-called ten lost tribes) in their place (Romans 1:16;
    Romans 2:9,10,17,28-29; Romans 3:1,9,29; Romans 9:24; Romans
    10:1-12; Romans 11:1-29).

(27) Blindness in part has happened to Israel until the Messiah comes to
    save them (Romans 11:25-29), but it was to the Jews that Christ said
    their house was left desolate until they would accept Him—at His
    second coming (Matthew 23:27-29).

(28) Paul said that Israel after the flesh were partakers of the altar of God
    (2 Cor. 10:18). This could only refer to those of Judah and the Jews
    of other tribes with them, for they were the only ones who had the
    true worship at Jerusalem. The ten tribes made golden calves as their
    gods which they worshipped until they were cut off and scattered
    among the nations (1 Kings 12:25-33; 1 Kings 13:33-34; 2 Kings
    17:7-23). The godly of the ten tribes left the idolatry and returned to
    Judah in great numbers.

(29) Paul speaks of the new covenant yet to be made with both houses of
    Israel (Hebrews 8:8-10). Jeremiah reveals that it would be made in
    the day of the second coming of Christ when all Israel will be
    gathered from among the nations to be under their Messiah in
    Palestine forever (Jeremiah 30:3-11,18-24; Jeremiah 31:1-40;
    Jeremiah 32:37-44; Jeremiah 33:3-26; cp. Ezekiel 36-37).

(30) Jews will be the missionaries of the gospel in the Millennium and
    go from Jerusalem to evangelize the world (Isaiah 2:2-4; Isaiah 52:7;
   Zech. 8:23).

(31) The gospel was first to the Jew, and then to the Gentile (Romans
    1:16; Romans 2:9-10,17-29; Romans 3:1; Romans 10:12). Where is
    any third class called Israel apart from the Jews?

(32) The apostles did not recognize any other class of people besides
    Jews and Gentiles (Romans 1:16; Romans 2:9-10; Romans 3:9,29;
    Romans 9:24; 1 Cor. 1:22-24; 1 Cor. 10:32; 1 Cor. 12:13; Galatians
    2:13-15; Galatians 3:28; Col. 3:11; 1 Thes. 2:14; Rev. 2:9; Rev. 3:9).

(33) Paul's former religion was that of the Jews (Galatians 1:13-14),
    proving that they and not some other people who were lost and
    unknown, were Israel—the custodians of religion.

(34) Jesus said, "salvation is of the Jews" (John 4:22).

(35) The feasts of the law of Moses given to all Israel were called feasts
    of the Jews in the days of Christ, proving that they alone had
    preserved the law and its rituals and were the custodians of the
    program of God (John 2:13; John 5:1; John 6:4; John 7:2,11; John
    11:55; John 19:42)

(36) The Jews were the only people who had the first responsibility of
    hearing and obeying the gospel from John the Baptist (John 1:19;
    John 3:25); from Christ (John 1:11; John 3:1; John 4:9-24; John 5:1-
    18; John 6:4,41,52; John 7:1-35; John 8:22-57; John 9:18-22; John
    10:19-33; John 11:8-54; John 12:9-11; John 13:33; John 18:12-39;
    John 19:3-40; John 20:19); and from the apostles and early
    Christians who were mainly all Jews (Matthew 10:5; Acts 2:5,10,22-
    36; Acts 9:22-23; Acts 10:22,39; Acts 11:19; Acts 13:5,42-50; Acts
    14:1-13; Acts 16:3,20; Acts 17:1-17; Acts 18:2-28; Acts 19:10-33;
    Acts 20:3-21; Acts 21:11-27; Acts 22:12-30; Acts 24:5-27; Acts
    25:2-24; Acts 26:2-21; Acts 28:17-29; Romans 1:16; Romans 2:9-29;
    Romans 3:1-9; Romans 9:24; Romans 10:12; 1 Cor. 1:22-24; 1 Cor.
    9:20; 1 Cor. 10:32; 1 Cor. 12:13; 2 Cor. 11:24; Galatians 2:13-15; 1
    Thes. 2:14; Rev. 2:9; Rev. 3:9). Jews, not an unknown nation of
    Israelites, are mentioned in all these passages.
  (37) Jews had the responsibility of passing on the religion of Jehovah to
      others, but failed; so it was taken from them and given to the
      Gentiles—the only other class of human beings mentioned in
      Scripture, other than Jews (Matthew 21:33-46; Romans 11; 1 Cor.
      10:32; Galatians 1:13-14).

  (38) Jews were the ones who arrested Jesus, tried Him, and condemned
      Him as worthy of death (John 18:12-19:40; Acts 2:22,36).

  (39) No man was ever called to go to a separate people from the Jews
      and Gentiles who are mentioned so often together. Not one reference
      can be found of a third class of people other than these. The church
      (which is often referred to) is made up of both Jews and Gentiles (1
      Cor. 10:32). So it is clear that there is not an Israel separate and
      distinct from the ones known as Jews.

  (40) The Jews of the days of Christ and the apostles are the only people
      considered the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel (Acts 3:12-
      13,25; Acts 4:1-8; Acts 7:1,44-54; Acts 13:17) and the children of
      the covenant with God (Acts 3:25; Romans 3:1-2; Romans 9:3-5).

  (41) Paul and others called themselves both Jews and Israelites (Acts
      16:20; Acts 21:39; Acts 22:3; Romans 9:3-5,24; Romans 10:1;
      Romans 11:1-29; 2 Cor. 11:22; Phil. 3:4-6).

  (42) In the N.T. the term Jews and Greeks, Jews and Gentiles, and Jews,
      Gentiles and church of God are found, but never Jews, Israel, and
      Gentiles (Acts 18:4,12-17,28; Acts 19:10,17; Acts 21:20-26; Romans
      3:9; 2 Cor. 10:32; 2 Cor. 12:13; Galatians 3:28; Col. 3:11).

79. The Anglo-Saxon theory is not scriptural from any standpoint.

 Thirty Scriptural Ideas Wrongly Applied in the Anglo-Saxon
                           Theory
  (1) Israel to be a great nation (Genesis 18:18). This has been true in the
      past and will be in the future when Israel becomes great under the
      Messiah who will reign in Jerusalem, not London or elsewhere. This
    applies to all twelve tribes, including Judah and all Jews (Isaiah 2:2-
    4; Isaiah 9:6-7; Ezekiel 36-37; Micah 4; Zech. 14; Luke 1:32-33;
    Rev. 11:15).

(2) Israel's name to be "great" (Genesis 12:2). This refers to Abraham,
    not Israel, so it proves nothing as far as Great Britain is concerned.
    Suppose we used the same argument in other scriptures: we could
    have Great Ishmael (Genesis 17:20), the Great nations of Canaan
    (Joshua 23:9), Great Babylon (Jeremiah 6:22; Jeremiah 50:41), and
    other Great people, all of whom would be identified with Israel
    because great was used of them.

(3) Israel was to be exceedingly fruitful (Genesis 28:14). This does not
    prove Anglo-Saxons to be Israel any more than the fruitfulness of
    China, India or other large nations.

(4) Israel was to spread abroad in four directions (Genesis 28:14). This
    was to be done only in the bounds of the promised land (Genesis
    15:18-21; Ezekiel 47:13-48:29). Many other nations have spread in
    four directions in larger countries than the promised land, yet we do
    not seek to identify them as Israel on this basis.

(5) Israel to have a Davidic king (2 Samuel 7; Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel
    37:24; Hosea 3:4-5). This is true but it does not identify Israel as
    Britain, or America which has no king. It will come to pass when all
    Israel is regathered from the nations to be back in their own land
    under their Messiah, as is clear in these scriptures and many others.

(6) Israel will be the first of the nations (Genesis 49:22-26; Deut. 4:7;
    Deut. 14:2). These scriptures applied to the whole nation of Israel in
    Moses' day, except Genesis 49:22-26 which applies to this one tribe
    of twelve that will be fruitful and great under the Messiah when He
    comes in the last days (Genesis 49:1).

(7) Israel was to continue a nation forever (2 Samuel 7; Jeremiah 31:35-
    37). This is true but will not be fulfilled until all Israel is regathered
    (as in the points above). These scriptures prove nothing concerning
    England and America.
(8) Israel to have a new home north of Palestine (2 Samuel 7:10; 1
    Chron. 17:9; Isaiah 24:15; Jeremiah 3:18; Jeremiah 31:8). There is
    nothing in any of these scriptures to give the idea that Israel would
    be moved to a place north. The land for Israel has been settled by
    God as between the Mediterranean and the Euphrates, and from
    northern Palestine to the river of Egypt in the south (Genesis 15:18-
    21). In the future restoration of all Israel to Palestine the north and
    south borders are to be enlarged to be from Hamath on the north to
    the Indian Ocean on the south, taking in all the Arabian peninsula
    (Ezekiel 47:13-48:29). The isles referred to do not mean the British
    Isles any more than in Genesis 10:5 where we have the isles of the
    Gentiles. In Esther 10:1 we read of the king of Persia taxing the isles
    of the sea, and we know he did not rule Britain. The term isles in
    many places simply means the coastlands surrounding the
    Mediterranean or any other large body of water. Regarding the
    bringing of Israel from the north, the Bible teaches that Israel was to
    have invaders from the north who would take them captive; the
    reference means they would be gathered again from the north in the
    last days when they will also be gathered from other countries
    (Jeremiah 23:3,8; Ezekiel 20:33-39; Ezekiel 37:11-28).

(9) Israel's home was to be uninvadable and undefeatable (Isaiah 41:11-
    14). This scripture and others like it merely teach that when Israel
    comes to repentance and is gathered to Palestine under their Messiah
    in the Millennium, no enemy will hurt them anymore. It doesn't
    mean that Israel could never be defeated, for the nation was defeated
    and the land invaded numerous times. They were finally led captive
    among all nations where they are today and from where they will be
    gathered by Christ at His second coming. This has nothing to do with
    England and America. The promise of victory over enemies was
    conditional—according to their obedience to God (Leviticus 26;
    Deut. 28). Dispersion was predicted if they sinned (Leviticus 26:32-
    34).

(10) Israel like a lion (Numbers 23:24; Numbers 24:9). This does not
    prove that England is Israel anymore than the same symbol makes
   Assyria (Jeremiah 50:17-18), Babylon (Daniel 7:1-6,17), Satan (1
   Peter 5:8), or Christ (Rev. 5:5) Israel.

(11) Israel to be the mistress of the uttermost parts of the earth (Deut.
    33:17; Psalm 2; Psalm 98:3). These passages are Millennial. The first
    refers to Joseph's tribe only. Psalm 2 refers to Christ reigning over
    the nations of the earth at His second coming, and Psalm 98:3 refers
    to His salvation.

(12) Israel to be immensely wealthy (Deut. 28:14; Isaiah 60:16). The
    first passage was to be fulfilled with all twelve tribes to whom it was
    given, and that only if they obeyed God. This was true when they did
    obey, and not true when they sinned. The last passage will be
    fulfilled in the Millennium when all Israel is fully restored to
    Palestine.

(13) Israel was to be a company of nations, or have a great colonial
    empire (Genesis 17:4-16; Genesis 35:11). The Hebrew word for
    nations means troops, tribes, or peoples, meaning that Israel was to
    consist of a company of tribes. This has been fulfilled and will be
    fulfilled in all eternity when the twelve tribes will be under Christ
    and the apostles (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:29-30; Ezekiel 47-48).
    Israel was never to have colonies of her own people all over the
    earth; she was to remain one nation upon the mountains of Israel
    (Ezekiel 37), and be the head of all Gentile nations (Deut. 28:13;
    Isaiah 60:16; Isaiah 61:5; Rev. 11:15). England and America
    certainly have not been the head of all nations and never will be as
    God promised Israel.

(14) Israel to lend to other nations, and borrow from none (Deut. 28:12).
    This was promised to Israel upon obedience only (Deut. 28:1), and it
    was true of them when they served God, but not true when they
    sinned.

(15) Israel was to possess the gates of her enemies, said by some to be
    Gibralter and the Suez Canal (Genesis 22:17). This passage means
    that Israel will conquer the city gates of her enemies in siege. Out of
    275 times the word gate is used it never means canals or strategic
    points, as one can see in Exodus 32:27; Deut. 21:19; Deut. 22:24;
    Deut. 25:7; Joshua 2:71, etc.

(16) Israel was to be an island or a coast people (Isaiah 24:15). This
    passage does not speak of Israel being an island people; it merely
    refers to them singing among many other peoples while in
    dispersion. See point (8), above. Such passages where isles is found
    means maritime countries, not any one country in particular.

(17) Israel was to lose all trace of her lineage and be blind as to her
    origin (Hosea 1:9-10; Hosea 2:17; Isaiah 42:16). The first scripture
    refers to the cutting off of Israel as God's people, not to the losing of
    their identity as Israelites, for the very next verse (Hosea 1:11)
    predicts that both Israel and Judah would be gathered as one people
    again. The second scripture has nothing to say about the name of
    Israel, but refers to the names of Baal as not being remembered
    anymore. The passage in Isaiah 42:16 speaks of the spiritually blind.

(18) Israel was to keep sabbath forever (Exodus 31:13-17). Keeping
    sabbath could not possibly identify race, color, or creed. Israel has
    not kept sabbath forever up until now, for God promised to do away
    with all her sabbaths (Isaiah 1:13; Hosea 2:11). England and
    America are surely not sabbath-keeping nations, as is well known by
    those who have lived in these countries.

(19) Israel was to have a great heathen empire (Psalm 2). This refers to
    Christ, not Israel. We could not substitute England for Son in this
    passage and be logical.

(20. Israel was to be the custodian of the oracles of God (Isaiah 59:21).
    The Jews of the N.T. were (Romans 3:1-2; Romans 9:4-6).

(21) Israel was to carry the gospel to all the world (Genesis 28:14). True,
    and it will be the Jews that do it (Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 2:2-4; Isaiah 52:7;
    Zech. 8:23).

(22) Israel was to be called by the name of Isaac—Isaac's sons (Genesis
    21:12). This scripture refers to all twelve tribes, not just ten of them.
   This is a shallow argument, for in the N.T., not only Jews but
   Gentiles also are said to be in Isaac in the sense that they are children
   of the promise like Isaac (Romans 4:9-25; Romans 9:8,23-33;
   Romans 10:9-21; Romans 11:1-32; 1 Cor. 12:13; Galatians 3:6-
   16,25-29; Galatians 4:28-31; Col. 3:11).

(23) The singular name Great Britain, "Brit" or "Brith," is Hebrew for
    "covenant," and "Ish" means "man," so British means covenant-man,
    and Britain means covenant land. The Bible teaches that Palestine is
    the covenant land and the Israel to whom this land belongs are the
    covenant people (Genesis 12:1-3; Genesis 5:18-21; Genesis 17:1-17).

(24) Israel was to pray toward Jerusalem (1 Kings 8:44-48). There is no
    connection between this scripture and England any more than other
    countries that pray in all directions, including the East.

(25) Israel was to deliver Jerusalem in the last days (Ezekiel 35:14;
    Ezekiel 36:8-12; Luke 21:24). These passages say nothing about
    Israel delivering Jerusalem, much less England. When Christ comes
    He will deliver Jerusalem (Zech. 14:1-21).

(26) Israel's teachers, pastors, and shepherds were to be blind (Ezekiel
    34:1-16). This really refers to Judah and her leaders, for Ezekiel
    prophesied to the Jews during the captivities, and not one word was
    said of an Israel apart from Judah.

(27) Israel will ever live under a monarchy (Numbers 23:21; 1 Kings
    7:13-15). The first passage refers to Israel 450 years before they had
    a king, and the last one does not mention a monarchy; so this claim is
    based on theory only. Israel has been without a king for over 2,500
    years and will not have one again until the Messiah comes to reign
    forever over them; then, they will always have a monarchy (Isaiah
    9:6-7; Jeremiah 30-31; Ezekiel 36-37; Daniel 2:44-45; Daniel 7:13-
    14; Zech. 14; Luke 1:32-33; Rev. 11:15; Rev. 20:1-10).

(28) Israel was always to be separated from the Gentile nations (1
    Samuel 12:22). This says nothing about being separated from
    Gentiles, but simply states that God had made them His people. This
      applies to all the tribes, not just to ten. Jews are the only separated
      people of Israel today; Anglo-Saxons mix with other races all the
      time.

   (29) Israel's soldiers in the latter days were to wear scarlet uniforms
       (Nahum 2:3-4). This refers to the Assyrian soldiers of Nineveh
       (Nahum 1:1,11; Nahum 2:1,3,7,8,13; Nahum 3:7), not soldiers of
       England.

   (30) Israel was to live part of their history without a king (Hosea 3:4-5).
       This proves nothing regarding England, but it does say that after this
       in the last days Israel will return to God and seek David and be
       established again as a nation (Hosea 1:10-11; Hosea 2:14-23; Acts
       15:13-18).

   We have given these 30 so-called scriptural arguments of the Anglo-
   Saxon theory to show how utterly unsound the teaching is in the light of
   hundreds of passages.

80. The theory is unhistorical. No genuine and authentic history has ever
   been found to show that the kings of England are direct descendants of
   the kings of Judah, or that Anglo-Saxons are the ten tribes. Anglo-
   Saxons are of Japheth, not Shem (see The Sons of Japheth and The Sons
   of Shem). There have been some attempts to attach some human records
   of Irish and Scottish kings to Bible genealogies but the efforts have been
   in vain for lack of proof.

81. The theory is not true from a national and racial standpoint. As to the
   language, there is no affinity between Hebrew and English. As to history,
   the British are a totally distinct people from Israel. As to manners and
   customs (both religious and social), there has been a great contrast
   throughout the ages. If there was an Israelite emigration to England there
   is not the slightest scriptural or historical evidence. The pages of English
   history have no trace of such mighty tribes ever landing in England

How vastly different is the record of the short Roman invasion and
occupation.
82. The theory is not logical, practical, or beneficial in any way except to
   exalt the British Empire and America:

   (1) None of the arguments are aimed to lead souls to Christ and personal
       salvation.

   (2) The blood of Christ and the new birth are not emphasized.

   (3) It leads to division and strife.

   (4) It classifies other biblical knowledge as shallow and elementary.

   (5) It fosters a clannish spirit and discourages fellowship with those who
       oppose it.

   (6) It is a latter-day delusion, to draw men away from spiritual and
       eternal matters.

   (7) It fosters excessive national pride.

   (8) It nationalizes the promises and covenants of the Bible.

   (9) It is dispensationally wrong, requiring that Britain must enlarge to
       become the kingdom of God on earth.

   (10) It robs Christ of His Millennial work in the world.

   (11) It does away with the coming kingdom of heaven and of David.

   (12) It clouds Christian and Jewish destiny and links destiny to race
       instead of grace.

   (13) It makes mental acceptance of its claims a source of justification
       without demanding personal holiness.

   (14) It robs the Jewish nation of their place in the plan of God.

   (15) It misinterprets prophecy and many sections of Scripture.
    (16) It diverts the use of God's money and the right use of time and talent
        to other things when they should be used for the winning of souls.

    (17) It is of no benefit to salvation and a Christian life. Nationality has
        nothing to do with God's plan to save men now.

    (18) It erroneously satisfies the hearts of some Anglo-Saxons who do not
        know Jesus as a personal Savior.

    (19) It cannot make men holy or cause them to live right in carrying out
        the Christian program.

    (20) It esteems national blessings as a special mark of God's favor and
        carnalizes and degrades our privileges in Christ.

One thing is certain: all latter-day events of prophecy in the Bible center
around Jerusalem and Palestine, not London and Washington which are not
once mentioned in Scripture (Psalm 102:21; Psalm 135:21; Isaiah 1:1;
Isaiah 2:1-4; Isaiah 4:1-6; Isaiah 11:3-16; Isaiah 12:6; Isaiah 16:1-5; Isaiah
24:23; Isaiah 27:12-13; Isaiah 30:19; Isaiah 31:5,9; Isaiah 40:9-11; Isaiah

a [Ish-Bosheth] Ishbosheth, man of shame. Saul's youngest and only
 remaining son, he was made king over Benjamin and the rest of Israel
 (except Judah) by Abner (2 Samuel 2:8-15; 2 Samuel 3:7-15; 2 Samuel
 4:5-12). Also called Esh-baal, man of Baal (1 Chron. 8:33; 1 Chron. 9:39).
 This may have been his original name, with Baal changed to bosheth
 meaning shame—a popular nickname because of the idol for which he
 was named.

b [forty years old when he began to reign over Israel]

                       Ishbosheth's Chronology
This says he was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he
reigned two years. This could mean that it took Abner five years to
consolidate the rest of Israel sufficiently, and for them to recover from the
defeat in the north by the Philistines when Saul died, for them to be willing
to make Ishbosheth king. It must be remembered that when Saul and Israel
were defeated, the Philistines occupied the major cities of Israel in the
Mount Gilboa and Jezreel areas, the Israelites having fled across Jordan (1
Samuel 31:7). These facts being true, then he was born after Saul had been
king for five years, and he actually reigned only two years over Israel
before the war between Israel and Judah as in 2 Samuel 2:12-32. This
would harmonize with 2 Samuel 3:1 about a long strife between the house
of David and that of Saul. The strife no doubt lasted the entire seven and a
half years David was reigning in Hebron. In his scheme of dividing Israel,
Abner saw the need to have the tribes east of Jordan behind him, so he took
time to consolidate them; then, after at least five years' delay, made Saul's
son king at Mahanaim. Then Ashurites, Jezreelites, Ephraimites, and other
tribes accepted Ishbosheth as king (2 Samuel 2:8-10). David did not contest
Abner's act, or force matters, but was content to wait God's time to make
him the king of all Israel. He avoided any war with Abner until trouble was
threatened from that direction. It came when Abner and his servants went
from Mahanaim to Gibeon in Benjamin. There the two rival armies met,
and in the battle Abner was defeated (2 Samuel 2:12-32).

                        Michal Restored to David
Ishbosheth acted immediately on David's request and took Michal from her
present husband, Phaltiel, and sent her to David (2 Samuel 3:15-16). After
driving David away from home, Saul had given her to Phaltiel to be his
wife (1 Samuel 25:44). Michal may have lost some of her love for David in
the meantime, or her pride and slavery to etiquette caused her to make fun
of him when he danced publicly before the ark without his kingly robes on
(2 Samuel 6:14-16). This was called despising him in her heart, and was
such a serious offense that it became the reason for her being childless until
her death (▪ 2 Samuel 6:21-23, notes).

                        The Meaning of "Agency"
This is a simple example of how Hebrews expressed the idea of agency.
David spoke as if he personally took hold of the young man and killed him,
but in reality he had a young man do it for him (2 Samuel 1:15). So it is in
many cases where they expressed the idea of God doing certain things
(Genesis 12:17; Exodus 32:35; Deut. 28:59; 2 Samuel 12:15; etc.). It seems
as if God personally sent sickness, plagues, and curses, when in reality He
only permitted or gave the command for proper agents to carry out His will
concerning people who had committed sin worthy of punishment (Galatians
6:7-8).

    confirmed that the young man who fabricated a story to impress him did
    so to get a reward (see notes, ▪ 2 Samuel 1:2,5,6,13).

                         David's Thirty Years
This thirty years of David when he began to reign answers a number of
questions:

1. How old he was when he began to reign

2. How old he was when he killed the giant. He could not have been more
   than 18-20 years of age (1 Samuel 17)

3. How long he was driven away from home and chased by Saul. It could
   not have been more than 6-10 years (1 Samuel 18-31)

   old (1 Kings 1:1-4), being 30 when he began to reign for 40 years (2
   Samuel 5:4)

He evidently was only 20-24 years old when he gathered his men in the
cave of Adullam and became captain over them.

a [when the Philistines heard]

                            New War with Philistia
The Philistines had not been heard from for at least eight years now, the last
time being in the battle of Gilboa when Saul was defeated (1 Samuel 31). It
seems they were unconcerned all the time David was ruling over Judah for
seven and a half years, perhaps because this was only a part of Israel.
Furthermore, since David had lived among them for more than a year, as
one of them, and had simply settled in Hebron as ruler of his own tribe—the
Judah portion—they no doubt considered it lightly, though watching to see
what would develop between him and all Israel. Now, since he had been
accepted and crowned king over all Israel, they mobilized their armies to
seek him and destroy him before he could consolidate his hold upon Israel
and make his own war preparations.

b [seek David] Compare 1 Samuel 26:1-2.

c [David heard of it] David no doubt had spies among the Philistines, or
    other means of intelligence. Since Saul's defeat nearly eight years before,
    the Philistines had controlled the greater part of Israel, so Israelites living
    among them would naturally know about some of their plans.

d [hold]
                               David's Hold
All that is known of this hold is that he went down to it instead of up,
suggesting that it might be the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1). If he had
already conquered Zion and made it his city, as in 2 Samuel 5:6-10, then the
hold must have been some convenient defense south of Zion and the city of
David. Adullam was a large cave about 12 miles southwest of Jerusalem
(see The Cave of Adullam). The valley of Rephaim was a fertile one
southwest of Jerusalem, just beyond the low ridge which skirts the valley of
Hinnom and extended southward along the road to Bethlehem (about 15
miles away), being surrounded on all sides by rocky hills and ridges (Joshua
15:8; Joshua 18:16; Isaiah 17:5). Here the first battles between David and
the Philistines took place, and from this hold David had to go up to meet
them; so it was south of this valley. Josephus says the valley of Rephaim
was between Jerusalem and Bethlehem. Baal-perazim of 2 Samuel 5:20
means the lord of breakings through. It was a spot in the valley of Rephaim
where the first victory over the Philistines was won (2 Samuel 5:18-21; 1
Chron. 14:11). It could have been the same as Mount Perazim of Isaiah
28:21.

                           The Davidic Covenant
This chapter records the Davidic covenant promising David an eternal seed
and throne, as the 12th, 15th, and 17th chapters of Genesis record the
Abrahamic covenant promising an eternal seed and land. Both covenants
are conditional upon faith and obedience to God. Many call them
unconditional, but this can be true only in the sense that the benefits
promised aren't earned by works. Like the gospel of today, one does not
earn salvation by works (Ephes. 2:8-9); yet no man receives benefits
without obedience in the initial as well as the final stage of salvation (1
John 1:7). The whole program of requirements is that of obedience and
living soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world (2 Cor. 5:17-18;
2 Cor. 7:1; Titus 2:11-13; Hebrews 12:14; 1 John 1:7). If these covenants
were entirely unconditional and Israel did not have to obey God to receive
their benefits, then why are they not blessed according to these benefits
now? The people to whom they were promised went into sin, apostasy,
captivity, and dispersion and will not receive fulfillment of the promises
until they are regathered in repentance and obedience to God (Leviticus 26;
Deut. 28). God plainly said to David concerning his son, "If he commit
iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men" (2 Samuel 7:14). This is
what happened. His sons and all Israel sinned and they are now in the
process of chastening. See the many scriptures proving a regathering and
conversion of Israel in the latter days under the Messiah in Anglo-Saxon
Theory. See covenants 6 and 14 under Fifteen Great Covenants.

                        Israel's Millennial Land
This refers to the final appointment of the promised land to all the house of
Israel, at the second coming of Christ. From then on they will dwell in their
own place and move no more; neither shall the wicked afflict them anymore
(2 Samuel 7:10). One reading of this should be sufficient to make it clear
that this has a future fulfillment. Furthermore, many other prophecies state
the time of such fulfillment. God did appoint them the promised land
(Genesis 13:14-17; Genesis 15:18-21; Genesis 17:7-8; Genesis 26:3-4;
Genesis 28:4,13-15; Genesis 35:11-12), and He planted them in this land
twice: first, in the settlement of the land under Moses and Joshua (Numbers
32; Joshua 13:1-21:45); second, after the captivities to Assyria and Babylon
(Ezra, Nehemiah, and Haggai). They sinned after the first settlement until
God had to remove them (2 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 24). Then they sinned
after the second settlement until He had to remove them again and scatter
them among the other nations (Daniel 9:26-27; Matthew 23:37-39; Matthew
24:2-3; Luke 21:20-24). God has predicted that He will make for them a
second regathering and final appointment and settlement of the land when
they shall move no more; and wicked men will not afflict them anymore, as
before (2 Samuel 7:10; Deut. 4:25-30; Deut. 30:1-10; Isaiah 11:10-16;
Isaiah 60:8-22; Isaiah 66:19-21; Jeremiah 3:14-25; Jeremiah 16:14-21;
Jeremiah 23:3-8; Jeremiah 30:1-24; Jeremiah 31:18-40; Jeremiah 32:37-44;
Jeremiah 33:6-26; Ezekiel 11:17-21; Ezekiel 20:33-44; Ezekiel 34:11-31;
Ezekiel 36:1-37:28; Matthew 24:31).

c [place of their own]

                          A Place of Their Own
To associate this scripture with the idea that ten so-called lost tribes moved
to England and America (as some teach) where they will move no more is
unscriptural. No such thing could be understood here; certainly David did
not understand that God would do away with his tribe of Judah and rob
them of the original covenants promises, causing them to have no part in
the fulfillment of the predictions made to him and his house. It being true
that the English and Americans will not move anymore only proves they are
not Israel, for all Israel will be moved or regathered from the other nations
where they are now scattered so as to be back in their own land in the latter
days. See The Anglo-Saxon Theory. The children of wickedness are still
afflicting England, America, Israel, and many other lands, which proves
that the verse has not yet been fulfilled with any people as yet.

One of the most interesting facts in this chapter is that on the occasion of

eternally. God did make David a house, but it was destroyed along with all
Israel. It is now in destruction and unknown among the nations. Prophecy
declares that God will come and rebuild the house of David and set it up
again (after the church age) in the future (Isaiah 11:1-16; Hosea 3:4-5;
Amos 9:11-15). James said that all the prophets agree with this (Acts 15:13-

          David's Eternal House, Kingdom, and Throne
House here refers to household or family, the line of succession to the
throne. This line ended in Jehoiachin (called Coniah) at the time of the
captivities (Jeremiah 22:23-30). No man of his seed shall ever reign again
in Judah and Jerusalem. This literally happened as Zedekiah, his uncle, was
made king after him—a man not in the direct line of the kings of Judah (2
Kings 24:6-20). Zedekiah is not in the royal genealogy of Matthew 1 or the
other line of David through Nathan in Luke 3 (from which Mary came).
Christ, who was not of the direct royal line, inherited the throne right
through Joseph. See note, ▪ Matthew 1:6. It is therefore out of the question
that a daughter of Zedekiah should have continued the throne rights of the
house of David down to the present Queen and royal family of England.
Concerning the small remnant of Jews who were to escape from Egypt
(Jeremiah 44:28), which those who teach the Anglo-Israelite theory say
included the daughter of Zedekiah who continued the royal line of David,
no mention is made of any of the king's seed at all. No kingly line of Israel
was ever preserved through a woman, and the specific prophecy was that if
the Judahites stayed in the land of Judea they would be built up (Jeremiah
42:10). This would exclude a lone woman going to another country where
the house of David and his royal line would be built up. The strange land
the Judahites were to go into (as in Jeremiah 15:11-14) is explained: "into
all the kingdoms of the earth" (Jeremiah 15:4), not England alone.
David's kingdom was made up first of Judah (2 Samuel 2:7) and later the
other tribes of Israel (2 Samuel 5:1-5). This is what constituted the original
kingdom of David and this is what it will consist of in the future when all
the tribes will be gathered under the Messiah who will reign over them in
Palestine forever (2 Samuel 7:16; Isaiah 9:6-7; Isaiah 11:10-16; Jeremiah
30:9; Ezekiel 36-37; Hosea 3:4-5; Luke 1:32-33; Rev. 11:15; Rev. 19:11-
20:10).

All three things in this passage are eternal—the house, the kingdom, and the
throne of David (2 Samuel 7:16; Isaiah 9:6-7; Luke 1:32-33; Rev. 11:15;
Rev. 20:1-10). All three were done away with when Jerusalem was taken by
Nebuchadnezzar and not one of them has ever been restored. The throne
and crown were to be removed from Zedekiah and remain removed until
the Messiah came, whose right it is to rule (Psalm 2; Isaiah 9:6-7; Isaiah
16:4; Jeremiah 3:14-18; Jeremiah 16:14-21; Jeremiah 23:3-8,20; Jeremiah
30:3-24; Jeremiah 31:8-14,27-40; Jeremiah 32:37-44; Jeremiah 33:3-26;
Jeremiah 50:19-20; Ezekiel 1:17-21; Ezekiel 20:33-44; Ezekiel 21:27;
Ezekiel 28:25-26; Ezekiel 34:11-31; Ezekiel 36:3-38; Ezekiel 37:1-28;
Ezekiel 38:8-21; Ezekiel 39:1-39; Ezekiel 43:7; Ezekiel 47:13-48:35;
Daniel 2:44-45; Daniel 7:13-14,27; Hosea 3:4-5; Joel 2-3; Amos 9:11-15;
Obadiah 17-21; Micah 4-5; Zech. 12-14; Luke 1:32-33; Acts 15:13-18; Rev.

   7:24).

15. You have become their God.

                             The Syrian War
According to this passage David slew the men of 700 chariots, or 2,100
(allowing 3 to a chariot), besides 40,000 horsemen and their commander. In
the parallel passage (1 Chron. 19:18) it is said that David slew of the
Syrians seven thousand men which fought in chariots, which would make
10 men to each chariot. The 7,000 count is more probable with a vast army
like this, but we cannot be sure. There may have been a mistake in copying.
The Jews expressed numbers by single letters of the alphabet. For instance,
the Hebrew letter zayin (z) with a dot above it stood for 7,000, and nun
stood for 700. It was easy for a copyist to make an error, especially if one
letter was marred slightly. Such a system accounts for various mistakes in
numbers.

a [weight whereof was a talent of gold with the precious stones]

                           Weight of the Crown
A talent of gold weighed 125 lbs. troy, valued at $600,000. How a crown
weighing this much could be worn by a man is hard to understand.

Four Explanations of This:

1. The crown was placed only temporarily upon David, being held up by
   others, to signify that he was king of the Ammonites.

2. The crown was not actually worn at all by the king, but suspended over
   the head, being fixed to the canopy of the throne.

3. The crown was that of the idol god Milcom or Malcom and was taken off
   him and given to David as part of the spoils. This seems to contradict
   facts in the case, for the Hebrew word for king's here is melek (HSN-
   4428) which is the ordinary one for "king" as translated of men about
   2,091 times, and not once as Malcom or Milcom.
4. The value of the gold and jewels in the crown was equal to that of a
   talent of gold; therefore, the crown was light enough to be worn by a
   man.

Absalom, father of peace. He was David's third son by his wife Maacah, a

a [so vexed, that he fell sick for his sister Tamar]

                       Amnon's Lust for Tamar
Amnon had developed a violent lust for Tamar. The law forbade sexual
relations with close relatives (Leviticus 18:11); but, with the example of
Abraham and others in all pagan countries, he seems to have convinced
himself that it would be permissible for a man to have his half-sister. He
had no way of making his feelings for Tamar known, for virgins were kept
in seclusion from the company of men—even those who were close
relatives—not being permitted to see them without the presence of
witnesses. How to contact her was his brooding problem; so much so that
Amnon became sick and sore vexed daily in his great desire for her; yet, he
was held in check by a thought which made him doubt that it would be right
to touch her (2 Samuel 13:1-2).

                                Joab's Plan
Joab stepped into the picture here, for he knew David longed for Absalom
and wanted to pardon him (2 Samuel 13:39-14:1). He and a certain woman
plotted to get David to invite him back home. Being strongly attached to
Absalom, and having recovered from his sorrow over Amnon's violent
death, David now desired to see his exiled son again, after three years of
absence. Perhaps the dread of public opinion and his regard for public
interests made him hesitate to recall his son. Joab, seeing this struggle due
to royal duty and parental affection, decided it was time to act as a mediator
and relieve the king of the pressure he was under. He sent for a wise woman
of Tekoah to cooperate with him in pleading for Absalom's return. He
directed her to seek an audience with David so as to point out to him that
under certain circumstances it was better to spare the life of a murderer.

Seven Parts to the Plan:
1. Joab sent to Tekoah (a city about 12 miles south of Jerusalem and about 7
    miles south of Bethlehem) for a wise woman who would be actress
    enough to deceive David and get from him an expression of willingness
    to pardon Absalom (2 Samuel 14:2)

2. She was to play the part of a widow; her condition of life was designed to
   excite compassion in David

3. She was to come before the king and speak the words Joab put into her
   mouth, and make a plea for Absalom under the guise that it was actually
   her own experience (2 Samuel 14:3)

4. She was to be far enough from Jerusalem to make it hard to inquire into
   the circumstances of her case, so as to avoid detection of referring to
   Absalom until David had committed himself (2 Samuel 14:4-12)

5. Her case was to be similar enough to that of David's experience to
   awaken in the king a desire to act quickly to save her son—before the
   story was applied to him (2 Samuel 14:5-12)

6. After David gave his word to spare the murderer the application was to
   be made to himself and Absalom (2 Samuel 14:13-20)

7. The whole case was not to be plain or visible enough to David to be
   discovered before he gave his word to spare the murderer (2 Samuel
   14:13-20)

Thus, the mournful tale, her posing as an aged widow in distress, and her
impressive manner—all combined to move the heart of David and secure
his help in this case of protecting the son.

                              David's Promise
David promised to give charge concerning her case, but this did not satisfy
her. It was too far distant and by delay she could not bring her present
business to a conclusion. She proposed that if the public resented justice in
this case, the whole blame would fall upon her and her father's house with
the king being guiltless. This brought a further promise of protection for her
and the murderer (2 Samuel 14:9-10); but it did not yet bring the case to a
final conclusion, for the plan was to get the king to promise that the whole
case would be dropped where it was. The woman then pressed him for a
definite promise, pointing out that when God is approached for forgiveness
He responds before it is too late, and that if David waited any longer it
would be too late to help her son. The king then made a promise that her
son would not be touched (2 Samuel 14:11). This brought the matter to the
desired conclusion so she then applied the story to David himself (2 Samuel
14:12-20).

                        The Woman's Argument
The whole argument of the woman for the pardon and recall of Absalom
could be paraphrased: You have granted a pardon to my son who slew his
brother, and yet you hesitate to pardon Absalom whose sin was no greater
or different from that of my son. He was provoked and slew his brother for
the crime against his sister when you did nothing in accordance with the
law to punish for the crime. If you can set aside the law in one case, can you
not set it aside in another? The death of my son would be only a private loss
to my family, but the loss of Absalom would be a loss to all Israel, who
look to him to succeed you on the throne. Whatever is done must be done
quickly (2 Samuel 14:13). Amnon is dead and any punishment to Absalom
would not repair the damage done; it is like water poured out that cannot be
gathered up again. God shows no partiality; He provides means to pardon
those who sin. Should you not do likewise—you who are supposed to act in
His stead as ruler of His people (2 Samuel 14:14)? I have come to speak to
the king because the people have made me afraid regarding what they might
do in resenting the action of my king. I will now make my request and it
may be that the king will grant it (2 Samuel 14:15) to deliver his handmaid.
I have concluded that the word of my lord will be granted concerning the
request that I shall make to my king (2 Samuel 14:16-17).

a [Let him turn to his own house, and let him not see my face] David did
    have some excuses for pardoning Absalom, but none could justify his
    failure to execute the law of Moses impartially regarding the death-
    penalty sins of both Amnon and Absalom. In granting such a pardon he
    acted as an eastern despot, not as a righteous king of Israel. He now made
    his next regrettable mistake—refusing to see Absalom on his return.

                              David's Mistake
David relented enough to send Joab to Geshur to get Absalom, but he made
the serious mistake of refusing to see him when he returned home (2
Samuel 14:21-24). It would have been better not to let him come back at all
than to treat him this way. Absalom naturally resented David's attitude, and
later confessed that coming home to a partially unforgiving father to live
year after year without even seeing him was a miserable life (2 Samuel
14:32). What David hoped to gain by this stubbornness we do not know. It
estranged Absalom from him permanently, and eventually caused the
greatest trouble of David's career. This should be a lesson to all parents
when forgiving wayward children. Forgiveness should be wholehearted and
complete, not in word only with the heart remaining reserved and
implacable.

Whether Absalom would have plotted against David if he'd been received
wholeheartedly, we cannot say. History only records his vain attempt to
rebel against David. Absalom might have gained the throne by right of
succession and popularity, for all Israel loved him (2 Samuel 14:25-15:6);
but it would have been impossible after the rebellion, had he lived. It is true
that David promised the throne to Solomon, the son of Bathsheba, but this
might have changed with Absalom being so popular (1 Kings 1:13). His
death, however, resolved the issue of throne rights where he was concerned.

                The Fifteen Steps in Absalom's Rebellion
1. He prepared chariots and horses and fifty men to run before him.

2. He arose early and stood in the way of the gate (2 Samuel 15:2).

3. Every man who came to David for justice was approached and the cause
   of his coming to the king inquired about. Absalom would flatter the man
   and tell him his cause was just, but there was no one appointed by the
   king to give him justice. Then Absalom would declare that if he were
   king he would see to it that everyone received justice (2 Samuel 15:2-4).

4. He posed as the real champion of the people, kissing every man who
   came to him and stealing the hearts of the people of Israel (2 Samuel
   15:5-6).

5. He begged leave of David to go to Hebron that he might pay vows to
   God and serve the Lord, as he had promised while in exile (2 Samuel
   15:7-8).

6. He set up headquarters in Hebron and sent spies throughout all the tribes
   of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then
   you shall say that Absalom reigns in Hebron" (2 Samuel 15:10).

7. He took two hundred men from Jerusalem to help him, but kept all plans
   secret from them (2 Samuel 15:11).

8. He sent for Ahithophel, David's counselor and the grandfather of
   Bathsheba with whom David had sinned. Ahithophel was now ready to
   turn against David to avenge the harm done to his son's family. The
   conspiracy was then strong enough to cause David much trouble (2
   Samuel 15:12).

9. Absalom and the rebels with him marched on Jerusalem to take over the
   city (2 Samuel 16:15-19).

10. He asked counsel of Ahithophel who advised him to lie with his father's
   concubines so that all Israel would know that he was abhorred by his
   father; then all followers would be strong for him (2 Samuel 16:20-21).

11. He laid with his father's concubines, as advised (2 Samuel 16:22-23).

12. He asked counsel of Ahithophel and Hushai regarding the next step to
   take in the rebellion (2 Samuel 17:1-14).

13. He mobilized all Israel (2 Samuel 17:11-14).

14. He pursued David across the Jordan and camped in the land of Gilead (2
   Samuel 17:24-26).

15. He fought David and his men in Mount Ephraim and was killed, thus
   ending the rebellion (2 Samuel 18:1-18).

c [chariots and horses, and fifty men to run before him] Chariots and
 horses were a sign of pride (Deut. 17:16,20), and a mark of royalty; their
 running before anyone meant to clear the way before him. This was
 characteristic of Absalom. He was bold, violent, revengeful, proud,
 enterprising, handsome, eloquent, flattering, ambitious, and vain—a
 popular and rich prince who saw no hindrance to getting the throne after
 the death of Amnon and the reconciliation with his father. He despised the
    boy Solomon because of his birth to a woman who had sinned with David
    being himself born of the king and a princess of Geshur. In his own
    opinion Absalom was of sufficient age, authority, and wisdom to rule.

                               Shimei's Curse
Shimei's curse against David was one of the most untrue and unjust
accusations in human history. Shimei knew full well that David had never
shed one drop of the blood of Saul's house, nor was he reigning in Saul's
place; and above all, God had nothing to do with delivering the kingdom of
Israel to Absalom. There was some truth in David reaping for shedding the
blood of Uriah and taking his wife, as was predicted in 2 Samuel 12:10-14.
Shimei could have referred to the many Benjamites who were slain—Saul
and his sons (1 Samuel 31), the 360 in the battle between Joab and Abner (2
Samuel 2:12-32), Ishbosheth as a result of Abner turning to David (2
Samuel 4:1-12), and perhaps a few others not recorded; but it must be
remembered that David was not responsible for any of these deaths. In fact,
he spared the life of Saul twice, and refrained from open war with Benjamin
for seven and a half years while he was king of Judah only (2 Samuel 2:8-
11; 2 Samuel 3:1). David had never deliberately hurt the house of Saul; and
even in the case of Shimei's cursing, which deserved death, the king had
mercy on him and kept him from dying on this and other occasions. He did
finally tell Solomon not to hold him guiltless. In his last charge to the new
king he said, "thou art a wise man, and knowest what thou oughtest to do
unto him; but his hoar head bring thou down to the grave with blood" (1
Kings 2:8-9).

                         David's Patient Suffering
Abishai, David's nephew, wanted to go over the brook and kill Shimei for
his insults to the king, but David refused to listen to any offer that would
cause such bloodshed. He suffered this as part of the chastening of God for
his sin with Bathsheba. His answer to Abishai expressed a deep and humble
resignation to the course of providence. One thing is certain: he acted more
firmly toward the sons of his sister Zeruiah during his period of humiliation
and seeming defeat than in the days of his prosperity and power (2 Samuel
16:9-14). Insults like this would be hard to endure from such a helpless one,
but they were easy for David, for he fully recognized himself as under the
divine hand of chastening for his sin. He never forgot this cursing by
Shimei, but he was determined not to avenge it in his lifetime. He left the
matter to the wisdom of Solomon, as one of the last things he mentioned in
his dying hour (1 Kings 2:8-11).

                 The Counsel of Ahithophel and Hushai
Moreover—besides the counsel he gave in 2 Samuel 16:21-23, he advised
the choice of 12,000 men to pursue David immediately, before he could
find refuge and while he was weary and short of soldiers. The people with
him would flee and only the king would be killed. Then the rebellion would
be over (2 Samuel 17:1-3). This sounded like an easy victory to Absalom
and all the elders of Israel; but they changed their minds when they got
Hushai's advice. Note the contrast between the counsels of Ahithophel and
Hushai:

Sevenfold Counsel of Ahithophel:

1. Let me now choose 12,000 men (2 Samuel 17:1).

2. I will pursue David this very night.

3. I will come upon him while he is weary and weak-handed (2 Samuel
    17:2).

4. I will make him afraid.

5. All the people that are with him shall flee.

6. I will smite the king only.

7. I will bring back all the people to you so all the people shall be in peace
    (2 Samuel 17:3).

Sevenfold Counsel of Hushai:

1. The counsel of Ahithophel is not good at this time (2 Samuel 17:7).

2. You know your father and his men, that they are mighty (2 Samuel 17:8).

3. They are chafed in their minds, as a bear robbed of her whelps in the
   field.

4. Your father is a man of war, and will not lodge with the people.

5. He is hidden even now in some pit, or in some place of refuge (2 Samuel
   17:9).

6. If you go after him now and some of your men are overthrown, it will be
    reported that there is slaughter among the people that follow Absalom;
     this will cause the most valiant among your men to lose heart and give
     up (2 Samuel 17:9-10).

7. All Israel knows what a mighty man your father is, and that those who
   are with him are valiant men (2 Samuel 17:10).

Sevenfold Counsel of Hushai:

1. Therefore, I counsel that all Israel be gathered from Dan to Beersheba, as
   numberless as the sand by the sea (2 Samuel 17:11).

2. You go out to battle and personally lead the army of Israel.

3. We shall come upon David in some place where he shall be found (2
   Samuel 17:12).

4. We will light upon him as the dew falls on the ground.

5. There will not be left one man that follows your father.

6. If he takes refuge in some city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city
    (2 Samuel 17:13).

7. We will draw it into the river until there be not left one stone upon
   another.

Of the two plans, this advice sounded better to Absalom and the elders of
Israel; God allowed this in order to defeat the counsel of Ahithophel (2
Samuel 17:14). When Ahithophel saw that his advice was not taken, he
went home and committed suicide (2 Samuel 17:23). This gave David time
to flee and make proper preparations for war.

b [twelve thousand men] Absalom must have many thousands of soldiers
    with him at this time if 12,000 could have been chosen out of them.

                      Restoration of the Kingdom
The kingdom was completely disorganized at this time. The man whom
they rebelled with was dead and they were uncertain what to do next. The
tribes, other than Judah, first reasoned that David had saved them out of the
hands of their enemies—especially the Philistines—and had now fled from
the land before Absalom who was dead. They apparently wanted to speak to
David and welcome him back as king (2 Samuel 19:9-10).

Sentiments of three different parties are seen in 2 Samuel 19:9-10—the
royalists, the numerous followers of Absalom, and others who were
indifferent to David. Under these circumstances it was wise of David not to
return to Jerusalem hastily as a conquering hero to take over the kingdom
without the full consent of the people.

This invitation was in the making at least, from all the tribes except Judah,
when David sent the two priests, Zadok and Abiathar, to speak with the
elders of Judah and ask why they were the last to invite the king back. He
seemed to be vexed with Judah, his own tribe, because of their apparent
apathy in this matter. He appealed to them from the standpoint of being
their own flesh and blood, and even promised that Amasa would be
commander of the army in place of Joab (2 Samuel 19:11-13). This appeal
brought Judah together and united them as one man in the invitation (2
Samuel 19:14).

However, this separate message to Judah and the preference given them by
David seemed to create jealousy in the hearts of the other tribes who were
ready to welcome him as king. David played politics here in that he wanted
his own tribe to be the first to welcome him. He appealed to Amasa, the
only man of Judah that could hinder them from inviting David back, by
offering to pardon Amasa and make him captain in place of Joab whose
overbearing haughtiness had become intolerable. David thought Amasa
would make a better man for the job and would have a great influence over
the whole tribe of Judah in cementing it back to him. The appeal was a
success, for those who had stood aloof were the first ones to welcome him
back (2 Samuel 19:14).
