b [famine in the days of David three years]

                            Famine in the Land
It seems that David did not inquire of the Lord by the Urim and Thummim
until the third year of famine, perhaps thinking that the first two years might
be a natural consequence of recent events and therefore nothing to be
alarmed about. But when the famine continued the third year it caused great
concern and he sought an answer from God, who said that it was because of
the bloody house of Saul and his slaying of the Gibeonites. What happened
between Saul and the Gibeonites or when it happened is not recorded in
Scripture; all we know about it is this story in 2 Samuel 21:1-14. We know
that Saul, in his zeal, slew some peaceable Amorites whom the children of
Israel swore to protect in the days of Joshua (2 Samuel 21:2; Joshua 9:3,16-
17). The Gibeonites were called by David so that proper amends could be
made to them. Their requirement was that seven sons of Saul be hung by
them in Gibeon (2 Samuel 21:3-6). This was granted by David and the
plague was stayed (2 Samuel 21:7-14). See Thirteen Famines in Scripture.

Some have supposed that the experiences of 2 Samuel 21 took place early
in David's reign, but there is no evidence for this. The word "then" in 2
Samuel 21:1 proves that the time was after the preceding events of
Absalom's rebellion. The mention of the slaying of Gibeonites (2 Samuel
21:1), the reference to the destruction of Saul's family (2 Samuel 16:7-8),
Mephibosheth's statement that all of Saul's house were dead men (2 Samuel
19:28)—all these can be understood as coinciding with the events of this
chapter. Regardless of the time, though, David was obligated to meet the
demands of the Amorites, according to the customs of that time and place.
The severity of the punishment on Saul's line emphasizes the truth of the
narrative concerning the league between Israel and the Gibeonites (Joshua
9).

    own hurt (2 Samuel 21:1-2; Joshua 9; Psalm 15:4).

b [Michal] This should be Merab, not Michal who had no sons (2 Samuel
    6:23). Merab, the daughter of Saul and sister of Michal, was given to
    Adriel and she bore him five sons (2 Samuel 18:19). An ancient copyist
    mistakenly substituted Michal's name for Merab's. One theory is that the
    translators let this remain in the text on the grounds that Michal may have
    raised these sons for Adriel who perhaps became a widower by the death
    of Merab. But the Hebrew for "brought up" here is yalad (HSN-3205)
    which is translated beget 201 times, bare 110 times, born 79, bring forth
    25, bear 23, travail 16, midwife 10, child 8, delivered 5, borne 3, birth 2,
    and labour 2. Yalad is only translated brought up twice—here and Genesis
    50:23—so this explanation will not do. Josephus says that Michal bore
    them to Adriel after a second divorce from David, but this contradicts 2
    Samuel 6:23. Some MSS (which the Moffatt and Berkeley versions both
    agree with) read Merab instead of Michal, which is no doubt the original
    wording.

a [anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel]

                          Satan Provoked David
The anger of the Lord would not have been against Israel if He had been the
one to move David to number Israel. The real power that provoked him to
do this was Satan (1 Chron. 21:1), so we must understand "He moved
David" in 2 Samuel 24:1 to mean that God allowed David to be moved by
Satan without interfering. By Hebrew idiom (and also modern usage) a
person is said to do that which he permits to be done. Here we have God's
permission and in 1 Chron. 21:1 we have the report of Satan's actual
temptation and moving of David to number the people. God was justly
displeased with the action of David and punished him for it (2 Samuel
24:10-17).

                                       Tyre
Tyre at this early day was a great stronghold or fortress (Joshua 19:29).
Later it became much stronger; it took Nebuchadnezzar thirteen years to
overthrow it. Afterward it was built on an island in the Mediterranean,
finally being completely destroyed by Alexander the Great who built a
causeway from the mainland. At one time Tyre controlled all the rich
commerce with India and the treasures of the world were poured into it; but
such glory is now gone. Hiram, king of Tyre, was ever a lover of David and
Solomon (2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Kings 5:1; 1 Kings 7:13-14; 1 Kings 9:11-12; 1
Chron. 14:1; 1 Chron. 22:4; 2 Chron. 2:3,11-14). The city is mentioned with

Isaiah 23; Jeremiah 25:22; Jeremiah 27:3; Jeremiah 47:4; Ezekiel 26-29;
Hosea 9:13; Joel 3:4; Amos 1:9-10; Zech. 9:2-3). See Matthew 11:21-22;

                SUMMARY OF 2 SAMUEL
                         ____________________

Author: Samuel, David, Nathan, and Gad no doubt kept the original
records from which Isaiah compiled the book about 743-683 B.C.

Proof of Authorship: It is necessary to treat 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel as one
book because, in the Hebrew canon and early editions of the Hebrew text,
they were one. The division came with the Septuagint translators about 289-
94 B.C. and this has been followed in all editions since then. Samuel
perhaps wrote 1 Samuel 1-24; David, Nathan, and Gad, 1 Samuel 25-2
Samuel 24 (1 Samuel 10:25; 1 Chron. 29:29). There is a reference to the
book of Jasher in 2 Samuel 1:18, which may have also been used in the
final writing of the book of Isaiah, who wrote the history of the kings of
Judah and Israel (▪ 2 Chron. 32:32, note).

Date and Place: The records which make up 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel were
written by Samuel, David, Nathan, and Gad from 1204-1035 B.C. in
Palestine, but were perhaps finally made into one book by Isaiah the
prophet, about 743-683 B.C. He perhaps compiled Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel
and 2 Samuel, 1 Kings and 2 Kings, and 1 Chron. and 2 Chron. in their final
form, according to ▪ 2 Chron. 32:32, note.

Theme: In 1 Samuel we have the record of the failure of Israel under Eli,
Saul, and Samuel. In 2 Samuel we have the record of the restoration of
order in Israel through David, God's choice as ruler of His people; the full
establishment of the kingdom of Israel with Jerusalem as the political and
religious center (2 Samuel 1:1-6:23); the making of the Davidic covenant as
the basis of all earthly kingdom truth (2 Samuel 7:1-29); the full conquest
of the enemies of Israel (2 Samuel 3:1; 2 Samuel 5:17-25; 2 Samuel 8:1-
10:19); David's sin and repentance (2 Samuel 11:1-12:31); family troubles
of David (2 Samuel 13:1-14:33); rebellion of Absalom (2 Samuel 15:1-
19:43); and the last days of David (2 Samuel 20:1-24:25).

Purpose: See Summary of 1 Samuel.

Statistics: 10th book of the Bible; 24 chapters; 695 verses; 20,600 words;
125 questions; 679 verses of history; 9 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 7 verses
of unfulfilled prophecy; 11 distinct messages from God (2 Samuel 2:1,2; 2
Samuel 5:19,23; 2 Samuel 7:4; 2 Samuel 12:1,7; 2 Samuel 21:1; 2 Samuel
24:11,16,18); 70 commands; 25 predictions; and 13 promises.

                         Conditions of Blessing
When and how long did God bless the kings of David's house? As long as
they met the conditions laid down here. Even David was dealt with because
of sin (2 Samuel 11-18). Solomon his son, the second king of David's
house, was blessed as long as he obeyed; but when he sinned judgment was
pronounced upon him and his kingdom (1 Kings 11:1-40). Rehoboam, the
third king, had his kingdom divided and ten whole tribes were lost to him in
one day because of pride and sin (1 Kings 12:1-24). And so it continued for
the next 433 years following David. One king after another sinned and was
judged—cut off in many cases—until the whole nation was finally
destroyed (2 Kings 23-25). Even when the nation was restored it still
continued in sin until it was finally destroyed again, in A.D. 70. It has never
recovered from this. God will never bless Israel again with a king until they
come to complete repentance (Zech. 12:10-13:1; Matthew 23:37-39; Acts
15:13-18; Romans 11:25-29).

                         Burying Place of David
This was a departure from the ordinary custom, as the dead were usually
buried outside the cities. It was therefore a mark of high honor to be buried
in the city, and a special honor to David to be buried in the city called by his
name. Other kings of David's line were buried here also (1 Kings 11:43; 2
Chron. 32:33). Some were buried in the city, but at different places (2 Kings
21:18,26). The sepulchre of David was known in apostolic times (Acts
2:29). Its location today is pointed out on the southern hill of Jerusalem
(commonly called Zion), under the Mosque of David. It is jealously
guarded by Muslims.

a [he will not say thee nay] Adonijah was mistaken, for Solomon had the
    greatest respect and love for his father; it was not customary to give the
    father's wives to another. Solomon took that request as a great insult to
    David, and put Adonijah to death (1 Kings 2:23-25). Kings' wives either
    became widows for the rest of their lives or became the wives of the
    deceased monarch's successor (2 Samuel 12:8; 2 Samuel 16:22).

                     Adonijah's Treacherous Request
Public opinion so closely connected the title of the crown and the
possession of a deceased king's wives that to have granted Adonijah's
request would have encouraged his pretension of being king. Knowing this,
Solomon assumed that Adonijah had a guilty purpose, that there had been a
fresh plot to get the kingdom for himself, and that Abiathar and Joab,
Adonijah's counselors in the former conspiracy, were parties to a new plan
to seize the throne. He considered the severest measures necessary to crush
the new treason. This is why Solomon said to his mother (who evidently
saw no harm in the request) that she might as well ask for the kingdom also
—for Adonijah as well as Abiathar and Joab (1 Kings 2:22).

This request was sinful according to the customs for another reason: the
oriental mind held the monarch to be sacred, and whatever he owned was
set apart from common use. This was especially true of the royal harem.
Hence, for Adonijah to ask for one of David's widows, who now belonged
to the new king, was like asking Solomon for one of his own wives. Either
way it was unpardonable and could only be satisfied by the death penalty.
Solomon therefore commanded Benaiah to slay Adonijah. Abiathar the
priest (and one of the conspirators with Adonijah) was told to go to his
fields in Anathoth. He was also worthy of death, but was spared for having
carried the ark of the Lord before David, and because he suffered much
with him in all his afflictions. However, though Solomon spared Abiathar's
life, he took away his priestly office (1 Kings 2:26-27). As for Joab, the
other conspirator, Solomon commanded that he be executed (1 Kings 2:28-
34).

The fact that both Abiathar and Joab were judged at this time strongly
suggests that behind Adonijah's request was a new plot to seize the
kingdom. The statement in 1 Kings 2:22 linking them with Adonijah and
his desire for the kingdom also indicates it. These men may have thought
that such a young king—perhaps only twenty years old—would be easily
deposed. They were wrong, however, and the possibility of a revolt was
thus ended for the time being.

                        God's Promise to Solomon
God told Solomon to ask whatever he wanted, and it is plainly implied that
the request would be granted. Those who wish God would say to them what
He did to Solomon should realize that He does—and even more. Consider
these unlimited promises of God: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and
ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you: for every one that
asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it
shall be opened. . . . If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto
your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give
good things to them that ask him?" (Matthew 7:7-11). "If ye have faith as a
grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to
yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto
you" (Matthew 17:20). "Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt
not, ye shall not only do this (which is done) to the fig tree, but also if ye
shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the
sea; it shall be done. And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer,
believing, ye shall receive" (Matthew 21:21-22). "If thou canst believe, all
things are possible to him that believeth" (Mark 9:23). "Have faith in God.
For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be
thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart,
but shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass; he
shall have whatsoever he saith. Therefore I say unto you, What things
soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall
have them" (Mark 11:22-24). "If ye abide in me, and my words abide in
you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you" (John 15:7).
"Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye
should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that
whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you"
(John 15:16). There are many such promises in the N.T. which amount to
far more than Solomon was promised here.

                            Solomon's Request
This request of Solomon set the pattern for all who desire to please God and
be blessed by Him (1 Kings 3:10-14). Too often men pray for gifts which
they think will make them great in the eyes of others. They want to imitate
some other great man and they aren't called or qualified for that particular
work. Their motive is selfish. Solomon, on the other hand, asked for
wisdom and understanding in the science of government, to give true justice
to Israel. One of the chief functions of the eastern monarch has always been
to hear and decide causes. Hence, Solomon desired gifts that would best
qualify him for his work and calling in life.

                       Chronology of the 480th Year
This does not account for the entire time between the exodus and the 4th
year of Solomon's reign. It really refers to the 480th year of Israel's security
as a nation. It doesn't include the 41 years at Sinai and the wandering in the
wilderness, the conquest of Canaan and division of the land (about 10
years), or the 3 years of confusion under Abimelech and the 111 years of
servitudes during the judges. The entire period from the exodus to the 4th
year of Solomon was 645 years. Some chronologists have made the mistake
of basing their whole system upon this 480-year period. There are at least
twelve different chronological opinions, ranging 330 to 680 years for the
period from the exodus to the 4th year of Solomon. These differences raise
obvious questions as to the proof for their conclusions. Scripture verifies
the lengths of most periods, proving some modern scholars to be off as
much as 300-400 years in their figuring of the time from the exodus to
Christ (see Dispensation of Law). Chronological conclusions in this work
are reached by exhaustively searching the Scriptures, offering chapter and
verse as proof when possible.

                              The Brazen Sea
The brazen sea was an immense vase of solid brass. It was 7' 6" deep, with
a 15' diameter and a 45' circumference, weighing about 25-30 tons. Cast in
the foundry like the pillars of 1 Kings 7:16, it had 2 rows of knobs around
the rim of the bowl (1 Kings 7:24). It stood on 12 brazen oxen: 3 looked in
each of the 4 directions with their hind parts under the brazen laver which
was about 4" thick, with the brim like that of a cup, decorated with lilies (1
Kings 7:25-26). Filled with 16,750 gallons of water, the laver would weigh
about 100 tons. The small lavers were thought to contain 300 gallons of
water, which, with the lavers, would weigh about 2 tons each. Jewish
writers say that the water was changed daily, to stay pure for use in
ceremonial worship.

a [When thy people Israel be smitten down before the enemy]

               Prophetic Aspects of Solomon's Prayer
Inspired by the Holy Spirit in prayer, Solomon apparently sensed several
aspects of Israel's future:

1. When Israel is smitten down before the enemy, because of sin (1 Kings
   8:33)

2. Bring them again unto their land (plainly implying captivity, 1 Kings
   8:34)

3. When heaven is shut and there is no rain, because of sin (1 Kings 8:35)

4. When You afflict them (1 Kings 8:35)

5. If You send famine, pestilence, blasting, mildew, locust, and caterpillar (1
    Kings 8:37)

6. If their enemy besiege them in their land (1 Kings 8:37)

7. If plagues and sicknesses come (1 Kings 8:37)

8. If You deliver Israel to the enemy to carry them captives unto another
    land, and they repent in the land of their enemy, then give their enemies
    compassion on them (1 Kings 8:46-53)

These things couldn't have been mere guesswork on Solomon's part, for
Israel experienced all that he referred to. Technically, then, they are
prophetic. However, we do not list them as definite predictions since they
are so general and were given in connection with conditions of answered
prayer.

b [because they have sinned agsinst thee] This is the only reason Israel
 was defeated prior to Solomon, and the only reason they were defeated
 after him. Sin is to blame for all the troubles and curses among men.
 These verses not only state the results of sin, but also reveal the remedy
 for it.

                     Eight Ways to Get Rid of Sin
1. Turn again to God—be converted (1 Kings 8:33)

2. Confess the name of God (1 Kings 8:33,35)

3. Make supplication to Him (1 Kings 8:33)

4. Turn from sin (1 Kings 8:35)

5. Fear God (1 Kings 8:43)

6. Repent, and make supplication (1 Kings 8:47)

7. Acknowledge sins committed

8. Return to God with all the heart, and with all the soul (1 Kings 8:48)

Eight Blessings for Obedience

1. God will hear from heaven and forgive all sins confessed (1 Kings
   8:34,36,38)

2. One will be taught the good way wherein he should walk (1 Kings 8:36)

3. Will be given material blessings

4. Will receive answers to prayers (1 Kings 8:38,52)

5. Will be rewarded according to works (1 Kings 8:39)
6. Will learn to fear God and know His name (1 Kings 8:40,43)

7. Will have his cause maintained by God (1 Kings 8:45,49)

8. Will be shown mercy by men (1 Kings 8:50)

a [Ophir]

                                   Ophir
A country of the East, celebrated for its production of gold and precious
stones (1 Kings 10:11; 2 Chron. 8:18; 2 Chron. 9:10). Supposedly settled by
the sons of Joktan (Genesis 10:29), it produced gold in the time of Job (Job
22:24; Job 28:16). From the time of David to the time of Jehoshaphat Israel
traded with Ophir. The Jewish fleet spent three years on their voyage to this
place and brought back gold, apes, peacoks, spices, ivory, ebony, and almug
trees. Its location is uncertain; no less than sixteen sites are suggested by
Bible scholars. If it took three years for the journey and trading it was no
doubt a long way off (1 Kings 10:22). Perhaps Ophir was in Africa, for the
same fleet is called the navy of Tarshish (2 Chron. 9:21), which would be in
Spain. There was no Suez Canal in those days and the navy was located in
the Red Sea. To get from here to the Atlantic Ocean and then to Spain
would require a trip around Africa; a stop at Ophir could be made on the
voyage to Spain and the return trip. In three years, no doubt many places
were visited.

Two opinions are held about the queen of Sheba. Some say she came from
southeast Arabia, and others contend she came from Ethiopia. This is partly
founded on Ethiopian history. Sheba, the grandson of Cush, for whom the

a [temple]

                             Solomon's Temple
According to a report of the Illinois Society of Architects in 1925, the cost
of Solomon's temple according to existing values would have been about
$87 billion. The cost of the temple, its internal decorations, and the
paraphernalia was one of the wonders of ancient times. According to
Vallapardus, the talents of gold, silver, and brass used in the construction
were valued at $34,399,110,000. The jewels are generally valued as high.
The vessels of gold, according to Josephus, were valued at 140,000 talents,
which, when reduced to everyday coinage according to Chapel's reduction
tables, would equal the sum of $1,876,481,515. The vessels of silver,
according to the same authority, were still more valuable, being reckoned at
$3,246,720,000. The priests' vestments and robes of the singers were worth
$10,050,000. The trumpets alone were worth $1 million.
Added to the above expenses are building materials and labor. There were
10,000 men cutting cedars, 70,000 bearers of burden, 80,000 hewers of
stone, and 3,850 overseers. In addition to their wages for 7 years, Solomon
gave them $33,669,885 as a bonus. The daily cost of food for this army of
workmen for the 7 years and 6 months it took to complete the temple has
been estimated at $344,385,440. And besides the gold, silver, jewels, etc.
mentioned above, additional materials have been estimated at
$12,726,685,000.

Combining these estimates, the temple and its furnishings were valued at
more than $87 billion in 1925. (Editor's note: We have endeavored
throughout this work to update as many of Dake's facts and figures as
possible. However, we were unable to locate all of Dake's sources for the
above information. Therefore, the best solution we have for current price
equivalents is to track the consumer price index since 1925. Based on that,
the 1997 equivalent of the 1925 figures would be estimated at over $985
billion.)

a [But king Solomon loved many strange women]

                        Five Steps in Solomon's Fall
1. Wealth (1 Kings 10:14-27)

2. Weapons (1 Kings 10:26-29)

3. Women (1 Kings 11:1-3)

4. Turning his heart from the Lord (1 Kings 11:4)

5. Outright idolatry (1 Kings 11:5)

Wealth can be a blessing if properly used for the Lord; but if "consumed
upon lusts" and turned into "provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts
thereof," it becomes a curse (James 4:3; Romans 13:14). Solomon's great
riches contributed to his downfall. As to weapons, no king who has God as
his helper the way Israel once did needs to multiply them for his protection.
God miraculously fought Israel's battles when they obeyed Him. As to
women, the law forbade a king to multiply wives to himself (Deut. 17:17).
These three W's—wealth, weapons, and women—were temptations
Solomon yielded to, and they led to his complete downfall.
b [loved many strange women] Two things Solomon loved:

1. The Lord (early in life when he was godly and first blessed, 1 Kings 3:3)

2. Many strange women (later in life, when backslidden, 1 Kings 11:1-3)

c [strange women] Strange—particularly foreign women of heathen
 nations whom God commanded Israel not to marry, lest they turn the heart
 after other gods (Exodus 34:15-16). In Proverbs there are many warnings
 against strange women. If Solomon had heeded his own warnings the
 record would be different.

             Eight Warnings Against Strange Women
1. To deliver you from the strange woman, even the stranger who flatters
   with her words (Proverbs 2:16)

2. The lips of a strange woman drop as a honeycomb, and her mouth is
   smoother than oil . . . . Remove your way far from her (Proverbs 5:3-8)

3. Why will you, my son, be ravished with a strange woman and embrace
   the bosom of a stranger? (Proverbs 5:20)

4. To keep you from the evil woman, from the flattery of the tongue of a
   strange woman (Proverbs 6:24)

5. That they may keep you from the strange woman, from the stranger who
   flatters with her words (Proverbs 7:5)

6. The mouth of a strange woman is as a deep pit: he that is abhorred of the

7. For a whore is a deep ditch, and a strange woman is a narrow pit

8. Your eyes shall behold strange women, and your heart shall utter

Either Solomon (the writer of Proverbs) did not live up to his own

                             Dynasty of Hadad
The dynasty of Hadad continued to rule until the time of David who
completely conquered Edom and ordered Joab to stay there six months to
kill all the males (2 Samuel 8:13). Hadad was rescued from Joab as a mere
boy and carried into Egypt where he was well cared for; he became allied
with the house of the Egyptian king. Eventually, Pharaoh gave him his own
sister-in-law for a wife. Hadad's son Genubath was also brought up in
Egyptian court circles.
This war on Edom was brought about by the Edomites attacking Israel
when David and his army were fighting in northern Syria. The sneak attack
was met by David taking his army into Edom and winning a great victory in
the valley of Salt. He took vengeance on them and the slaughter was terrible
(1 Kings 11:15-17; 2 Samuel 8:13-14; 1 Chron. 18:12; Psalm 60:6-12).

This destruction of Edom deeply embittered Hadad toward Israel. After
Solomon's death he was ready for vengeance at any opportunity. Having
asked leave of the king of Egypt to return to his own country, after the death
of David and Joab (1 Kings 11:17-22), and he caused much trouble for
Israel in spite of the fact that the Edomites paid tribute to Israel up to the
time of Jehoshaphat (1 Kings 22:47).

                                   Shechem
Shechem lay on the flank of Mt. Gerizim, directly opposite Mt. Ebal, the
mounts of curses and blessings (Deut. 11:29; Deut. 27:1-8). It was a
national sanctuary (Joshua 24:1) and the site of Abraham's first altar
(Genesis 12:6). Isaac and Jacob both lived here. Joseph was buried here.
Jacob's well was here (John 4:5). The modern town called Neapolis has two
long streets running parallel with the valley, six mosques, a church of Greek
Christians, public baths, and a variety of factories, a synagogue of
Samaritans, and other points of interest.

           Fourteen Assassinations—Kings and Queens
1. Servants slew Ishbosheth (2 Samuel 4)

2. Baasha slew Nadab (1 Kings 15:27-28)

3. Zimri slew Elah (1 Kings 16:8-10)

4. Omri slew Tibni (1 Kings 16:21-22)

5. Jehu slew Jehoram (2 Kings 9:14-26)

6. Jehu slew Ahaziah (2 Kings 9:27-29)

7. Eunuchs at Jehu's command slew queen Jezebel (2 Kings 9:30-37)

8. Captians slew Athaliah (2 Kings 11:13-16)

9. Servants slew Joash (2 Kings 12:19-21)

10. Servants slew Amaziah (2 Kings 14:17-20)

12. Menahem slew Shallum (2 Kings 15:14)

13. Pekah slew Pekahiah (2 Kings 15:25)

14. Hoshea slew Pekah (2 Kings 15:30)

It is interesting that only one king and one queen of Judah were killed by
conspirators. Another, Ahaziah, happened to be in Israel when Jehu
assassinated Jehoram, king of Israel; Ahaziah also was killed. The others
were murdered by conspirators who wanted the throne for themselves or
another. One king of Israel committed suicide because conspirators had him
trapped and would have killed him (1 Kings 16:18). This is another
indication of the utter wickedness of Israel compared to Judah, during the
time of the division of the kingdom. And yet, some today contend that God
cut Judah off, not Israel, and that Israel is now enjoying the covenants and
blessings exclusive of Judah. On the basis of wickedness it was Israel that
was cut off as a nation even until now; but Judah survived and was restored.
Thus it will be in the future—Judah along with the ten tribes will be
restored again under the Messiah. Acts 15:13-18 verifies this, speaking of
David and his kingdom of Judah in particular, not the ten tribes—although
they will be included, according to all the prophets.

                                     Elijah
He is mentioned 69 times (1 Kings 17:1-19:21; 1 Kings 21:17-28; 2 Kings
1:1-17; 2 Kings 2:1-15; 2 Kings 3:11; 2 Kings 9:36; 2 Kings 10:10,17; 2
Chron. 21:12; Malachi 4:5). He is called Elias 30 times in the N.T.
(Matthew 11:14; Matthew 16:14; Matthew 17:3-12; Matthew 27:47-49;
Mark 6:15; Mark 8:28; Mark 9:4-13; Mark 15:35-36; Luke 1:17; Luke
4:25-26; Luke 9:8,19,30,33,54; John 1:21-25; Romans 11:2; James 5:17),
this being the Greek form of the name.

Elijah is considered one of the greatest of the prophets. He is not called a
writing prophet because he didn't leave a book like the ones from Isaiah to
Malachi, but he did write four verses (2 Chron. 21:12-15). No prophet has
been more vividly described as he has been, nor have any been so
counterfeited. Many throughout the ages have claimed to be Elijah, since he
is clearly predicted to return to the earth to help restore Israel just before the
second coming of Christ (Malachi 4:5-6; Rev. 11:3-12). Elijah is also
revealed as one of two anointed men who now stand before God,
symbolized by two olive trees and two candlesticks (Zech. 14:11-14; Rev.
11:3-12). He is the only prophet whom people tried to identify with John
the Baptist (Matthew 16:14; Mark 6:15; Mark 8:28; John 1:21-25), and the
only one whom John the Baptist imitated in spirit, power, and ministry
(Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:11-12; Mark 9:12-13; Luke 1:17).

Fourteen Points of Similarity Between Elijah and John the Baptist:

1. Both were anointed with the same Spirit and power (2 Kings 1:9; Luke
   1:17)

2. Both were familiar with deserts and solitude (1 Kings 17:3; 1 Kings 19:4;
   Luke 1:80)

3. They wore the same kind of garments and lived simply (2 Kings 1:8;
   Matthew 3:4)

4. Both were fearless and bold to rebuke kings (1 Kings 18:17-18; 2 Kings
   1; Matthew 14:4)

5. They were sought to be killed by kings (2 Kings 1:9-16; Matthew 14:3-4)

6. Both were prone to discouragement (1 Kings 19:4; Matthew 11:1-6)

7. They were preachers of righteousness (1 Kings 18:20-24; Matthew
   21:32)

8. Both incurred enmity of a queen (1 Kings 19:1-7; Matthew 14:3-12)

9. Both were fruitful in their ministry (1 Kings 18:17-41; Matthew 3:5-6)

10. Both had a great influence over Israel (1 Kings 18:25-41; Mark 11:32)

11. Both were subjects of prophecy (Malachi 4:5-6; Isaiah 40:3; Malachi
   3:1)

12. Both have been or will be a forerunner of the Messiah—John before the
   first advent (Malachi 3:1), and Elijah before the second (Malachi 4:5-6)
13. Both had a lapse of faith but quickly recovered (1 Kings 19:1-7,18;
   Romans 11:1-4; Matthew 11:1-6)

14. Both were prophets (1 Kings 18:22; Matthew 11:9)

                                 Ravens
The Hebrew Ê½oreb (HSN-6158), translated only as raven, is related to, but
not identical with, the root Ê½arab (HSN-6150). Some, trying to downplay
the miraculous in Scripture, have suggested that Arabians fed Elijah twice
daily during his long stay at the brook Cherith. Nothing is really gained
from this effort, though, for it would still be miraculous for strangers to
bring two meals a day to such an isolated spot. Furthermore, it is
linguistically incorrect. Oreb and arab have distinct meanings and are never
used interchangeably in Scripture. Finally, these interpreters aren't
consistent in their approach. Imagine how ridiculous it would be to read
Arabian for raven in other scriptures:

1. Noah would have sent out an Arabian from the ark to see if the flood was
   gone (Genesis 8:7)

2. Arabians would have been regarded as clean food (Leviticus 11:15; Deut.
   14:14)

3. The beloved's hair would be as black as an Arabian (Song 5:11)

4. Young Arabians would cry for food along with other beasts and birds
   (Psalm 147:9)

5. The one who mocked his father disobeyed his mother would have his
   eyes picked out by the Arabians of the valley (Proverbs 30:17)

                            Elijah and Immortality
Without the scores of simple passages we now have in the Bible, Elijah
knew more about the body, soul, and spirit than many today. To teach that
the soul is not immortal, or that body and soul are the same and both go to
the tomb at death, is to reject many scriptures. The soul is immortal and
fully conscious after leaving the body; it can go out and return to the body,
as clearly demonstrated here. When Elijah prayed, the soul came back and
the body revived and lived again (1 Kings 17:21-22), which proves that the
soul is the life of the body. The soul and spirit must be in the body in order
for it to live (James 2:26). At physical death the soul goes to one place and
the body to another. See Hell.

a [sealed them with his seal]

                                Ancient Seals
Seals were more important than signatures, often used in their place. No
document was valid without one. Ordinarily, a seal was covered with ink
and pressed on the paper, pressed into hot wax to leave its impression.

Ancient seals have been found in various shapes and sizes—cylindrical,
square, pyramidal, and round. Some were made into rings (Genesis 41:42).
A common style among Egyptians was a stone, rounded on one side and
flat on the other. The inscription was on the flat side, and the convex
surface was skillfully crafted into the form of a beetle. The beetle was
worshipped by the Egyptians, and their example was followed by the
Phoenicians, after whose deities Ahab had gone. Some, therefore, think
Ahab's seal may have been like this.

Some seals had holes in them through which a string was passed so they
could be worn around the neck. It is thought that Judah's seal was worn this
way (Genesis 38:18). Many ancient seals were cylinders set in a frame
fastened at both ends so that they could be rolled to make the impression.
Some of these have been found in both Chaldea and Assyria. The figures
carved on them vary. Seals were made of pottery, stone, brass, silver, and
gold.

                        Deception Allowed by God
Ahab was in rebellion against God and in league with idol gods, listening to
their prophets instead of the true prophets of Jehovah. Therefore, God
allowed him to be deceived instead of saving him from it. There was very
little that could be done with such a stubborn man. Micaiah had been sent to
Ahab, but the king wouldn't receive God's instructions. Ahab thus clearly
illustrates 2 Thes. 2:8-12. Because he and his associates had no love for the
truth that they might be saved, God sent them a strong delusion that they
should believe a lie. God permitted such deception to take the place of
rejected truth. If men will not receive the truth, they will automatically get a
substitute that corresponds with their wicked ways. Ahab wouldn't listen to
Jehovah, but he would listen to the prophets of Baal.

This passage gives an insight into the spirit realm, showing that behind all
human acts there are good and bad spirits working to carry out the
respective wills of their masters. The Lord protects as long as He can, but
when there is nothing else He can do to turn men from their wicked ways,
He lets demons deceive them, causing them to go further astray.

                    SUMMARY OF 1 KINGS
                           ____________________

Date and Place: The records which make up 1 Kings and 2 Kings were
written in Palestine (1046-606 B.C.), by scribes or prophets who were
responsible for recording events during the reign of the king or kings under
whom they served. These records were put into one book by the final author
or authors, and the one book was divided into 1 Kings and 2 Kings by the
Septuagint translators, around 294-289 B.C. If the final authors were Isaiah
and Jeremiah, the book was finished around 743-683 B.C. and 782-606
B.C.

Author: It seems that Isaiah and Jeremiah were the authors or final
compilers, using the public records of the kings of Israel. Among the
recorders were Nathan, Gad, Iddo, Ahijah, Jehu, and others (2 Chron. 9:29;
2 Chron. 12:15; 2 Chron. 20:34; 2 Chron. 26:22; 2 Chron. 32:22).

Proof of Authorship: Jewish tradition says that Jeremiah was the author.
However, 2 Chron. 32:32 indicates that Isaiah was the writer. Perhaps Isaiah
wrote the book of Kings up to Hezekiah's time, and Jeremiah completed it,
telling of the events from then to the captivity.

Theme: History of the kings of Israel and Judah from the time of Solomon
to the captivity by Babylon—a period of 413 years. The books of 1 Kings
and 2 Kings begin with a record concerning King David and end with one
regarding the king of Babylon. They open with an account of the building
of the temple and close with its destruction. They begin with the story of
David's first successor and end with the last one released from captivity.
The character of all the kings of Israel and Judah is tested by the litmus test
—David.

Purpose: To show the reason for the Davidic kingdom not being
perpetually continued and to reveal why God sent Israel into captivity.

Statistics: 11th book of the Bible; 22 chapters; 816 verses; 24,524 words;
66 questions; 1 verse of unfulfilled prophecy; 71 verses of fulfilled
prophecy; 36 distinct messages from God (1 Kings 3:5,11; 1 Kings 9:2; 1
Kings 11:11,30; 1 Kings 12:22; 1 Kings 13:1,9,20; 1 Kings 14:5,7; 1 Kings
16:1; 1 Kings 17:1,2,8,13; 1 Kings 18:1; 1 Kings 19:5,7,9,11,13,15; 1 Kings
20:13,14,22,28,36; 1 Kings 21:17,21,28; 1 Kings 22:17,19,25,28); 92
commands; 73 predictions; 6 promises.

a [Then Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab]

                         The Rebellion of Moab
Then—after the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against the northern
kingdom of Israel. The word "then" indicates the book is a continuation of 1
Kings. The two books were one up to the time of the Septuagint translators
in the third century B.C. It was then that the book of Kings was divided into
two sections.

Moab had been subdued by David (2 Samuel 8:2; 2 Samuel 23:20). After
the division of the kingdom, the Moabites were under the northern
kingdom. Omri and Ahab greatly oppressed them. When Ahab died,
however, Mesha, king of Moab, rebelled and gained independence.

The Moabite stone discovered in 1868 at Dibon in Moab is revealing. The
writing is in ancient Hebrew characters down to the time of 140 B.C. when
it was replaced by the square characters used today. According to the stone,
Mesha, son of Chemosh-Melech, king of Moab of Dibon, carried out his
desire upon his enemies after Omri and Ahab had oppressed them for many
days. It tells of his victories at Ataroth, Kerioth, Nebo, Jahaz, and other
places. It gives all credit for past defeats and slavery to Israel to Chemosh,
the national god of Moab, because he was angry; the god is also credited for
the victories won after this. See 2 Kings 3:1-27.

a [sons of the prophets]

                         The Sons of the Prophets
The prophets were the divine philosophers, instructors, and guides of the
Hebrews in piety and virtue. They generally lived in solitude, being seen in
public mainly when they had to deliver some message from God. Their
lifestyle and dwellings were plain, simple, and consistent.

Sons of the prophets were pupils of the prophets, being trained in religious
and spiritual matters. They were not a monastic order but a group of
theological students studying the law and the history of God's people, along
with sacred poetry and music. There were several schools of the prophets
from the days of Samuel to the N.T. times when Israel was a nation (1
Samuel 10:5,10-12; 1 Samuel 19:20,24). Elijah was headmaster of several
schools—at Gilgal (2 Kings 4:28); at Bethel where Jeroboam had his altar
and one of his golden calves (1 Kings 12:29; 1 Kings 13:1-32); at Jericho,
and other places (2 Kings 2:3-7,15; 1 Kings 20:35; 1 Kings 21:10). Elisha
succeeded Elijah over these schools and even enlarged them (2 Kings
4:1,38; 2 Kings 5:22; 2 Kings 6:1-7; 2 Kings 9:1).
b [Knowest thou that the LORD will take away thy master from thy
    head to day?] Question 7. Next, ▪ 2 Kings 2:5.

c [Yea, I know it] Twice Elisha testified that he knew Elijah was to be
    translated that day (2 Kings 2:3,5). This revelation may have come
    through prophets other than Elijah, but Elijah knew it too, for he was
    translated by faith like Enoch (Hebrews 11:5). He had to have received a
    word from God to have such faith (Romans 10:17). This whole story is
    one of absolute acceptance of revelation as fact.

                           Elijah Taken to Heaven
Elijah was the second man to be taken to heaven in a natural body, Enoch
being the first (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5; see Enoch). Both now reside in
heaven in their natural bodies, having never died. However, they will die
their own appointed death on earth as the two witnesses of the future
tribulation period (Zech. 4:11-14; Malachi 4:5-6; Rev. 11:3-12; see
Eighteen Facts Identifying the Two Witnesses). Since their time at least two
other men have been taken to heaven and brought back (2 Cor. 12:1-5; Rev.
4:1). Christ also went to heaven and came back after His resurrection (John
20:17-19); then returned to heaven leading many resurrected men, and souls
and spirits of just men whose bodies were not resurrected (Matthew 27:53-
54; Ephes. 4:8-10; Hebrews 12:23). Before this, all righteous souls and
spirits went into Sheol-Hades where they were fully conscious while their
bodies went to qeber (HSN-6913), the grave. Now, when a Christian dies he
no longer goes into the underworld of departed spirits to be held by the
devil against his will (Hebrews 2:14-15); instead he goes immediately to
heaven to await the resurrection day (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:21-24; Hebrews
12:23).

                             Eastern Chambers
Hebrew: Ê½aliyah (HSN-5944), generally refers to an upper room of an
Eastern house, sometimes built on the roof or as a second story to the porch,
accessed by stairs. It is called "the chamber over the gate" in 2 Samuel
18:33. The chamber here is "on the wall," perhaps because a window
opening to the street was the only evidence that a new room had been
added. Such a room was usually well furnished and kept for the
entertainment of honored guests. This is where the Shunammite entertained
Elisha. It was in such a room that Elijah dwelt with the widow in Zeraphath
(1 Kings 17:19,23). In that passage `aliyah is unfortunately translated "loft",
conveying the idea of a bare, desolate garret—far from the truth. Poorer
homes had no `aliyah, so the widow who entertained Elijah was not of the
poorest class. Rather, her extreme destitution was due to the dreadful
famine at the time.

Such a room made a desirable place of retirement for the master of the
house. Ahaziah was in an Ê½aliyah (HSN-5944) in the palace of Samaria
when he fell through the lattice work of the window and injured himself (2
Kings 1:2). Eglon was in a room like this when he was assassinated by
Ehud (Judges 3:20, where `aliyah is rendered "summer parlor," a parlor of
cooling). It was on the roof of an `aliyah in the palace of Ahaz that the
kings of Judah had altars erected for idolatrous worship (2 Kings 23:12). It
was in an `aliyah that Daniel prayed daily in the midst of idolatry (Daniel
6:10). In the N.T. it is called an upper room (Acts 1:13; Acts 9:37,39; Acts
20:7-8). In such a place Christ ate the passover with His disciples (Mark
14:15; Luke 22:12).

b [stool] "Stool" is a misleading translation for modern readers. The
    Hebrew comes from a root verb meaning "to cover"; it refers to a
    canopied seat or throne, as it is translated 127 times. This was no doubt
    the best piece of furniture the rich woman could get for the prophet.

a [if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not
    have done it] Naaman was so angry he might have started a war with
    Israel. The king of Israel had done nothing for him, and now the prophet
    hadn't even shown him the courtesy of meeting him personally. He'd only
    dealt with the prophet's servant. His initial hopes were high, and he was
    willing to make a man rich who would heal him. But after this kind of
    treatment he was enraged; it was too much for his pride. His servants
    simply pointed out that if the prophet had told him to do some great thing
    he would have done it.

    How much easier to just dip in the Jordan seven times and be clean? Was
    he here to be healed, or to do something great? Was he not even willing to
    try what the prophet said would make him clean? Such reasoning pacified
    Naaman and he decided to follow the suggestions. He'd have to cross the
    Jordan on the return trip anyway, so he agreed to dip seven times. When
    he did, he was healed (2 Kings 5:14).

a [he returned to the man of God] Naaman was like the one leper out of
    ten whom Christ healed (Luke 17:12-17). He was glad to return and show
    his gratitude. He confessed faith in Jehovah before everyone, declaring
    there was no God like Him in any other nation. This was God's original
    motive in choosing Abraham and his descendants—that through them all
    the nations of the earth would be blessed. If Israel had continually obeyed
    God they would have evangelized the world centuries ago, and people
    everywhere would have experienced the power of God. Likewise, the
    church was to carry on the work Israel failed to finish, and the work Christ
    and the early believers began (Matthew 28:20; Mark 16:15-20; John
    14:12-15; John 15:7,16; 2 Cor. 12; Hebrews 2:3-4). Then nations today
    would know of complete deliverance from sin, poverty, sickness and
    disease.

b [I pray thee, take a blessing of thy servant] Naaman begged Elisha to

b [kings of the Hittites]

                       The Kings of the Hittites
 The kings of the Hittites ruled from the Euphrates to Asia Minor. They
 were divided into several tribes with a king over each one. The Assyrian
 monuments speak of twelve such tribes at this time. In the day of
 Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob they were powerful in Canaan (Genesis 15:20;
 Genesis 23:10; Genesis 25:9; Genesis 26:34; Genesis 36:2; Genesis
 49:29-30; Genesis 50:13). They were dispossessed by Israel under Joshua
 (Exodus 3:8,17; Exodus 13:5; Exodus 23:23,28; Exodus 33:2; Exodus
 34:11; Numbers 13:29; Deut. 7:1; Deut. 20:17; Joshua 1:4; Joshua 3:10;
 Joshua 9:1; Joshua 11:3; Joshua 12:8; Joshua 24:11). Their kingdom was
 extended northward after this, although some remained in the land (Judges
 1:26; Judges 3:5; 2 Samuel 11:3,6,17,21,24; 2 Samuel 12:9-10; 2 Samuel
 23:29; 1 Kings 9:20; 1 Kings 10:29; 1 Kings 11:1; 1 Kings 15:5; 2 Kings
 7:6; 1 Chron. 11:41; 2 Chron. 1:17; 2 Chron. 8:7; Ezra 9:1; Neh. 9:8;
 Ezekiel 16:3,45).

c [kings of the Egyptians] Elsewhere in Scripture Egypt seems to have had
 a single monarch. Here "kings" probably refers to a number of princes
 ruling with the Pharaoh at this time, or to allied kings—those of Ethiopia,
 Libya, the Lubims, Sukkiims, and others under the king of Egypt (cp. 2
 Chron. 12:3; 2 Chron. 16:8; Jeremiah 46:9; Ezekiel 30:5; Ezekiel 38:5).

                                Ancient Makeup
    It was an ancient custom to color the eyelids, eyebrows and lashes with
    black powder called kohl. It was made by burning liban, a kind of
    frankincense, and the shells of almonds. This was purely for ornamental
    purposes whereas another kind made from powder of ore or lead was used
    as much for medicinal purposes as for beauty. In the use of kohl the arch
    of the brows was darkened and elongated, and the edges of the eyelids,
    both above and below, were colored. This, by contrast, made the white of
    the eyes look larger. Such painting was practiced as far back as the days of
    Job, from which fact one of his daughters was called Keren-happuch,
    meaning paint horn (Job 42:14). Kohl was applied to the eyelids with a
    small piece of wood, ivory, or silver made for this purpose; it was shaped
    like the bodkin. It was first moistened in rose water then dipped into the
    black powder and drawn over the eyelids. See Proverbs 6:25; Jeremiah
    4:30; Ezekiel 23:40.

                               Queen Athaliah
    Queen Athaliah was the granddaughter of Omri (2 Chron. 22:2), and the
    daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. The marriage between Jehoram, king of
    Judah, and Athaliah, daughter of Jezebel, was part of Satan's design to
    introduce idolatry into Judah, so that Athaliah might do for Judah what
    Jezebel did for Israel. Jehoshaphat began his reign by strengthening
    himself against Israel (2 Chron. 17:1), but married his son to the
    idolatrous daughter of Israel's worst rulers—Ahab and Jezebel. The leaven
    worked morally and politically, and was used by Satan in an effort to
    destroy the Seed of the woman, the Messiah, whom he was determined to
    prevent from coming into the world. Jehoram, king of Judah, began this
    destruction by killing all his brethren (2 Chron. 21:4). The Arabians came
    and destroyed all his sons, except the youngest, Azariah (2 Chron. 22:1).
    Then Athaliah killed all the sons of Ahaziah after his death (2 Kings 11:1-
    2; 2 Chron. 23:3), or thought she did. The infant Joash was rescued,
    however, being the only one left in the line of the coming Messiah. He
    was hidden for six years, while the faithfulness of God's word depended
    upon the divine preservation of the child's life. Athaliah's was a case of
    "like mother like daughter"—both were wicked queens, idolaters and
    murderers. Imagine a woman killing her grandchildren and other close
    relatives as Athaliah did, to further her political ambitions!

                         Israel's Repeated History
    During a period of 450 years God delivered Israel from servitudes under
    surrounding nations. They would serve other gods and go into the greatest
    of sins until the Lord would let them be defeated. Then, in their distress
    they would call upon Him for mercy and deliverance, and He would raise
    up a deliverer to set them free again. They would serve God all the days of
    the deliverer, but when he died they would go back into sin, be brought
    down as before, and call upon the Lord for help.

                              Bows and Arrows
    The bow was very ancient. Ishmael was an archer (Genesis 21:20), as was
    Esau (Genesis 27:3). Used early as weapons of war (Genesis 48:22), bows
    were made of various materials—wood, horn, ivory, and steel (Job 20:24;
    Psalm 18:34)—and were of various shapes. The Egyptian bow was about
    six feet long and nearly straight, having a slight curve at each end, or a
    curve in the center when unstrung. The Assyrian bow was sometimes
    curved and sometimes angular, and shorter than the Egyptian bow. Strings
    were of leather thongs, horse hair, hide, or catgut. There were various
    methods of bending the bow—with the hand, the knee, or the foot. The
    foot was probably used the most, since darak, the Hebrew word
    commonly used in speaking of bending the bow, literally means to tread.
    Arrows were made of wood or reed and tipped with metal or horn. Some
    were feathered and had barbed points. See Fourteen Examples of Archery.

Ten Prophets and One Prophetess to Judah:

4. Jehu (2 Chron. 19:1-3)

These—twenty-five prophets and one prophetess—are the only ones
mentioned in the books of Kings and Chronicles during the division of
Israel into two kingdoms. In the introduction to Isaiah many others are
listed which are mentioned elsewhere. Only seven of the fifteen writing
prophets from Isaiah to Malachi lived and prophesied during this time of
national division. Only Hosea and Amos were prophets to the ten tribes

a [Topheth] Topheth (Tophet elsewhere) could be derived from toph (HSN-
    8596), a drum (tabret), because of the cries of the children being burned in

    cries so the worship could be tolerated. Or, the word is derived from taph,
    to burn. Topheth was a spot in the valley of the son of Hinnom where
    continual fires were kept to burn the refuse of Jerusalem, and where such
    idolatry was carried on. This place had been given to the priests of Molech
    by kings of Judah—Ahaz, Manasseh, and Amon; and the idolatrous
    worship had flourished here.

a [horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun] Dedicating a
    chariot and horses to the sun was a Persian practice. When he made
    sacrifices, the king of Persia offered a white horse to the sun. They
    mounted their horses early in the morning and rode toward the rising orb
    of the sun as if to salute it, then offered the horses in sacrifice. The wicked
    Manasseh heard of this custom and imitated it to some extent, maybe not
    actually slaying the horses but dedicating them to the sun. The idea came
    from regarding the sun as a charioteer who drove his horses daily across
    the sky. The Greeks and Romans may have taken this idea from the
    Persians. Such chariots were used mainly in Israel in religious
    processions.

                     SUMMARY OF 2 KINGS
                         ____________________

Date and Place: The records which make up 1 Kings and 2 Kings were
written in Palestine, 1046-606 B.C., by scribes and prophets whose duty it
was to record events during the reign of whatever king or kings they served
under. These records were put into one book by the final author or authors,
and that book was divided by the Septuagint translators about 294-289 B.C.
If written by Isaiah and Jeremiah in its final form the book was so compiled
about 743-683 B.C. and 782-606 B.C.

Author: It seems that Isaiah and Jeremiah were the authors or final
compilers using the public records of the kings of Israel. Among the
recorders were Nathan, Gad, Iddo, Abijah, Jehu, and others (2 Chron. 9:29;
2 Chron. 12:15; 2 Chron. 20:34; 2 Chron. 26:22; 2 Chron. 32:32).

Proof of Authorship: Jewish tradition says that Jeremiah was the author. It
seems from 2 Chron. 32:32 that Isaiah was the chief writer, so it could be
that Isaiah wrote the book of Kings up to the time of Hezekiah (1 Kings
1:1-2 Kings 20:21) and Jeremiah completed it, telling of the events from
then to the captivity (2 Kings 21-25).

Theme: History of the kings of Israel and Judah from the time of Solomon
to the captivity to Babylon.

Purpose: To show the reason for the Davidic kingdom not being
perpetually continued and to reveal why God sent Israel into captivity.

Statistics: 12th book of the Bible; 25 chapters; 719 verses; 23,532 words;
118 questions; 560 verses of history; 58 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 1
verse of unfulfilled prophecy; 65 predictions; 118 commands; 3 promises;
and 20 distinct messages from God (2 Kings 1:3,15; 2 Kings 2:21; 2 Kings
3:16; 2 Kings 4:43; 2 Kings 7:1; 2 Kings 8:1,10; 2 Kings 9:1,6,26; 2 Kings
10:30; 2 Kings 19:6,20; 2 Kings 20:1,5,16; 2 Kings 21:10; 2 Kings 22:15; 2
Kings 23:27).

                    The Uniqueness of Chronicles
The two books of Chronicles are not new history; they cover many things
written before. They belong to quite another part of the O.T. because they
do not sequentially follow the books of Kings. They are, according to the
Jewish canon, the conclusion of the O.T., and the genealogies here lead to
those of the N.T. They begin with the first Adam and end looking forward
to the second Adam. They deal primarily with the kingdom of Judah,
because Christ was to be the successor of David on an eternal throne. As
compared with 1 Kings and 2 Kings which give the history from the human
standpoint, the two books of Chronicles give the history from the divine
standpoint. The former records are as man ruled the history; the latter, as
God overruled it. Compare Saul's death in 1 Samuel 31:6 with 1 Chron.
10:13-14. Also note that only four verses are devoted to Hezekiah's
reformation in 2 Kings 18:4-7, whereas three whole chapters are given to it
in 2 Chron. 29-31. The books of Chronicles give God's standpoint, pointing
to the moral issues and giving reasons for both judgments and mercies. The
books of Kings are chronological in order; in Chronicles chronology is
sometimes ignored in order to bring out causes or consequences for the
purpose of comparison and contrast between records. In Kings we have the
complete history of both houses of Israel; in Chronicles we have only that
which pertains to the house of David and Judah, as being founded on the
covenant God made with David (2 Samuel 7; 1 Chron. 17). The Chronicles
are entirely independent of the books of Samuel and Kings and the
differences between them are intentional. Many critics create their own
difficulties by first assuming that all the books should be alike; because
they're not, they conclude that there are many discrepancies and corruptions
in the text when actually the writings are full of divine instruction, with
occasional additions for our benefit. The following list of parallel passages

    one time joined together. Indeed, they fit together like a jigsaw puzzle.
    The east coastline of South America matches the west coast of Africa with
    the rounded corner of Brazil fitting into the Gulf of Guinea. Facing coasts
    of the United States and Europe also fit, and so on. Science has finally

    earth (Genesis 10:25; Genesis 11:7-9). Without this truth there would be
    no explanation for the presence of the American Indian and inhabitants of
    numerous islands before the discoveries made by explorers from the old

the Messiah (1 Chron. 3:17; Matthew 1:12).

              SUMMARY OF 1 CHRONICLES
                           ____________________
Date and Place: The records which make up 1 Chron. and 2 Chron. were
written in Palestine, 1279-461 B.C., by scribes and prophets whose duty it
was to record events during the time of whatever king or kings they served
under. These records were put into one book by the final author or authors.
The book was divided into two by the Septuagint translators about 294-289
B.C. If written by Isaiah and Ezra in its final form the book was compiled
about 743-683 B.C. and 546-461 B.C.

Author: It seems that Isaiah and Ezra were the authors or the final
compilers using the public records of the nation of Israel. Among the
recorders were Nathan, Gad, Iddo, Ahijah, Jehu, and others (2 Chron. 9:29;
2 Chron. 12:15; 2 Chron. 20:34; 2 Chron. 26:22; 2 Chron. 32:32; 2 Chron.
36:22-23 with Ezra 1:1-4; 1 Chron. 9:10-16 with Neh. 11:10-17).

Proof of Authorship: It seems from 2 Chron. 32:32 that Isaiah wrote the
history of the kings of Israel and Judah. This not only applies to Samuel and
Kings, but also could apply to 1 Chron. 1:1-2 Chron. 32:33. Ezra completed
the history by writing 2 Chron. 33-36. Ezra was president of the Great
Synagogue, a college of learned Jews which originated with him and
formed the O.T. Canon of Scripture. The books passed upon then are the
ones making up the complete Old Testament as found in the Septuagint (the
Greek translation of the O.T.), the Hebrew Bibles, and the versions in many
other languages which we have copies of today. See the discussion of the
canon of Scripture in Bible Introduction.

Theme: Genealogical background of Israelite leaders and of the coming
Messiah, and a history of the kingdom of Judah and of the ancestors of
Jesus Christ, according to the flesh. The Hebrew name for Chronicles is
dibrey (HSN-1697) hayamim (HSN-3117), words of the days. The Greek
name, Paraleipomena, means things omitted. It is from the Latin name
Chronicon that we get our word Chronicles. The Hebrew meaning is
literally "the daily acts or occurrences," a title originally applied to the
accounts of the reigns of the kings of Israel and Judah. Afterward,
Chronicles was applied to the book taken from these narratives. See The
Uniqueness of Chronicles.

Purpose: To show the divine reason for the dealings of God with Israel and
why the Davidic kingdom was not allowed to continue perpetually.
Statistics: 13th book of the Bible; 29 chapters; 941 verses, 20,369 words;
927 verses of history; 8 1/2 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 7 1/2 verses of
unfulfilled prophecy; 30 predictions; 53 commands; 19 questions; 9
promises; and 8 messages from God (1 Chron. 14:10,14; 1 Chron. 17:3; 1
Chron. 21:9,18; 1 Chron. 22:8; 1 Chron. 28:3,6).

b [cannot contain him]

                            God Not Contained
Such statements in Scripture give some people an overly mystical
impression of God. They view Him as so great, large, invisible, and
omnipresent that their theories are out of proportion with the truth
expressed in other passages. Many seem to concentrate their teaching on
making Him a mystery instead of simplifying the facts so that He can be
understood by man. Yet God never revealed Himself so mysteriously, and it
is hardly believable that Solomon and others intended to do so. When
Solomon said "the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain Him," he
wasn't referring to God's size or substance, but to the simple fact that God
cannot be limited to heaven. Solomon wasn't saying that the physical
temple would be too small to hold God's body, nor was he suggesting that
outer space wasn't big enough for Him. (Indeed, it is plainly stated in many
scriptures that the different members of the Trinity will literally, visibly, and
bodily dwell with men; the very soles of their feet will walk in the
millennial temple throughout eternity: Ezekiel 43:7; Ezekiel 48:35; Zech.
6:12-13; Zech. 14:4-5,9,16-21; 2 Thes. 1:7-10; Jude 1:14-15; Rev. 20:1-10;
Rev. 21:1-7; Rev. 22:1-5). God is of ordinary size as proved by His many
personal appearances to men (see Forty-four Appearances of God). All of
God's manifestations, traits, acts, passions, attributes, and powers—
wherever they are mentioned in Scripture—are shown to be exactly like
those of angels and men, only more unlimited (see Anthropomorphism).
They can be understood by comparison with those of other beings, as Paul
plainly states in Romans 1:20 where he says that all the invisible things,
even the eternal power and Godhead, are clearly seen by man, being
understood by the visible things on earth, so that no man is excused for his
ignorance of God and other invisible things.

a [cedar trees] Cedar trees—among the most valuable and majestic trees in
    eastern forests. They grow 70 to 80 ft. tall, and have thick branches which
    grow up to 20 ft., spreading out in all directions. The red wood is so bitter

    2,000 years. The mountains of Lebanon were famous for such trees. See
    note b, ▪ 1 Kings 5:6.

b [fir trees] Fir Trees—well-known evergreens which grew abundantly in
    Mt. Lebanon and other parts of the East. The wood was used for musical
    instruments, as framing material for houses, and in ship building (2 Chron.
    3:4; 2 Samuel 6:5; 1 Kings 5:8-10; Rev. 6:15,34; Rev. 9:11; Ezekiel 27:5;
    Song 1:17). Storks made nests in such trees (Psalm 104:17). Being tall and
    straight they were used to illustrate power and grandeur (2 Kings 19:23;
    Isaiah 14:8; Isaiah 27:24).

b [twenty thousand measures of beaten wheat, and twenty thousand
    measures of barley, and twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty
    thousand baths of oil]

                    Yearly Wages for Hiram's Workers
1. Beaten wheat—20,000 measures. At 6.25 bushels to the measure, this
   would be 125,000 bushels. At $6 a bushel, this would be $750,000 worth
   of flour.

2. Barley—20,000 measures. Again, 125,000 bushels. If beaten into flour
   like the wheat, at an estimated price of $4 a bushel, this would be worth
   $500,000.

3. Wine—20,000 baths. At 72 pints to a bath, this would be 1,440,000 pints
   or 720,000 quarts which, at $5 each, would be $3.6 million worth of
   wine.

4. Oil—20,000 baths. Again, 1,440,000 pints or 720,000 quarts. At $8 each,
   this would be $5,760,000 worth of oil.

Thus, total yearly wages for the Tyrian workers would be $10,610,000.

                Prophetic Aspects of Solomon's Prayer
Inspired by the Holy Spirit in prayer, Solomon apparently sensed several
aspects of Israel's future:

1. If and when Your people Israel are defeated because of their sins (2
    Chron. 6:24)

2. Bring them again unto their own land (plainly implying captivity, 2
   Chron. 6:25)

3. When heaven is shut and there is no rain, because of sin (2 Chron. 6:26)

4. When You afflict them
5. When you have taught them the good way, and send rain again (2 Chron.
   6:27)

6. If You send drought, pestilence, blasting, mildew, locusts, and caterpillars
    (2 Chron. 6:28)

7. If the enemy besieges Your people in their own land

8. If there be sicknesses and diseases

9. If Your people go to war (2 Chron. 6:34)

10. If You are angry with them and deliver them to their enemies, and they
   are carried away captives unto another land (2 Chron. 6:36)

11. If they turn to You while in captivity (2 Chron. 6:37)

These things couldn't have been mere guesswork on Solomon's part. (Had
Solomon been guessing he most likely would have made more favorable
statements, for everything at this time pointed to a long and happy period
under the blessing of God.) Israel eventually experienced all of them, so the
prayer was prophetic. They aren't listed as definite predictions, however,
since they are so general and were made in connection with conditions of
answered prayer.

                          221 Prayers of the Bible
In the following list of Bible prayers (176 in O.T. and 45 in N.T.) we give
only actual, worded prayers, not references to prayer. All statements as "he
prayed, he entreated the Lord, he called upon the name of the Lord, " etc.,
are not prayers; they merely mention that certain people prayed.

Six Prayers in Genesis:

1. Abraham for an heir (40 words; Genesis 15:2-3). Answered because God
    had promised (Genesis 21:1-8).

2. Abraham for Ishmael to be his heir (7 words; Genesis 17:18).
    Unanswered because it was not in harmony with God's word and plan.

3. Abraham for Sodom to be spared if 10 persons were righteous (176
    words; Genesis 18:23-32). Unanswered because 10 righteous persons
   weren't found (Genesis 19:24).

4. Eliezer, steward of Abraham, for a bride for Isaac (110 words; Genesis
    24:12-14). Answered because it was according to God's word (Genesis
    12:1-3,7; Genesis 13:15; Genesis 15:18; Genesis 17:7,19; Genesis
    21:12).

5. Jacob for a blessing (Genesis 28:20-22). Answered because of God's plan
    for him (Genesis 32:1-33:17).

6. Jacob for deliverance from Esau (130 words; Genesis 32:9-12).
    Answered because of God's word and plan for him (Genesis 25:19-23;
    Genesis 26:3; Genesis 27:28-29; Genesis 28:3-4,13-15; Genesis 32:9).

References to prayer, entreating the Lord, calling on the name of the Lord,
and groaning and being afflicted (Genesis 12:7-8; Genesis 13:4; Genesis
16:11; Genesis 20:17-18; Genesis 25:21-23).

Four Prayers in Exodus:

7. Moses for Aaron to go with him (16 words; Exodus 4:13). Answered
    because God wanted to please Moses (Exodus 4:14-17).

8. Moses in complaint to God for not delivering Israel (42 words; Exodus
    5:22-23). Answered because of God's word (Exodus 3:8,12,17-22).

9. Moses for forgiveness for Israel (39 words; Exodus 32:31-32). Answered
    because of atonement and intercession (Exodus 32:11-14,30-35) and
    because of God's word (Exodus 33:1-6,12-14).

10. Moses for God's presence to go with Israel to Canaan (138 words;
    Exodus 33:12-13,15-16). Answered because of God's word (Exodus
    33:12-14) and His grace (Exodus 33:17).

References to groaning, sighing, crying, and entreating the Lord (Exodus
2:11,23-25; Exodus 3:7,9; Exodus 10:16).

Nine Prayers in Numbers:
11. Aaron for the blessing of God upon the people (32 words in the form of
    benediction; Numbers 6:24-26). Answered because of God's promise
    (Numbers 6:27).

12. Moses for God to bless on the journey (27 words; Numbers 10:35-36).
    Answered when Israel lived free from sin, but unanswered when they
    sinned, which was according to God's word (Exodus 32:32-33).

13. Moses in complaining to God because the burden was too heavy (136
    words; Numbers 11:10-15). Answered because of God's words

                           Ancient Fortifications
Fortifications are as ancient as cities. Some writers say the only difference
between ancient cities and villages was whether they were walled or
unwalled. To build a city often meant to build walls around a town already
inhabited—not to build a town in a new location. Some of the fenced cities
of Scripture are thought to have been protected by wooden stockades.
Sometimes there was more than one wall to a fortified city, as in the case of
Jerusalem (2 Chron. 32:5; 2 Kings 25:4). There was a ditch outside some
walls and a low wall or rampart protecting that. At regular distances on the
wall there were towers for the purpose of watching and defense (2 Chron.
26:15; 2 Kings 9:17). ÷

From Hiram he received $72 million (1 Kings 9:14). From the queen of
Sheba he received $72 million in gold, besides other riches (1 Kings 10:10).

                             Increase of Judah
Note the steady increase of Judah and the decrease of the 10 tribes. These
were 400,000 chosen men of Judah, Benjamin, and the 10 tribes that were
in Judah, many of whom had gone to Judah when Rehoboam destroyed the
true worship of Jehovah in the 10-tribe kingdom (2 Chron. 11:16-17). Just
18 years before this Rehoboam could muster only 180,000 chosen men (2
Chron. 11:1), indicating that thousands from the 10 tribes had become a
part of the kingdom of Judah (called "all Israel" in 2 Chron. 12:1). Asa, 6
years later, had 580,000 (2 Chron. 14:8); 32 years after that Jehoshaphat had
1,160,000 besides those in the fenced cities throughout Judah (2 Chron.
17:14-19). On the other hand, Jeroboam could muster 800,000 when Judah
had only 400,000 (2 Chron. 13:3), while Ahab's army in Jehoshaphat's day
was compared to two little flocks of kids which couldn't stand against the
Syrians (1 Kings 20:27). This increase of Judah was caused mainly by a
constant emigration of the 10 tribes to Judah (see note, ▪ 1 Kings 12:17).

                 Three Eternal and Unchangeable Facts
1. The Lord is with you, while you are with Him.

2. If you seek Him, He will be found by you.

3. If you forsake Him, He will forsake you.

These eternal facts are true of an individual or a nation, Jews or Gentiles,
people under law or under grace, and in one age or another. Whoever seeks
God with a whole heart finds Him; and as long as he remains in that
relationship with Him, not forsaking Him, God won't forsake him. There is
no such thing, however, as God being with those who don't remain with
Him. God has forsaken both angels and men when they have forsaken Him,
many of them being eternally doomed. See Twenty-one Examples of Beings
Fallen From Grace.

               God's Patience With the House of David
In spite of Jehoram's sin, God chose to continue the kingdom of David
because of the covenant made with him. It was the devil's plan to break into
the royal line to hinder and destroy the possibility of the Seed of the woman
coming into the world (Genesis 3:15; 2 Samuel 7:16; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah
9:6-7). This started with Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 18:1) and continued with
Jehoram (2 Chron. 21:6). Later the Arabians continued the assault (2 Chron.
21:17; 2 Chron. 22:1), then wicked Athaliah nearly destroyed all the royal
descendants (2 Chron. 22:10). This promise of giving a light to David
forever was based on the obedience of his descendants (see note b, ▪ 2
Kings 8:19); how much sin would be tolerated before cutting off David's
sons from the throne was in God's hands. He no doubt hoped there would
be more good kings in Judah who would justify sparing the nation from
complete destruction or, at least enable Him to salvage part of it. Indeed,
there were six more godly kings in Judah after Asa and Jehoshaphat;
because of them, destruction was postponed. However, sin gradually
became more open in Judah, as in the northern kingdom. God finally had to
abandon them also and permit their captivity. Just before the captivity to
Babylon God cut off the throne rights of the royal line (▪ Jeremiah 22:24-30,
notes). These rights were inherited by Jesus Christ from Joseph of the royal
line, yet He Himself did not come of that line, but of another line of David,
so that He could fulfill all the throne-right promises as well as all the other
Davidic rights in the eternal program, with the house of David, with Judah
and the other tribes of Israel (see note a, ▪ Matthew 1:6).

a [Behold, the king's son shall reign]

                              Jehoiada's Plan
After telling his plans to the chief classes of Israel, and revealing to them
that the king's son was alive and should become their king according to the
Lord's word to David, final plans were made as to how to take over the
kingdom and get rid of the wicked queen Athaliah:

1. A third of the priests and Levites were to be porters of the doors (2
   Chron. 23:4).

2. A third part were to be at the king's house (2 Chron. 23:5).

3. A third part were to be at the foundation gate.

4. All the people were to be in the courts of the house of God.
5. None were to go into the temple itself, except the priests and Levites who
   ministered (2 Chron. 23:6).

6. The people in the courts were to keep watch.

7. The Levites were to surround the king with weapons to protect him (2
   Chron. 23:7).

8. Anyone else who tried to enter the temple itself was to be executed.

9. The Levites were to protect the king in his going and coming.

10. The courses of the priests weren't dismissed (2 Chron. 23:8).

11. The soldiers were armed and ready for battle (2 Chron. 23:9-11).

12. They brought out the king's son, put the crown upon him, gave him the
   testimony (the law of Moses), and made him king (2 Chron. 23:11).

a [Manasseh]

                                 Manasseh
Manasseh was one of the wickedest of Israel's forty-two kings. Yet his reign
of fifty-five years was fourteen years longer than any other except Uzziah,
and three years longer than his. This can only be explained by the mercy of
God. How many years he was wicked is not known. Manasseh did repent,
however, and serve God faithfully after his captivity to Babylon. This is the
difference between him and others, such as Saul, Solomon and Uzziah:
Manasseh began his reign as a wicked king but ended it as a good one; they
began as good kings and ended their rule as bad ones.

Eighteen Sins of Manasseh:

1. He lived in all the abominations of the heathen whom the Lord had cast
   out of the land before Israel (2 Chron. 33:2)

2. Built again the high places which Hezekiah his father had broken down
   (2 Chron. 33:3)

3. Reared up altars for Baal

4. Made groves (see Asherah under Biblical Facts About False Gods)

5. Worshiped and served all the host of heaven

6. Built altars in the temple where God said His name should be forever (2
   Chron. 33:4)

7. Built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the temple (2
   Chron. 33:5)

8. Caused his children to pass through the fire as burnt sacrifices to Moloch
   in the valley of the son of Hinnom (2 Chron. 33:6)

9. Observed times
10. Used enchantments

11. Used witchcraft

12. Dealt with familiar spirits

13. Dealt with wizards

14. Lived wickedly to provoke God to anger

15. Set up a carved image which he had made, in the temple (2 Chron. 33:7)

16. Made Judah and Jerusalem to err (2 Chron. 33:9)

17. Made them do worse than the heathen whom the Lord had destroyed for
   such sins

18. Would not listen to God (2 Chron. 33:10)

Four Things Manasseh Did to Find God:

1. Sought God to deliver him from his affliction (2 Chron. 33:12)

2. Humbled himself greatly before God

3. Prayed until God heard him (2 Chron. 33:13)

4. Made supplication to Jehovah to bring him again to Jerusalem and his
   kingdom

Ten Good Deeds After Conversion:

1. Manasseh built a high wall outside the city of David on the west side of
   Gihon and in the valley to the entering in of the fish gate, and encircled
   Ophel (2 Chron. 33:14).

2. He put captains of war in all the fortified cities.

3. Took away the strange gods (2 Chron. 33:15).
4. Took the idol he had made from the temple.

5. Took away all the altars he had built in the mount of the temple and in
   Jerusalem.

6. Cast them out of the city.

7. Repaired the altar of the Lord (2 Chron. 33:16).

8. Sacrificed on the altar of the Lord in the temple.

9. Commanded Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel.

10. Permitted his people to use high places for making sacrifice to Jehovah
   only (2 Chron. 33:17).

                               SUMMARY
                            ____________________

Date and Place: The records which make up 1 Chron. and 2 Chron. were
written in Palestine, 1279-461 B.C. by scribes and prophets whose duty it
was to record events during the time of whatever king or kings they served
under. These records were put into one book by the final author or authors.
The one book was divided into two by the Septuagint translators about 294-
289 B.C. If written by Isaiah and Ezra in its final form the book was
compiled 743-683 B.C. and 546-461 B.C.

Author: It seems that Isaiah and Ezra were the authors or final compilers
using the public records of the nation of Israel. Among the recorders were
Nathan, Gad, Iddo, Ahijah, Jehu, and others (2 Chron. 9:29; 2 Chron. 12:15;
2 Chron. 20:34; 2 Chron. 26:22; 2 Chron. 32:32; 2 Chron. 36:22-23 with
Ezra 1:1-4; 1 Chron. 9:10-16 with Neh. 11:10-17).

Proof of Authorship: It seems from 2 Chron. 32:32 that Isaiah wrote the
history of the kings of Israel and Judah. This not only applies to Samuel and
Kings, but could also apply to 1 Chron. 1:1-32:33. Ezra completed the
history by writing 2 Chron. 33-36. Ezra was president of the Great
Synagogue, a college of learned Jews which originated with him and
formed the O.T. Canon of Scripture.

Theme: Genealogical background of the Israelite leaders and of the coming
Messiah, and a history of the kingdom of Judah and of the human ancestors
of Jesus Christ. See Summary of 1 Chronicles.

Purpose: To show the divine reason for God's dealings with Israel and why
the Davidic kingdom was not allowed to continue perpetually.

Statistics: 14th book of the Bible; 36 chapters; 822 verses; 26,074 words;
583 verses of history; 32 verses of fulfilled prophecy; 7 verses of unfilled
prophecy; 42 predictions; 45 commands; 8 promises; and 21 messages from
God (2 Chron. 1:7,11; 2 Chron. 3:12; 2 Chron. 11:4; 2 Chron. 12:5,7; 2
Chron. 15:1; 2 Chron. 16:7; 2 Chron. 18:16,18,24; 2 Chron. 19:2; 2 Chron.
20:15,37; 2 Chron. 21:12; 2 Chron. 24:20; 2 Chron. 25:7,16; 2 Chron. 28:9;
2 Chron. 34:23; 2 Chron. 36:21); 47 questions.
